The forced blowup theorem and its geometry

NS-BLOWUP N1. Independent exposition by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI). Authored lesson text is CC0.

A fluid velocity can become arbitrarily large while its total kinetic energy stays bounded. The size of the region carrying that velocity matters. The construction studied here concentrates its fastest flow near one point, controls its full momentum residual, and turns that residual into a force smooth through the singular time.

This lesson states the exact theorem and proves the coordinate, volume, energy, stress and scaling calculations that give its mathematical picture. The full profile and correction constructions have complete proofs in the linked audit. Subsequent lessons develop those proofs in teaching order. The existing summation lesson proves the infinite-sum step in full.

Prerequisites are multivariable differentiation, integration by parts, the implicit function theorem, and the definitions of curl, divergence and the Lebesgue norms. We give the specific coordinate and integral arguments used here. The source is OpenAI’s Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, Theorem 1.1 and Sections 2–3.

N1.1. What the theorem says

Write \(x=(x_1,x_2,z)\in\mathbb R^3\). For a vector field \(u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)\), the \(i\)-th component of \((u\cdot\nabla)u\) is \(\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u_i\); here \(x_3=z\). The Laplacian acts on each component. Fix a viscosity \(\nu>0\), and retain the full residual

\[ \mathscr R_\nu(u,p) =\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla p. \tag{N1.1} \]

A force \(f\) makes this an exact forced solution when \(\mathscr R_\nu(u,p)=f\) and \(\nabla\cdot u=0\).

The whole-space theorem. For every prescribed \(\nu>0\), there exist

\[ f_\nu\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3), \qquad \mathcal K_\nu\subset\mathbb R^3\ \text{compact}, \tag{N1.2} \]

and smooth velocity and pressure \(u_\nu,p_\nu\) on \(\mathbb R^3\times[0,1)\) satisfying

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathscr R_\nu(u_\nu,p_\nu)=f_\nu,\qquad \nabla\cdot u_\nu=0,\qquad u_\nu(\cdot,0)=0,\\ \operatorname{supp}u_\nu(\cdot,t)\cup \operatorname{supp}p_\nu(\cdot,t)\subset\mathcal K_\nu \quad(0\le t<1),\\ \sup_{0\le t<1}\|u_\nu(t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}<\infty,\qquad \limsup_{t\uparrow1}\|u_\nu(t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^3)}=\infty. \end{gathered} \tag{N1.3} \]

There is no smooth solution on all of \(\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)\) with the same force and initial velocity whose kinetic energy is uniformly bounded in time.

Here \(C_c^\infty\) requires one compact support in the open space–time domain and derivatives of every order. In particular the force vanishes on an initial time interval, vanishes after some finite time, and is smooth at \(t=1\). A function merely smooth at every \(t<1\) would not meet this requirement. Smoothness of \(u_\nu,p_\nu\) on \([0,1)\) means smoothness up to the initial time and on every shorter closed time interval. It does not assert finite limits of their derivatives at the singular point.

Kinetic energy is

\[ \mathcal E_\nu(t)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u_\nu(x,t)|^2\,dx. \tag{N1.4} \]

The factor \(1/2\) is retained throughout. The theorem’s force is part of the construction; the theorem does not assert the same behavior for every force.

The periodic statement. On the particular torus \(\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3\), for every \(\nu>0\) there is a smooth force compactly supported in time and a solution \((U,P_{\rm per})\) with zero initial velocity, smooth for \(0\le t<1\), such that

\[ \limsup_{t\uparrow1}\|U(t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb T^3)}=\infty. \tag{N1.5} \]

Velocity and periodic pressure have support in one fixed compact subset of the interior of \((-1/2,1/2)^3\) at all times before one. No global smooth periodic solution has the same datum and force. This is original Corollary 10.6; the exact map producing it appears in N1.7.

The complete supplying proofs for these statements are the local construction, I0–I7 and compact force and final argument, F0–F8, together with their included profile and operator proofs. N1.8 identifies every part of that chain. The theorem’s statement here is a reference to that completed mathematical argument, not a new assumption used to supply its missing steps.

N1.2. The original coordinates, with their exact inverse

The profile construction first works at viscosity one; N1.7 proves the full map to each \(\nu>0\). Keep its fixed parameters

\[ 0<h<\frac1{100},\qquad A=\frac12+h,\qquad D=\frac12-h,\qquad \tau=1-t>0. \tag{N1.6} \]

The three-dimensional cylindrical coordinates and unit vectors are

\[ \begin{gathered} x=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z),\quad r=(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{1/2},\\ e_r=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0),\quad e_\theta=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta,0),\quad e_z=(0,0,1). \end{gathered} \tag{N1.7} \]

The unit vectors at \(r=0\) are not used to define the Cartesian field. Its smooth extension there will be proved below.

Retain the source’s variables \(q,X,\eta\):

\[ \tau=q(1-\eta^2),\qquad z=q^D\eta,\qquad X=\frac{r^2}{2q},\qquad q>0,\quad |\eta|<1. \tag{N1.8} \]

Eliminating \(\eta\) gives

\[ q-z^2q^{2h}=\tau. \tag{N1.9} \]

For \(z\ne0\), the left side is zero at \(q=|z|^{1/D}\), tends to infinity as \(q\to\infty\), and has derivative

\[ 1-2hz^2q^{2h-1}\ge1-2h>0 \quad\text{on }q\ge |z|^{1/D}. \tag{N1.10} \]

The inequality follows because \(2h-1=-2D\), so \(z^2q^{2h-1}\le1\) on that interval. Any solution of N1.9 with \(\tau>0\) lies strictly above its left endpoint. The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity give exactly one positive solution. For \(z=0\), it is \(q=\tau\). The derivative at every solution is nonzero, proving smoothness by the implicit function theorem.

There are useful explicit comparisons. Put \(b=|z|^{1/D}\) and \(a=2^{1/(2D)}\). Then

\[ \max(\tau,b)\le q\le a(\tau+b). \tag{N1.11} \]

For the upper bound set \(Q=a(\tau+b)\). Since \((b/Q)^{2D}\le a^{-2D}=1/2\),

\[ Q-z^2Q^{2h}=Q\{1-(b/Q)^{2D}\}\ge Q/2\ge\tau. \]

Here \(a\ge2\), since \(D<1/2\). Monotonicity from N1.10 gives \(q\le Q\). The lower bounds follow directly from N1.9 and its positive left side. When \(z=0\), the bound involving \(b\) is interpreted with \(b=0\).

Let \(d=1-\eta^2\) and \(L=1-2h\eta^2\). At fixed physical coordinates, differentiation gives

\[ \begin{aligned} q_t&=-L^{-1},& q_z&=2\eta q^{1-D}L^{-1},\\ \eta_t&=D\eta(qL)^{-1},& \eta_z&=q^{-D}dL^{-1},\\ X_t&=X(qL)^{-1},& X_z&=-2\eta Xq^{-D}L^{-1},& X_r&=r/q. \end{aligned} \tag{N1.12} \]

For example \(q_t=-1/L\) follows by differentiating N1.9 with \(\partial_t\tau=-1\). From \(\eta=zq^{-D}\), \(\eta_z=q^{-D}(1-2D\eta^2/L)=q^{-D}d/L\), because \(L-2D\eta^2=1-\eta^2\). The remaining formulas follow by the same product rule. Every denominator stays positive, since \(L\ge1-2h\).

For a profile \(G(X,\eta)\) and any real \(b_0\), these formulas imply the complete first derivatives

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_t(q^{b_0}G) &=\frac{q^{b_0-1}}L \{-b_0G+XG_X+D\eta G_\eta\},\\ \partial_z(q^{b_0}G) &=\frac{q^{b_0-D}}L \{2b_0\eta G-2\eta XG_X+dG_\eta\}. \end{aligned} \tag{N1.13} \]

These operators retain the derivative of the radial profile coordinate \(X\); treating \(X\) as fixed during physical differentiation would change the equation.

At \(\tau=0\) with \(z\ne0\), N1.9 gives

\[ q=|z|^{1/D}>0,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{sgn}z,\qquad L=1-2h. \tag{N1.14} \]

The implicit derivative remains positive. Thus the endpoints \(\eta=\pm1\) with positive \(q\) describe terminal points away from the origin. Approaching \(q=0\) on a bounded \(X\) range instead forces \(r\to0\), \(z\to0\), and \(t\to1\).

N1.3. The leading velocity and its smooth axis

Use the actual leading profiles constructed in the audit. They have the form

\[ u_\theta^{(0)}=q^{-A}E(X,\eta),\qquad u_z^{(0)}=q^{-A}U(X,\eta),\qquad r u_r^{(0)}=V_0(X,\eta),\qquad p^{(0)}=q^{-2A}\Pi(X,\eta). \tag{N1.15} \]

Their complete existence proof is G/O/H/J/Q/V, ending with V7. In particular \(E/\sqrt{2X}\), \(U\), \(V_0/X\), and \(\Pi\) extend smoothly to \(X=0\), and \(E(X,\eta)>0\) for \(X>0\). These are properties of the supplied profiles; they are not properties of arbitrary choices of four functions.

Here is the exact relation that fixes the radial component. Set

\[ F_U(X,\eta)=\int_0^XU(y,\eta)\,dy,\qquad \mathcal A_XU=\int_0^1U(sX,\eta)\,ds. \tag{N1.16} \]

Then \(F_U=X\mathcal A_XU\), including at \(X=0\). The fixed-interval integral proves smoothness of \(\mathcal A_XU\) and each derivative. Since \(A+D=1\), N1.13 gives

\[ \nabla\cdot u^{(0)} =q^{-1}\left\{(V_0)_X+ \frac{-2A\eta U-2\eta XU_X+dU_\eta}{L}\right\}. \tag{N1.17} \]

Indeed the cylindrical radial contribution is \(r^{-1}\partial_r(ru_r^{(0)})=q^{-1}(V_0)_X\), and the angular contribution vanishes because the leading components are independent of \(\theta\).

Integrating the condition that N1.17 vanish, with \(V_0(0,\eta)=0\), gives

\[ V_0=\frac1L\{2\eta XU-2D\eta F_U-d\,\partial_\eta F_U\} =\frac X L\{2\eta U-2D\eta\mathcal A_XU -d\,\partial_\eta\mathcal A_XU\}. \tag{N1.18} \]

To check the coefficient of \(F_U\), use \(\int_0^XyU_y\,dy=XU-F_U\) and \(A-1=-D\). Differentiating N1.18 reproduces N1.17 exactly. The formula also proves that \(V_0/X\) is smooth at the axis.

Define \(F_E=E/\sqrt{2X}\) and \(v_0=V_0/X\), with their smooth axis values. The actual Cartesian components are

\[ \begin{aligned} u_1^{(0)}&=\frac{v_0x_1}{2q}-q^{-A-1/2}F_Ex_2,\\ u_2^{(0)}&=\frac{v_0x_2}{2q}+q^{-A-1/2}F_Ex_1,\\ u_3^{(0)}&=q^{-A}U. \end{aligned} \tag{N1.19} \]

At fixed \(t<1\), \(q\ge1-t>0\), and \(X=(x_1^2+x_2^2)/(2q)\) is smooth. Thus N1.19 is smooth across \(r=0\), with zero angular and radial components on the axis. The cylindrical factor \(1/r\) in N1.15 has not produced a Cartesian singularity.

The original pressure is fixed by its radial integral:

\[ \Pi(X,\eta)=-\int_X^\infty\frac{E(y,\eta)^2}{2y}\,dy, \qquad \Pi_X=\frac{E^2}{2X}=F_E^2. \tag{N1.20} \]

The supplied exterior has \(E=O(X^{-A})\), so the integrand is \(O(X^{-2A-1})\) at infinity and integrable, since \(A>0\). At zero it is the smooth function \(F_E^2\). Consequently

\[ \partial_rp^{(0)} =q^{-2A}\frac rq\,\frac{E^2}{2X} =\frac{(u_\theta^{(0)})^2}{r} \quad(r>0). \tag{N1.21} \]

This is the centrifugal radial balance. It cancels exactly those two terms. The time derivative, radial transport, and radial and axial viscous terms of the full residual still have to be included; the higher-order construction supplies them.

N1.4. An exact shrinking core and its energy

Let \(X_a>0\) be the supplied inner-profile radius. The local construction I6 fixes \(X_{\rm in}=X_a/2\). Choose fixed \(X_{\rm in}<X_c<X_a\) and \(0<\eta_c<1\) with \([0,X_c]\times[-\eta_c,\eta_c]\) inside that inner region. This choice also places the later growth point inside the core. At time \(t=1-\tau\), define the actual spatial region

\[ \mathcal C_\tau=\{x:0\le X(x,1-\tau)\le X_c,\ |\eta(x,1-\tau)|\le\eta_c\}. \tag{N1.22} \]

The variables \(X,\eta\) retain N1.8; this region is not a cylinder with arbitrarily assigned height. At fixed \(\tau\),

\[ q=\frac{\tau}{1-\eta^2},\quad r=\left(\frac{2\tau X}{1-\eta^2}\right)^{1/2},\quad z=\tau^D\eta(1-\eta^2)^{-D}. \tag{N1.23} \]

The derivative of \(z\) with respect to \(\eta\) is

\[ \frac{dz}{d\eta} =\tau^D(1-2h\eta^2)(1-\eta^2)^{-D-1}>0. \tag{N1.24} \]

Thus each allowed \(z\) corresponds to exactly one \(\eta\). The maximal radius and the positive axial extent are exactly

\[ r_{\max}(\tau)= \left(\frac{2X_c}{1-\eta_c^2}\right)^{1/2}\tau^{1/2}, \qquad z_{\max}(\tau)=\eta_c(1-\eta_c^2)^{-D}\tau^D. \tag{N1.25} \]

Their ratio is

\[ \frac{r_{\max}}{z_{\max}} =\frac{\sqrt{2X_c}}{\eta_c}(1-\eta_c^2)^{-h}\tau^h \longrightarrow0. \tag{N1.26} \]

Both lengths go to zero, and the radial extent goes to zero faster.

The drawing shows the ordering and formulas of N1.22–N1.31. It is a schematic, with no numerical velocity samples or substituted profile constants. The editable SVG is its reproducible source.

The full volume element follows from \(dx=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz\). At fixed \(\eta\), \(r\,dr=q\,dX\). The determinant in \((X,\eta)\mapsto(r,z)\) has no second term because \(z_X=0\). Combining N1.23–N1.24 gives

\[ dx=\tau^{1+D}L(\eta)(1-\eta^2)^{-D-2} \,dX\,d\theta\,d\eta. \tag{N1.27} \]

In particular

\[ |\mathcal C_\tau| =2\pi X_c\,\tau^{1+D} \int_{-\eta_c}^{\eta_c} L(\eta)(1-\eta^2)^{-D-2}\,d\eta. \tag{N1.28} \]

The integral is a finite strictly positive constant: its integrand is continuous and positive on a fixed compact interval. No part of that constant has been discarded. The volume power is \(1+D=3/2-h\).

Consider the kinetic energy of the leading field on this specific region. Its angular and axial contributions are exactly

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal E_{\rm tan}^{(0)}(\tau) &=\frac12\int_{\mathcal C_\tau} \bigl\{(u_\theta^{(0)})^2+(u_z^{(0)})^2\bigr\}\,dx\\ &=\pi\tau^{1+D-2A} \int_{-\eta_c}^{\eta_c}\int_0^{X_c} (E^2+U^2)L(\eta)(1-\eta^2)^{2A-D-2}\,dX\,d\eta . \end{aligned} \tag{N1.29} \]

Its radial contribution is

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal E_r^{(0)}(\tau) &=\frac12\int_{\mathcal C_\tau}(u_r^{(0)})^2\,dx\\ &=\frac{\pi}{2}\tau^D \int_{-\eta_c}^{\eta_c}\int_0^{X_c} \frac{V_0(X,\eta)^2}{X} L(\eta)(1-\eta^2)^{-D-1}\,dX\,d\eta . \end{aligned} \tag{N1.30} \]

For N1.30, use \((u_r^{(0)})^2=V_0^2/(2qX)\); the energy factor \(1/2\), angular integral \(2\pi\), and denominator \(2X\) give the coefficient \(\pi/2\). The integrand at \(X=0\) extends continuously as \(Xv_0^2\). Both integrals are finite. The first is strictly positive because \(E>0\) on \(X>0\).

The two time powers are

\[ 1+D-2A=\frac12-3h>0,\qquad D=\frac12-h>0. \tag{N1.31} \]

Thus this core’s leading kinetic energy tends to zero, even though its leading angular velocity grows. This exact calculation concerns \(u^{(0)}\) on \(\mathcal C_\tau\). The full corrected velocity also contains oscillations, higher coefficients and localization terms. N1.6 proves its uniform global energy bound from the exact equation, without assuming that the leading energy calculation controls every correction.

The region \(\mathcal C_\tau\) is defined by fixed profile coordinates. It need not be a material region transported by \(u\). For a smooth incompressible velocity, a material flow map \(Y(a,t)\) satisfies \(\partial_tY=u(Y,t)\). Differentiating in \(a\) gives \(\partial_tD_aY=(D_xu)(Y,t)D_aY\); hence the determinant obeys \(\partial_t\det D_aY=(\nabla\cdot u)(Y,t)\det D_aY=0\). With initial determinant one, it remains one. This volume preservation for material sets is consistent with N1.28: the sets \(\mathcal C_\tau\) are selected by N1.22, not by a fixed collection of moving fluid particles.

N1.5. Why oscillations can carry the missing stress

At fixed \(z,t\), write the two tangential residuals as \(R_\theta(r)\) and \(R_z(r)\). The original radial stress equations are

\[ R_\theta=-\left(\partial_r+\frac2r\right)T_{r\theta}, \qquad R_z=-\left(\partial_r+\frac1r\right)T_{rz}. \tag{N1.32} \]

Multiplication by \(r^2\) or \(r\), respectively, and integration from the axis give the axis-regular choices

\[ T_{r\theta}(r)=-r^{-2}\int_0^r s^2R_\theta(s)\,ds, \qquad T_{rz}(r)=-r^{-1}\int_0^r sR_z(s)\,ds. \tag{N1.33} \]

Indeed differentiating \(r^2T_{r\theta}\) and \(rT_{rz}\) recovers N1.32, including its minus signs. The homogeneous integration constants would give \(r^{-2}\) and \(r^{-1}\) terms and are excluded by axis regularity.

Suppose a residual is zero for \(r\le r_a\) and \(r\ge r_b\), with \(0<r_a<r_b\). The corresponding stress is zero for \(r\le r_a\). For \(r\ge r_b\), it is zero if and only if the appropriate full moment vanishes:

\[ \int_0^\infty s^2R_\theta(s)\,ds=0,\qquad \int_0^\infty sR_z(s)\,ds=0. \tag{N1.34} \]

Necessity and sufficiency both follow from the constant numerators of N1.33 outside the support. These exact moments explain why radial matching is part of the construction.

An oscillation can have zero mean velocity and nonzero mean momentum flux. To see every coefficient, let \(a,b\in\mathbb R^3\), let \(\varphi\) range over a circle, and define

\[ w(\varphi)=a\cos\varphi+b\sin\varphi,\qquad \langle H\rangle=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}H(\varphi)\,d\varphi. \tag{N1.35} \]

Direct integration gives

\[ \langle w\rangle=0,\qquad \langle w\otimes w\rangle=\frac12(a\otimes a+b\otimes b). \tag{N1.36} \]

The mixed integrals vanish and each square integrates to \(\pi\). Thus \(\langle w_rw_\theta\rangle=(a_ra_\theta+b_rb_\theta)/2\) and \(\langle w_rw_z\rangle=(a_ra_z+b_rb_z)/2\). Changing \(w\) to \(-w\) leaves both products unchanged.

The actual construction supplies two flux directions \(v_1,v_2\in\mathbb R^2\) and positive coefficients \(c_1,c_2\) with

\[ T=c_1v_1+c_2v_2. \tag{N1.37} \]

At any point where \(\det(v_1,v_2)\ne0\), the coefficients have the exact formulas

\[ c_1=\frac{\det(T,v_2)}{\det(v_1,v_2)},\qquad c_2=\frac{\det(v_1,T)}{\det(v_1,v_2)}. \tag{N1.38} \]

Multiplying these expressions out in coordinates proves N1.37; uniqueness follows from the nonzero determinant. Positivity is the additional restriction defining the interior of the cone spanned by these ordered vectors. The profile construction proves that its actual stress satisfies this restriction, and the covariance proof, C1–C8 constructs the amplitudes, including their edge behavior.

N1.36 is an averaging identity, not by itself a solution of the momentum equation. Actual waves have moving phases, varying envelopes, viscosity, pressure and compact cutoffs. Their exact divergence-free velocities come from curls, and their derivatives contain additional terms. The pulse proof, P0–P8 and the four-operation cycle, K0–K8 retain those terms. The later mean corrections restore the exact compatibility conditions. The single actual sum then has a residual whose every fixed derivative decays to arbitrary order near the singular point.

N1.6. Smooth forcing, energy, and the surviving growth path

For any smooth divergence-free \(v\), assigning \(f=\mathscr R_\nu(v,p)\) makes the equation true at times where \(v,p\) are smooth. That identity alone gives no smooth extension of \(f\) through a singular time. The construction proves that extension for the full residual, after all corrections.

Localization also has to preserve incompressibility. If \(v=\operatorname{curl}\mathcal A\) and \(c\) is a smooth cutoff, then

\[ u=\operatorname{curl}(c\mathcal A) =c\,v+\nabla c\times\mathcal A,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0. \tag{N1.39} \]

The first equality is the curl product rule. The second follows by cancellation of mixed partial derivatives in divergence of a curl. The term \(\nabla c\times\mathcal A\) is part of the localized velocity and its residual. If one instead used \(cv\), its divergence would be \(\nabla c\cdot v\), which generally does not vanish. The actual local field has the potentials and smooth extensions needed for N1.39; F0–F3 proves every cutoff term, every terminal force derivative and the compact extension after time one.

Now use that actual compactly supported solution, for the original prescribed viscosity \(\nu\). At every \(T<1\), integration of the exact equation against \(u_\nu\) is legitimate on its fixed compact support. The time term is the derivative of N1.4. Since \(\nabla\cdot u_\nu=0\),

\[ u_\nu\cdot((u_\nu\cdot\nabla)u_\nu) =\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{|u_\nu|^2}{2}u_\nu\right), \quad u_\nu\cdot\nabla p_\nu=\nabla\cdot(p_\nu u_\nu). \]

Both integrals vanish. Integrating the Laplacian by parts gives

\[ \frac12\frac d{dt}\|u_\nu(t)\|_2^2 +\nu\|\nabla u_\nu(t)\|_2^2 =\langle f_\nu(t),u_\nu(t)\rangle. \tag{N1.40} \]

Define \(F_\nu(t)=\int_0^t\|f_\nu(s)\|_2\,ds\). It is finite up to time one because the force is smooth with fixed compact support. For \(\delta>0\), divide N1.40 by \((\|u_\nu(t)\|_2^2+\delta^2)^{1/2}\), discard only the nonnegative dissipation in this inequality, and apply Cauchy–Schwarz. This yields

\[ \frac d{dt}(\|u_\nu(t)\|_2^2+\delta^2)^{1/2} \le\|f_\nu(t)\|_2. \]

Using \(u_\nu(0)=0\), integrate and let \(\delta\downarrow0\) to obtain \(\|u_\nu(t)\|_2\le F_\nu(t)\). Return to the full identity N1.40 and retain dissipation:

\[ \begin{aligned} \|u_\nu(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u_\nu(s)\|_2^2\,ds &\le2\int_0^tF_\nu'(s)F_\nu(s)\,ds\\ &=F_\nu(t)^2\le F_\nu(1)^2. \end{aligned} \tag{N1.41} \]

Monotone convergence of the nonnegative dissipation integrals gives \(\int_0^1\|\nabla u_\nu(s)\|_2^2ds\le F_\nu(1)^2/(2\nu)\). This is a global bound for the full corrected field.

The unbounded velocity is witnessed at a particular Cartesian point. At viscosity one, the actual construction supplies \(X_{\rm in}>0\), \(e_0=E(X_{\rm in},0)>0\), and one finite constant \(C\) such that

\[ x_\tau=(\sqrt{2X_{\rm in}\tau},0,0),\qquad u_\theta(x_\tau,1-\tau) =\tau^{-A}(e_0+\varepsilon_\tau),\qquad |\varepsilon_\tau|\le C\tau^{2h}. \tag{N1.42} \]

The unchanged inner profile and the full summation remainder give this estimate in I6 and F6. All annular oscillations vanish on that path, and both localization cutoffs are one there for sufficiently small \(\tau\). At \(x_\tau\), \(\theta=0\) and \(e_\theta=(0,1,0)\), so the displayed component is \(u_2\). Choose \(\tau\) small enough that \(C\tau^{2h}\le e_0/2\). Then

\[ \|u(1-\tau)\|_\infty\ge u_2(x_\tau,1-\tau) \ge\frac{e_0}{2}\tau^{-A}. \tag{N1.43} \]

Continuity implies that the essential supremum is at least this pointwise value: every smaller value is exceeded in a neighborhood of the point. Since N1.43 holds at every sufficiently small positive \(\tau\), the norm has full limit \(+\infty\), which implies the source’s stated limsup conclusion.

To exclude a different global smooth solution, one also needs a comparison theorem. For any \(T<1\), the constructed compact field is in \(L^\infty([0,T];L^2\cap L^6)\) and has \(\nabla u\in L^1([0,T];L^\infty)\). A smooth competitor with bounded kinetic energy supplies the other \(L^\infty_tL^2_x\) input. The complete whole-space comparison proof, equations (1)–(64) proves equality on \([0,T]\), without assuming decay of the competitor’s pressure. It retains the expanding spatial cutoff flux and proves its Sobolev and pressure estimates. Thus a global smooth competitor would equal \(u\) on every such interval. It would be bounded on a compact neighborhood of \((0,1)\), contradicting N1.43 along \(x_\tau\to0\). N1.7 transfers this conclusion to every viscosity.

N1.7. Every viscosity and the original periodic domain

Let \((u,p,f)\) be the constructed viscosity-one fields. For any \(\nu>0\), use the exact map

\[ u_\nu(x,t)=\sqrt\nu\,u(x/\sqrt\nu,t),\quad p_\nu(x,t)=\nu p(x/\sqrt\nu,t),\quad f_\nu(x,t)=\sqrt\nu\,f(x/\sqrt\nu,t). \tag{N1.44} \]

Writing \(y=x/\sqrt\nu\), the four momentum terms become

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_tu_\nu&=\sqrt\nu\,\partial_tu,& (u_\nu\cdot\nabla_x)u_\nu&=\sqrt\nu\,(u\cdot\nabla_y)u,\\ \nu\Delta_xu_\nu&=\sqrt\nu\,\Delta_yu,& \nabla_xp_\nu&=\sqrt\nu\,\nabla_yp. \end{aligned} \tag{N1.45} \]

They therefore satisfy \(\mathscr R_\nu(u_\nu,p_\nu)=f_\nu\). Velocity and spatial derivative factors cancel in divergence. Time and the zero initial datum are unchanged. A compact spatial set \(\mathcal K\) maps to \(\sqrt\nu\,\mathcal K\). Each force derivative retains

\[ \partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^m f_\nu =\nu^{(1-|\alpha|)/2} (\partial_y^\alpha\partial_t^m f)(x/\sqrt\nu,t). \tag{N1.46} \]

For each fixed positive \(\nu\) these are finite constant multiples of the original derivatives, so smooth compact support is preserved.

The volume change is \(dx=\nu^{3/2}dy\). Hence

\[ \begin{gathered} \|u_\nu(t)\|_2^2=\nu^{5/2}\|u(t)\|_2^2,\qquad \|f_\nu(t)\|_2=\nu^{5/4}\|f(t)\|_2,\\ \nu\int_0^t\|\nabla_xu_\nu(s)\|_2^2\,ds =\nu^{5/2}\int_0^t\|\nabla_yu(s)\|_2^2\,ds. \end{gathered} \tag{N1.47} \]

The full energy inequality N1.41 has the same factor \(\nu^{5/2}\) on both sides. At the point \(\sqrt\nu\,x_\tau\), the lower bound in N1.43 is multiplied by \(\sqrt\nu\). If a global competitor at viscosity \(\nu\) existed, the inverse map

\[ v(y,t)=\nu^{-1/2}v_\nu(\sqrt\nu y,t),\qquad P(y,t)=\nu^{-1}P_\nu(\sqrt\nu y,t) \tag{N1.48} \]

would produce a viscosity-one competitor with energy \(\nu^{-5/2}\|v_\nu(t)\|_2^2\), contradicting N1.6.

For the periodic statement, fix this viscosity and choose \(\lambda>1\) so large that the common support of velocity, pressure and force, after division by \(\lambda\), lies strictly inside \(Q_0=(-1/2,1/2)^3\). Such a choice exists by compactness. Put \(t_0=1-\lambda^{-2}\), and define

\[ \begin{aligned} \widetilde u(x,t)&=\lambda u_\nu(\lambda x,\lambda^2(t-t_0)),\\ \widetilde p(x,t)&=\lambda^2p_\nu(\lambda x,\lambda^2(t-t_0)),\\ \widetilde f(x,t)&=\lambda^3f_\nu(\lambda x,\lambda^2(t-t_0)). \end{aligned} \tag{N1.49} \]

The first two are used for \(t_0\le t<1\); the force continues beyond one. Extend all three by zero for \(t<t_0\). The original construction vanishes on an initial interval, so the extensions are smooth there. Every momentum term has factor \(\lambda^3\); divergence has factor \(\lambda^2\). The viscosity remains \(\nu\), and original time one is reached precisely at \(t=1\).

Set

\[ U(x,t)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}\widetilde u(x+k,t),\quad P_{\rm per}(x,t)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}\widetilde p(x+k,t),\quad F_{\rm per}(x,t)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}\widetilde f(x+k,t). \tag{N1.50} \]

The translates have disjoint closed supports with a positive gap. The sums are locally finite, all derivatives can be taken term by term, and all nonlinear products between distinct translates vanish. Thus

\[ (U\cdot\nabla)U =\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3} (\widetilde u\cdot\nabla)\widetilde u(x+k,t). \tag{N1.51} \]

This proves the exact periodic equation, including a periodic pressure. Compact time support of the force survives N1.49. The velocity and pressure are supported in the same fixed compact subset of \(Q_0\) before time one.

At

\[ \widetilde x_\tau=\lambda^{-1}\sqrt\nu\,x_\tau,\qquad \widetilde t_\tau=1-\lambda^{-2}\tau, \]

only the zeroth translate contributes, and

\[ U_2(\widetilde x_\tau,\widetilde t_\tau) \ge\frac{\lambda\sqrt\nu\,e_0}{2}\tau^{-A}. \tag{N1.52} \]

The periodic comparison needs no spatial cutoff. If \(V\) is a smooth periodic competitor, put \(w=V-U\) on a shorter interval. Subtract the equations in the form

\[ \partial_tw+(V\cdot\nabla)w+(w\cdot\nabla)U -\nu\Delta w+\nabla(P_V-P_{\rm per})=0. \]

Integration against \(w\), periodic integration by parts, and divergence zero give

\[ \frac12\frac d{dt}\|w\|_2^2+\nu\|\nabla w\|_2^2 \le\|\nabla U\|_\infty\|w\|_2^2. \tag{N1.53} \]

Multiply by \(\exp(-2\int_0^t\|\nabla U(s)\|_\infty ds)\). Its product with \(\|w(t)\|_2^2\) is nonincreasing, nonnegative, and initially zero, so \(w=0\). A global smooth competitor would therefore contradict N1.52. This proves the periodic implication from the supplied compact whole-space construction.

N1.8. How the construction supplies the theorem

The mechanism is a succession of exact constructions, not an inference from a picture or a sample of a flow. The table identifies the complete proofs available for each part; N2–N7 develop them in the corresponding lesson sequence.

Mathematical part What it supplies Complete proof
Leading profile Smooth Cartesian axis, positive angular profile, both exterior endpoints, all five moments and the admissible stress cone G/O/H/J/Q/V; V7 collects all six properties
Every-order background The actual coefficient sequence, one radial interval, compact moment corrections, and one divergence-preserving base with both stresses D/Y/Z; Z0–Z8
Oscillations and mean corrections Closed-support separation, the pulse equation, positive covariance, exact curls, radial and temporal inverses, and the five-moment solve K0–K6 with its complete W/P/C/R/M/T/S suppliers
All stages and one actual field One common domain, increasing residual decay, stage-independent derivative losses, and convergence of the actual potentials and pressure K7–K8, L0–L7 and I0–I7; summation lesson S1–S7
Compact force and breakdown Every localized residual term, all terminal force derivatives, compact smooth extension, energy, comparison and the original growth point F0–F8 and comparison (1)–(64)

The same pressure and velocity pass through these maps. In particular, the mean correction uses the reserved interval supplied by the actual profiles, the pulse inverse uses their actual shear margins, and the final localization uses the actual potential sum. The complete proof connections, Sections 2–3, check the order of choices and these receivers.

The human smooth-forcing programme provides essential context for the question. Alpöge, Buckmaster and Coiculescu’s IPM paper, arXiv:2609.16470v1, explicitly develops the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa approach and focuses on smoothness jointly in space and time. Its introduction and overview describe retained nonlinear residuals and oscillatory corrections. The source’s IPM theorem is a separate theorem about a transported density; it is not an input to the Navier–Stokes proof in the table. The Courant account of Alpöge and Buckmaster’s Euler and Boussinesq work identifies the companion smooth-forcing programme. Their complete mathematical treatments belong to the corresponding foundation lessons. Here the proved Navier–Stokes calculation N1.1, N1.32–N1.41 makes the relevant issue explicit: an exact residual must meet the required force class through the terminal time.

The workbench contribution used in this course is the independent derivation and comparison of these maps, including the full pressure comparison and the retained terms in the summation. Original author formulas remain identifiable. Transcription corrections restore what OpenAI wrote; editorial mathematical arguments stay in separate exposition.

N1.9. Five worked exercises

Exercise 1. Find the core’s exact horizontal section. Fix \(z\) and \(\tau>0\). Determine when this height meets \(\mathcal C_\tau\), and give the disk radius there.

Solution. The function \(\eta\mapsto\tau^D\eta(1-\eta^2)^{-D}\) is strictly increasing by N1.24. It maps \([-\eta_c,\eta_c]\) onto \([-z_{\max},z_{\max}]\). Thus the height meets the core exactly when \(|z|\le z_{\max}\). Solve that strictly monotone scalar equation for its unique \(\eta\), set \(q=\tau/(1-\eta^2)\), and use N1.22:

\[ x_1^2+x_2^2\le 2X_cq =\frac{2X_c\tau}{1-\eta^2}. \]

This is a disk, with the full factor \(2X_c\) and the same \(\eta\) determined by the height. At \(z=0\) it has radius \(\sqrt{2X_c\tau}\); at either endpoint height it has radius \(r_{\max}\). The boundary need not have the shape of a cylinder.

Exercise 2. Compare the two exact core-energy contributions. Denote the constant integrals, including their coefficients, in N1.29 and N1.30 by \(C_{\rm tan}\) and \(C_r\). Prove a formula for their ratio and show when it is zero.

Solution. The earlier proof gives \(0<C_{\rm tan}<\infty\) and \(0\le C_r<\infty\). Therefore

\[ \frac{\mathcal E_r^{(0)}(\tau)}{\mathcal E_{\rm tan}^{(0)}(\tau)} =\frac{C_r}{C_{\rm tan}}\, \tau^{D-(1+D-2A)} =\frac{C_r}{C_{\rm tan}}\tau^{2h}. \]

It tends to zero because \(h>0\). Since every factor in the radial integral is positive except \(V_0^2/X\), its value is zero precisely when \(V_0=0\) on the whole core profile rectangle. For necessity, a nonzero value at any \(X>0\) would, by continuity, give a neighborhood with positive integral. Axis continuity then includes \(X=0\). For sufficiency the integrand is identically zero. This statement concerns the leading field and does not omit corrections from the full-field energy estimate.

Exercise 3. Show why zero-mean waves can carry either sign of a cross flux. Construct two vector waves with zero mean, the same mean kinetic energy, and opposite radial–angular flux.

Solution. In the ordered components \((r,\theta,z)\), take

\[ w_+(\varphi)=(1,1,0)\cos\varphi,\qquad w_-(\varphi)=(1,-1,0)\cos\varphi. \]

Both means vanish. Their mean squared lengths are \(2\langle\cos^2\varphi\rangle=1\), and their mean kinetic energies are \(1/2\). Their radial–angular fluxes are respectively \(1/2\) and \(-1/2\); both radial–axial fluxes are zero. Negating all components of either wave preserves its flux, while changing just the angular sign reverses that cross flux. These are exact circle identities. Constructing waves with the required equation, support and pressure remains the pulse construction cited in N1.5.

Exercise 4. Prove that the theorem’s force cannot be zero. Use the exact energy identity and the initial datum.

Solution. If \(f_\nu=0\), N1.41 has right side zero. Each term on its left is nonnegative, so \(\|u_\nu(t)\|_2=0\) at every \(t<1\). Smoothness makes the field identically zero: any nonzero point would have a neighborhood with positive square integral. This contradicts N1.43 and its viscosity scaling. The same argument applies on the torus, using periodic integration by parts. Thus the force in this construction is nonzero, even though it extends smoothly through the singular time.

Exercise 5. Retain every constant in periodic energy and growth. Compute the periodic \(L^2\) energy from N1.49–N1.50, and express the lower bound N1.52 in terms of \(1-\widetilde t_\tau\).

Solution. At any \(t_0\le t<1\), disjoint translates and a fundamental cube give

\[ \begin{aligned} \|U(t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T^3)}^2 &=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\widetilde u(x,t)|^2\,dx\\ &=\lambda^{-1} \|u_\nu(\lambda^2(t-t_0))\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}^2\\ &=\lambda^{-1}\nu^{5/2} \|u(\lambda^2(t-t_0))\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}^2 . \end{aligned} \]

The kinetic energy is half this expression. The coefficient is \(\lambda^2\lambda^{-3}\), not one. Also \(\tau=\lambda^2(1-\widetilde t_\tau)\), so

\[ U_2(\widetilde x_\tau,\widetilde t_\tau) \ge \frac{\sqrt\nu\,e_0}{2} \lambda^{1-2A}(1-\widetilde t_\tau)^{-A} =\frac{\sqrt\nu\,e_0}{2} \lambda^{-2h}(1-\widetilde t_\tau)^{-A}. \]

The growth point is \(\widetilde x_\tau=(\sqrt{2\nu X_{\rm in}(1-\widetilde t_\tau)},0,0)\); this follows by substituting the same \(\tau\) into N1.42 and retaining both spatial scale factors. The factor \(\lambda^{-2h}\) is positive and fixed, so the lower bound diverges while the energy stays bounded.

The local-field construction, compact force extension and energy and comparison argument complete the proof of the theorem stated here.

From velocity profiles to stress and five exact moments

NS-BLOWUP N2.1. A leading velocity field is useful only if its full residual has the form needed by the later corrections. This lesson derives that form and proves how to alter the profiles without disturbing their exterior.

We answer three concrete questions:

  • How does the velocity profile determine the radial stress, with pressure and both viscous contributions retained?
  • Which five moments must be restored after changing a profile, and how can their nonlinear correction equations actually be solved?
  • Which stress directions can be supplied by positive wave covariances?

The opening lesson supplies the exact target theorem and its geometry. We recall the needed coordinates here, and give the complete calculations for the stress and finite correction mechanisms. These are tools for the actual outer, axis, joining and shear constructions; the complete leading-profile existence proof is supplied by the linked construction papers and is developed further in N2. This lesson does not replace those constructions with an assumption.

The original formulas come from OpenAI's Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, Sections 4.1–4.3, Lemma 4.7 and Appendix A.1. All arguments here are editorial exposition, separate from the diplomatic transcription. Original mathematical irregularities, if found, belong in separate editorial discussion.

P0. Coordinates, regularity and incompressibility

The starting data are velocity profiles \(E,U\) and one prescribed pressure value \(\Pi_{\rm ax}(\eta)\). They determine the radial velocity and pressure by exact integration. The angular profile contains a square root at the axis, so we work with its actual smooth coefficient \(F=\phi/\mathsf C\) when testing Cartesian regularity. The factor \(\mathsf C\) remains fixed and visible.

Keep the original parameters and variables

\[ \begin{gathered} 0<h<\tfrac12,\quad A=\tfrac12+h,\quad D=\tfrac12-h,\quad \tau=1-t,\\ z=q^D\eta,\quad \tau=q(1-\eta^2),\quad d=1-\eta^2,\quad L=1-2h\eta^2,\\ s=r^2/2,\qquad X=s/q. \end{gathered} \tag{P0.1} \]

For each \(\tau>0,z\in\mathbb R\), the equation \(q-z^2q^{2h}=\tau\) has exactly one solution \(q>|z|^{1/D}\). Indeed its left side vanishes at the lower endpoint, tends to infinity, and has derivative \(L\ge1-2h>0\) on that half-line. When \(z=0\), the endpoint is zero and the same argument applies. Thus \(|\eta|<1\). The implicit function theorem gives smooth \(q,\eta\) at every \(t<1\). Differentiation gives

\[ q_t=-L^{-1},\quad \eta_t=\frac{D\eta}{qL},\quad X_t=\frac X{qL}, \qquad q_z=\frac{2\eta q^{1-D}}L,\quad \eta_z=\frac d{q^DL},\quad X_z=-\frac{2\eta X}{q^DL}. \tag{P0.2} \]

The identity \(L-2D\eta^2=d\) proves the middle axial formula. For \(\mathcal D_X=X\partial_X\), any real \(b\), and a smooth profile \(f\), the chain rule therefore gives

\[ \begin{split} \partial_t(q^bf)&=q^{b-1}T_bf,&T_bf&=L^{-1}(-bf+D\eta f_\eta+\mathcal D_Xf),\\ \partial_z(q^bf)&=q^{b-D}Z_bf,&Z_bf&=L^{-1}(2b\eta f+df_\eta-2\eta\mathcal D_Xf). \end{split} \tag{P0.3} \]

All endpoint statements in \(\eta\) mean continuous one-sided derivatives.

Retain the fixed amplitude factor \(\mathsf C>1\) and set

\[ \begin{gathered} E=\mathsf C^{-1}\sqrt{2X}\phi=\sqrt{2X}F,\quad H=\sqrt{2X}E=2XF,\quad V_0=Xv_0,\\ (u_\theta^{(0)},u_z^{(0)},ru_r^{(0)},p^{(0)}) =(q^{-A}E,q^{-A}U,V_0,q^{-2A}\Pi). \end{gathered} \tag{P0.4} \]

The axis data are the smooth functions \(F=\phi/\mathsf C,U,v_0,\Pi\), with \(\phi>0\), on each finite closed \((X,\eta)\) rectangle. This does not require \(E\) to be smooth as a function of \(X\) at zero. In Cartesian coordinates the exact field is

\[ u_1^{(0)}=\frac{v_0x_1}{2q}-q^{-A-1/2}Fx_2,\qquad u_2^{(0)}=\frac{v_0x_2}{2q}+q^{-A-1/2}Fx_1,\qquad u_3^{(0)}=q^{-A}U,\qquad p^{(0)}=q^{-2A}\Pi. \tag{P0.5} \]

These expressions prove smoothness across the axis for \(t<1\).

The radial average is \(\mathcal A_Xf=\int_0^1f(aX,\eta)\,da\). Differentiation under this fixed finite integral proves its smooth extension with value \(f(0,\eta)\). Since \(A+D=1\), incompressibility is exactly

\[ 0=\partial_sV_0+\partial_z(q^{-A}U) =q^{-1}\left[(V_0)_X+L^{-1}(-2A\eta U+dU_\eta-2\eta XU_X)\right]. \tag{P0.6} \]

Integrate from zero, use \(V_0(0,\eta)=0\) and \(\int_0^XxU_X\,dx=XU-\int_0^XU\,dx\). This gives the original formula, including its sign,

\[ V_0=\frac X L\left(2\eta U-2D\eta\mathcal A_XU-d\partial_\eta\mathcal A_XU\right). \qquad \Pi_X=\frac{E^2}{2X}=F^2. \tag{P0.7} \]

The second identity equates the coefficients \(\sqrt{2X}\Pi_X\) and \(E^2/\sqrt{2X}\) of \(\partial_rp^{(0)}\) and \((u_\theta^{(0)})^2/r\), both with factor \(q^{-2A-1/2}\). It cancels precisely those radial terms. The remaining radial terms are retained in P1.6 below.

P1. Exact stress, including both kinds of viscosity

The momentum residual is \(\mathcal R_\nu(u,p)=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla p\). Its cylindrical components contain curvature terms. Angular momentum \(ru_\theta\) absorbs the angular transport curvature, while the radial viscous operators still retain their \(1/r\) terms. We first calculate the source's \(\nu=1\) field and then prove the full map for every original \(\nu>0\).

Define the original quantities

\[ \begin{gathered} l=\mathcal D_X\log H=1+XF_X/F,\qquad W=1-2D\eta\mathcal A_XU-d\partial_\eta\mathcal A_XU,\qquad H_c=D\eta+dU,\\ S_q=-Wl-h(1-2\eta U)-H_cF_\eta/F,\\ S_n=-W\mathcal D_XU-A(1-2\eta U)U-H_cU_\eta-d\Pi_\eta+4A\eta\Pi+2\eta\mathcal D_X\Pi. \end{gathered} \tag{P1.1} \]

Using P0.3 and \(V_0L=X(2\eta U+W-1)\), direct collection of the three derivatives proves the complete material-derivative formula

\[ (\partial_t+u_r^{(0)}\partial_r+u_z^{(0)}\partial_z)(q^bf) =\frac{q^{b-1}}L\left[b(-1+2\eta U)f+W\mathcal D_Xf+H_cf_\eta\right]. \tag{P1.2} \]

Here is the collection of terms in detail. At fixed \(z,t\), \(\partial_rX=r/q\), so

\[ u_r^{(0)}\partial_r(q^bf)=q^{b-1}\frac{V_0}{X}\mathcal D_Xf. \]

Also \(A+D=1\), and hence

\[ u_z^{(0)}\partial_z(q^bf) =\frac{q^{b-1}}L U(2b\eta f+df_\eta-2\eta\mathcal D_Xf). \]

The time derivative contributes \(q^{b-1}(-bf+D\eta f_\eta+\mathcal D_Xf)/L\). Thus the three coefficients are

\[ -b+2b\eta U,\qquad D\eta+dU,\qquad 1+LV_0/X-2\eta U=W. \]

This proves P1.2 term by term, including the radial transport.

For \(b=-h,f=H\), this is \(-q^{-h-1}HS_q/L\). For \(b=-A,f=U\), adding \(\partial_zp^{(0)}=q^{-A-1}Z_{-2A}\Pi\) gives \(-q^{-A-1}S_n/L\). The equality of pressure powers uses \(2A+D=A+1\).

The two radial equations have the unique axis-regular solutions

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal D_XQ_s+(1+l)Q_s=S_q,\qquad \mathcal D_XN_s+N_s=S_n,\\ Q_s=\frac{\int_0^XHS_q\,dx}{XH} =\frac1{F(X,\eta)}\int_0^1aF(aX,\eta)S_q(aX,\eta)\,da,\\ N_s=\frac1X\int_0^XS_n\,dx=\int_0^1S_n(aX,\eta)\,da. \end{gathered} \tag{P1.3} \]

Indeed the integrating factors are \(XH\) and \(X\). Their homogeneous constants would give \(X^{-2}\) and \(X^{-1}\) singularities, since \(H=2X\phi/\mathsf C\) and \(\phi(0,\eta)>0\). The displayed integrals are smooth and have values \(S_q(0,\eta)/2\) and \(S_n(0,\eta)\) at zero.

For \(r>0\), write \(D_\theta=\partial_r+2/r\), \(D_z=\partial_r+1/r\). The inviscid angular residual is \(-q^{-A-1}ES_q/L\), because angular momentum must first be divided by \(r\). Its negative radial primitive is

\[ \frac1{r^2}\int_0^r\rho^2q^{-A-1}\frac{E S_q}L\,d\rho =q^{-A-1/2}F\frac{XQ_s}L. \tag{P1.4} \]

Here \(\rho\,d\rho=q\,dx\), \(\rho=\sqrt{2qx}\), and \(\int_0^X\sqrt{2x}ES_q\,dx=XHQ_s\); thus all powers and factors of two are retained. The axial calculation similarly gives \(r^{-1}\int_0^r\rho q^{-A-1}S_n/L\,d\rho=q^{-A-1/2}XN_s/(L\sqrt{2X})\).

Put

\[ \begin{gathered} p_s=\left(\frac{XQ_s}L,\frac{XN_s}{LE}\right),\quad a=1-2\mathcal D_X\log E=2-2l,\quad b_s=\frac{2\mathcal D_XU}E,\quad \mathfrak s=(a,-b_s),\quad \mathcal T_0=F(p_s-\mathfrak s),\quad T=q^{-A-1/2}\mathcal T_0,\\ (\partial_ru_\theta^{(0)}-u_\theta^{(0)}/r,\partial_ru_z^{(0)})=-q^{-A-1/2}F\mathfrak s,\\ \mathcal R_1(u^{(0)},p^{(0)})\cdot e_j=-D_jT_j-\partial_z^2u_j^{(0)},\qquad j\in\{\theta,z\}. \end{gathered} \tag{P1.5} \]

The radial viscous operators are exactly \(D_\theta(\partial_ru_\theta-u_\theta/r)\) and \(D_z\partial_ru_z\). Subtracting them from the inviscid residual proves the last line and the stress sign. In particular, \(p_s\) is the integrated inviscid contribution, not the pressure. Axial viscosity has not vanished: its exact profile is \(\partial_z^2(q^{-A}f)=q^{-A-2D}Z_{-A-D}Z_{-A}f\), for \(f=E,U\).

For completeness set \(B_r=V_0/\sqrt{2X}\), so \(u_r^{(0)}=q^{-1/2}B_r\). After the centrifugal-pressure cancellation, the full radial residual is

\[ \begin{split} \mathcal R_1(u^{(0)},p^{(0)})\cdot e_r ={}&q^{-3/2}\left\{\frac{\frac12(1-2\eta U)B_r+W\mathcal D_XB_r+H_c(B_r)_\eta}{L} -2X(B_r)_{XX}-2(B_r)_X+\frac{B_r}{2X}\right\}\\ &-q^{-3/2+2h}Z_{-1/2-D}Z_{-1/2}B_r. \end{split} \tag{P1.6} \]

This follows from P1.2 and \((\partial_{rr}+r^{-1}\partial_r-r^{-2})(q^{-1/2}B_r)=q^{-3/2}(2X(B_r)_{XX}+2(B_r)_X-B_r/(2X))\). It retains every radial term. Its first power is larger than the cancelled leading power \(q^{-3/2-2h}\) by \(q^{2h}\); its axial-viscosity power differs by \(q^{4h}\). In P1.5 the axial viscosity differs from the leading tangential power \(q^{-A-1}\) by \(q^{2h}\). These are exact fixed-profile comparisons, not physical derivative estimates.

The stress vanishes exactly when \(Q_s=-2LF_X/F\) and \(N_s=-2LU_X\). Substitution in P1.3 gives

\[ -2L\frac{X\phi_{XX}+2\phi_X}{\phi}=S_q,\qquad -2L(XU_{XX}+U_X)=S_n. \tag{P1.7} \]

Conversely these equations make the displayed expressions for \(Q_s,N_s\) solve their radial equations and be smooth at the axis. Uniqueness in P1.3 then proves zero stress. Thus the equivalence uses the actual axis constants.

For any original viscosity \(\nu>0\), retain \(y=x_\nu/\sqrt\nu\), \(u_\nu(x_\nu,t)=\sqrt\nu u(y,t)\), \(p_\nu=\nu p(y,t)\), and \(T_\nu=\nu T(y,t)\). Direct differentiation gives \(\mathcal R_\nu(u_\nu,p_\nu)=\sqrt\nu\mathcal R_1(u,p)(y,t)\), \(D_{j,\nu}T_{j,\nu}=\sqrt\nu D_jT_j\), and \(\nu\partial_{z_\nu}^2u_{j,\nu}=\sqrt\nu\partial_z^2u_j\). P1.5 therefore retains exactly the same physical stress identity at every \(\nu\). The original coordinates are \(X_\nu=r_\nu^2/(2\nu q_\nu)\), \(\eta_\nu=z_\nu/(\sqrt\nu q_\nu^D)\), with \(q_\nu-z_\nu^2q_\nu^{2h}/\nu=\tau\). No viscosity factor is discarded.

P2. All five cumulative moments and the pressure datum

Changing a profile inside an annulus can change the stress beyond that annulus: the formulas in P1 integrate from the axis. We now identify exactly which accumulated data determine the exterior. The five entries below have different weights, and the pressure has an additional axis datum. Their distinct roles will matter when we restore them.

Use the original moments and prescribed axis pressure:

\[ \begin{gathered} M=\int_0^XU\,dx,\quad I=\int_0^XH\,dx,\quad J=\int_0^XUH\,dx,\\ S=\int_0^X(U^2-E^2/2)\,dx,\quad C_p=\int_0^X\frac{E^2}{2x}\,dx, \qquad \Pi=\Pi_{\rm ax}(\eta)+C_p. \end{gathered} \tag{P2.1} \]

The factor \(1/2\) in \(S\) and the weight \(1/(2x)\) in \(C_p\) remain distinct. Since \(XW=X-2D\eta M-dM_\eta\), \(\partial_X(XW)=1-2D\eta U-dU_\eta\). Integration by parts in \(-WXH_X\) yields

\[ \begin{split} \int_0^XHS_q\,dx ={}&-XWH+I-2D\eta J-d\int_0^XU_\eta H\,dx-hI+2h\eta J\\ &-D\eta I_\eta-d\int_0^XUH_\eta\,dx\\ ={}&-XWH+(1-h)I-D\eta I_\eta-dJ_\eta+2(h-D)\eta J. \end{split} \tag{P2.2} \]

The lower boundary vanishes because \(XWH=O(X^2)\). For the axial terms other than pressure, the identical integration by parts gives

\[ -XWU+D(M-\eta M_\eta)+4h\eta\int_0^XU^2\,dx-d\partial_\eta\int_0^XU^2\,dx. \tag{P2.3} \]

Indeed the coefficient of \(M\) is \(1-A=D\), that of \(\int U^2\) is \(2(A-D)\eta=4h\eta\), and the two copies of \(-d\int UU_\eta\) combine to the derivative shown. No axial boundary value has been omitted: \(XWU=O(X)\) at zero.

Writing \(K_E=\int_0^XE^2/2\,dx\), integration of \(x\Pi_x=E^2/2\) gives \(\int_0^X\Pi\,dx=X\Pi-K_E\). Hence the entire pressure contribution is

\[ \begin{split} \int_0^X(-d\Pi_\eta+4A\eta\Pi+2\eta x\Pi_x)\,dx &=X(4A\eta\Pi-d\Pi_\eta)+d(K_E)_\eta+(2-4A)\eta K_E\\ &=X(4A\eta\Pi-d\Pi_\eta)+d(K_E)_\eta-4h\eta K_E. \end{split} \tag{P2.4} \]

The axis pressure is included in \(X\Pi\). Combining P2.2–P2.4 and dividing by the exact integrating factors proves

\[ \begin{split} Q_s&=-W+\frac{(1-h)I-D\eta I_\eta-dJ_\eta+2(h-D)\eta J}{XH},\\ N_s&=-WU+\frac{D(M-\eta M_\eta)+4h\eta S-dS_\eta}{X} +4A\eta\Pi-d\Pi_\eta. \end{split} \tag{P2.5} \]

These are original (4.16), derived without discarding pressure or an integration constant.

P3. Exact exterior preservation and stability without radial derivative loss

There are two useful conclusions. Exact agreement of five moments preserves the exterior fields. Small differences of moments control the integrated inviscid vector without requiring small radial derivatives. The second fact allows a later construction to change the shear substantially while controlling the remaining part of the stress. Both conclusions are proved below with their domains.

For two profiles write \(\Delta f=f_2-f_1\) and \(\mathbf m_i=(M_i,I_i,J_i,S_i,C_{p,i})\). Their exact moment differences are

\[ \Delta\mathbf m= \begin{pmatrix} \displaystyle\int_0^X\Delta U\,dx\\ \displaystyle\int_0^X\Delta H\,dx\\ \displaystyle\int_0^X(U_2H_2-U_1H_1)\,dx\\ \displaystyle\int_0^X[U_2^2-U_1^2-(E_2^2-E_1^2)/2]\,dx\\ \displaystyle\int_0^X\frac{E_2^2-E_1^2}{2x}\,dx \end{pmatrix}, \tag{P3.1} \]

where every integral has measure \(dx\) and parameter \(\eta\) fixed. If the profiles agree for \(X\ge X_h>0\), all these integrands vanish there. Thus \(\Delta\mathbf m(X,\eta)=\Delta\mathbf m(X_h,\eta)\). When this latter function is zero for every \(\eta\), all its parameter derivatives vanish too. With the same \(\Pi_{\rm ax}\), P0.7 and P2.5 give equality of \(\Pi,V_0,Q_s,N_s\) on the entire exterior. Equality of the profiles on that interval also gives equality of their radial derivatives, including their common one-sided value at \(X_h\). P1.5 then proves equality of \(p_s,a,b_s,\mathcal T_0\) there. This proves the full preservation statement of Lemma 4.4(i).

The pressure datum is essential in this calculation. If instead its difference is \(g(\eta)\) while the five moments and exterior profiles agree, then

\[ \Delta\Pi=g,\qquad \Delta Q_s=0,\qquad \Delta N_s=4A\eta g-dg',\qquad \Delta\mathcal T_0=\left(0,\frac{X}{L\sqrt{2X}}(4A\eta g-dg')\right). \tag{P3.2} \]

These exact terms identify what preservation requires; there is no inference that the source neglects them.

On \(\mathcal R=[X_0,X_1]\times[-1,1]\), with \(0<X_0<X_1\), set \(\|f\|_j=\max_{0\le r\le j}\sup_{\mathcal R}|\partial_\eta^rf|\), using the componentwise maximum for tuples. Assume the source bounds \(E_i\ge e_{\min}>0\) and finite common \(k+1\) norms. The exact difference expressions are

\[ \begin{gathered} \Delta H=\sqrt{2X}\Delta E,\qquad \Delta W=-\frac{2D\eta\Delta M+d\partial_\eta\Delta M}{X},\\ \Delta\Pi=\Delta C_p,\qquad \Delta(H^{-1})=-\frac{\Delta H}{H_1H_2},\qquad \Delta(E^{-1})=-\frac{\Delta E}{E_1E_2}. \end{gathered} \tag{P3.3} \]

For clarity, let \(A_I=(1-h)I-D\eta I_\eta-dJ_\eta+2(h-D)\eta J\) and \(A_M=D(M-\eta M_\eta)+4h\eta S-dS_\eta\), retaining every summand. Then

\[ \begin{split} \Delta Q_s&=-\Delta W+\frac{\Delta A_I}{XH_2}-\frac{A_{I,1}\Delta H}{XH_1H_2},\\ \Delta N_s&=-U_2\Delta W-W_1\Delta U+\frac{\Delta A_M}{X} +4A\eta\Delta C_p-d\partial_\eta\Delta C_p,\\ \Delta p_{s,1}&=X\Delta Q_s/L,\qquad \Delta p_{s,2}=\frac X L\left(\frac{\Delta N_s}{E_2}-\frac{N_{s,1}\Delta E}{E_1E_2}\right). \end{split} \tag{P3.4} \]

This exposes the one differentiated moment in each term. To bound the other factors explicitly, use \(\partial_\eta^r(fg)=\sum_{a=0}^r\binom ra f^{(a)}g^{(r-a)}\), giving \(\|fg\|_r\le2^r\|f\|_r\|g\|_r\). If \(|f|\ge c>0\), its reciprocal derivatives are recursively

\[ (f^{-1})^{(r)}=-f^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^r\binom ra f^{(a)}(f^{-1})^{(r-a)},\qquad r\ge1. \tag{P3.5} \]

Start with \(\|f^{-1}\|_0\le c^{-1}\); this recursion gives a finite polynomial bound in \(c^{-1}\) and \(\|f\|_r\) for every \(r\). Apply it to \(E_i,H_i,L\), whose lower bounds are \(e_{\min},\sqrt{2X_0}e_{\min},1-2h\). Product differentiation of P3.4 therefore proves, with exactly the source dependence,

\[ \|\Delta(Q_s,N_s,p_s)\|_k \le C_k\left(\|\Delta(U,E)\|_{k+1}+\|\Delta\mathbf m\|_{k+1}\right). \tag{P3.6} \]

Here \(C_k\) depends only on \(k,h,X_0,X_1,e_{\min}\), the common input bounds, and \(\|\Pi_{\rm ax}\|_{k+1}\). No radial derivative of a difference occurs. This estimate does not control the changes of \(a,b_s\) without the corresponding radial derivatives; P1.5 retains that dependence in the full stress.

For the original joining radius \(\rho>0\), the exact comparison, not a replacement of the original objects, is

\[ \begin{gathered} X=\rho x,\quad \widehat U(x,\eta)=U(\rho x,\eta),\quad \widehat E(x,\eta)=E(\rho x,\eta),\quad H(\rho x,\eta)=\sqrt\rho\widehat H(x,\eta),\\ (M,I,J,S,C_p)(\rho x,\eta) =(\rho\widehat M,\rho^{3/2}\widehat I,\rho^{3/2}\widehat J,\rho\widehat S,\widehat C_p),\\ (\widehat Q_s,\widehat N_s)(x,\eta)=(Q_s,N_s)(\rho x,\eta),\quad \widehat p_s(x,\eta)=\rho^{-1}p_s(\rho x,\eta). \end{gathered} \tag{P3.7} \]

Changing the integration variable in each of P2.1 proves the five factors. Substitution in P2.5 and P1.5 cancels the same factors, so P3.6 holds in a fixed \(x\) rectangle with a constant independent of \(\rho\) whenever the listed hatted bounds are uniform. The shears obey \(a(\rho x)=\widehat a(x)\), \(b_s(\rho x)=\widehat b_s(x)\), whereas the full stress obeys

\[ \mathcal T_0(\rho x,\eta)=\rho^{1/2}\widehat F\widehat p_s-\rho^{-1/2}\widehat F\widehat{\mathfrak s}. \tag{P3.8} \]

Both different powers are necessary and are retained.

P4. Invertibility and the approaching-exponent bound

To change several moments independently, place smooth corrections on several disjoint radial intervals. The resulting matrix consists of weighted bump integrals. Its invertibility follows from the zero count of a sum of distinct powers. The proof also shows why a bound can deteriorate when two exponents approach each other.

Let distinct real \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m\) and nonnegative nonzero smooth \(\beta_j\) have supports in ordered disjoint compact subintervals \(I_1<\cdots<I_m\) of \((0,\infty)\). Define the actual matrix

\[ B_{ij}=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha_i}\beta_j(x)\,dx. \tag{P4.1} \]

A nonzero combination of \(n\) distinct powers has at most \(n-1\) distinct positive zeros. Here is the induction: divide by its least power, which does not change positive zeros. If \(n\) zeros exist, Rolle's theorem gives \(n-1\) zeros of the derivative. Unless that derivative is zero identically, it is a combination of at most \(n-1\) distinct powers and so has at most \(n-2\) zeros by induction. If it is zero identically, the divided function is a nonzero constant and has no zeros. The induction starts with one nonzero monomial. Consequently the evaluation determinant \(\det[x_j^{\alpha_i}]\) is nonzero when \(0<x_1<\cdots<x_m\). It has a constant sign on this connected domain. Expanding the determinant by permutations and applying finite Fubini gives

\[ \det B=\int_{I_1\times\cdots\times I_m}\det[x_j^{\alpha_i}]\prod_{j=1}^m\beta_j(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_m\ne0. \tag{P4.2} \]

There is no cancellation: the product is positive on a product of open sets of positive measure. This proves the matrix assertion of Lemmas 4.7 and A.1.

For a smooth compact family preserving these hypotheses, the determinant has a positive absolute minimum. The cofactor formula bounds \(B^{-1}\); all fixed parameter derivatives follow recursively from

\[ \partial_\eta^r B^{-1} =-\sum_{a=0}^{r-1}\binom ra(\partial_\eta^aB^{-1})(\partial_\eta^{r-a}B)B^{-1}. \tag{P4.3} \]

The assertion requires smooth dependence of the integrals, as in the source's smooth compact family. It supplies no uniform inverse at colliding exponents. For logarithmic coordinates the exact substitution is \(\int e^{\alpha_i y}\gamma_j(y)\,dy=\int x^{\alpha_i}\gamma_j(\log x)x^{-1}\,dx\). The Jacobian is part of the bump and does not change the ordering or sign.

The loss needed later is explicit. For fixed translated logarithmic bumps \(\beta(y-c_1),\beta(y-c_2)\), let \(\Delta=c_2-c_1>0\) and \(b(s)=\int e^{st}\beta(t)\,dt>0\). The original matrix and its determinant are

\[ B_{ij}^{\rm orig}=e^{s_ic_j}b(s_i),\qquad \det B^{\rm orig}=e^{(s_1+s_2)c_1}b(s_1)b(s_2)(e^{s_2\Delta}-e^{s_1\Delta}). \tag{P4.4} \]

The matrix displayed in original (A.1) is obtained by multiplying row \(i\) by \(e^{-s_ic_1}\); recovering the original inverse multiplies by this same diagonal factor on the right. For slopes in a fixed compact interval, those factors and the positive \(b(s_i)\) have two-sided bounds. The mean value theorem gives \(|e^{s_2\Delta}-e^{s_1\Delta}|=\Delta e^{\xi\Delta}|s_2-s_1|\). Cofactors are bounded, hence the original inverse is \(O(|s_2-s_1|^{-1})\).

For weights \(1,x^{-\lambda}\) and fixed ordered bumps \(\beta_1,\beta_2\), set \(m_j=\int\beta_j>0\) and \(\mu_j=m_j^{-1}\int\log x\,\beta_j(x)\,dx\). Separation gives \(\mu_1<\mu_2\). Taylor's formula on their compact positive supports, with its bounded second derivative \((\log x)^2x^{-\lambda}\), gives

\[ \det\begin{pmatrix}\int\beta_1&\int\beta_2\\\int x^{-\lambda}\beta_1&\int x^{-\lambda}\beta_2\end{pmatrix} =-m_1m_2(\mu_2-\mu_1)\lambda+O(\lambda^2). \tag{P4.5} \]

The remainder constant is finite on a fixed bounded \(\lambda\) interval. For sufficiently small positive \(\lambda\) it is at most half the magnitude of the displayed linear term, proving the required inverse bound \(O(\lambda^{-1})\). This is an analytic bound, with no numerical matrix sampling.

P5. Exact five-moment correction and the nonlinear solve

The matrix from P4 is the derivative of the moment map. The actual map also contains quadratic terms, which must be solved rather than dropped. We retain the complete original increments, give an invertible comparison map on their five rows, and solve the resulting finite equation. The parameter \(\rho\) remains in every original moment and in the support derivative estimates.

On a correction patch in \(X=\rho x\), keep the source base \(U_0=u_c(\eta)\), \(E_0=e_*f_*(\eta)x^\alpha\), where \(e_*>0\), \(f_*>0\). Use two fixed ordered axial bumps and three fixed ordered angular bumps, with additive perturbations \(u=\sum_{i=1}^2c_i\beta_i\), \(e=\sum_{j=1}^3c_{j+2}\gamma_j\). Each block has ordered disjoint supports inside the patch. The original five moment increments, integrated over the entire patch, are exactly

\[ \begin{split} \delta M&=\rho\int u\,dx,&\delta I&=\sqrt2\rho^{3/2}\int\sqrt x\,e\,dx,\\ \delta J&=\sqrt2\rho^{3/2}\int\sqrt x\,(u_ce+E_0u+ue)\,dx,\\ \delta S&=\rho\int(2u_cu+u^2-E_0e-e^2/2)\,dx,\\ \delta C_p&=\int(E_0e/x+e^2/(2x))\,dx. \end{split} \tag{P5.1} \]

In particular \(ue,u^2,e^2\) remain in the actual moment map. Introduce the explicitly invertible row map \(\mathscr L_\eta\) by

\[ \mathscr L_\eta(\delta\mathbf m)= \begin{pmatrix} \delta M/\rho\\ (\delta J-u_c\delta I)/(\sqrt2\rho^{3/2}e_*f_*)\\ \delta I/(\sqrt2\rho^{3/2})\\ -(\delta S-2u_c\delta M)/(\rho e_*f_*)\\ \delta C_p/(e_*f_*) \end{pmatrix}. \tag{P5.2} \]

Every factor is retained. Its inverse sends \(d=(d_1,\ldots,d_5)\) to

\[ \begin{gathered} \delta M=\rho d_1,\quad \delta I=\sqrt2\rho^{3/2}d_3,\quad \delta J=\sqrt2\rho^{3/2}(e_*f_*d_2+u_cd_3),\\ \delta S=2u_c\rho d_1-\rho e_*f_*d_4,\qquad \delta C_p=e_*f_*d_5. \end{gathered} \tag{P5.3} \]

Thus solving the transformed equation is proved equivalent to restoring the original moments; it does not replace them. The linear map is block diagonal with the actual entries

\[ B_U=\begin{pmatrix}\int\beta_1&\int\beta_2\\ \int x^{\alpha+1/2}\beta_1&\int x^{\alpha+1/2}\beta_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad (B_E)_{ij}=\int x^{a_i}\gamma_j\,dx,\quad (a_1,a_2,a_3)=(1/2,\alpha,\alpha-1). \tag{P5.4} \]

The exact remainder in the same row order is

\[ \mathscr Q_\eta(c,c)=\left(0,\frac{\int\sqrt x\,ue\,dx}{e_*f_*},0, \frac{-\int u^2\,dx+\frac12\int e^2\,dx}{e_*f_*}, \frac{\int e^2/(2x)\,dx}{e_*f_*}\right). \tag{P5.5} \]

Polarization supplies a smooth bilinear map with this diagonal. P4 proves invertibility precisely when \(\alpha\notin\{-1/2,1/2,3/2\}\): the two axial exponents and the three angular exponents are then distinct. At an excluded value the indicated block actually has equal rows, so this particular additive Jacobian is singular. No conclusion about other constructions is inferred. If \(u_c=0\) and \(u=0\), then P5.1 gives exactly \(\delta M=\delta J=0\), while the three angular coefficients control \((I,S,C_p)\).

Here is the full quantitative solve of Lemmas 4.7 and A.2. In \(C^j([-1,1];\mathbb R^m)\), use the source maximum norm, let \(\nu_j\) be the multiplication norm of \(B^{-1}\), and let \(q_j\) be the bilinear norm of \(\mathscr Q\), including all product-rule constants. For a prescribed smooth discrepancy \(d\), set \(r_j=2\nu_j\|d\|_{C^j}\). The iteration

\[ c_0=0,\qquad c_{n+1}=B^{-1}(d-\mathscr Q(c_n,c_n)) \tag{P5.6} \]

maps the closed ball of radius \(r_j\) into itself and has Lipschitz constant at most \(1/2\) whenever \(8\nu_j^2q_j\|d\|_{C^j}\le1\). In fact

\[ \begin{aligned} \|B^{-1}(d-\mathscr Q(c,c))\|_{C^j} &\le r_j/2+\nu_jq_jr_j^2\le3r_j/4,\\ \|\Phi(c)-\Phi(\widetilde c)\|_{C^j} &\le2\nu_jq_jr_j\|c-\widetilde c\|_{C^j}\\ &\le\tfrac12\|c-\widetilde c\|_{C^j}. \end{aligned} \tag{P5.7} \]

The case \(r_j=0\) gives the exact zero solution. Completeness and the geometric bound on successive differences give convergence and uniqueness in the specified ball. Applying this for \(j=0\) and one preselected finite \(j=k\) gives the same limit: the iterates are literally identical and convergence in \(C^k\) implies convergence in \(C^0\). Therefore \(\|c\|_{C^k}\le2\nu_k\|d\|_{C^k}\).

Smoothness requires no simultaneous smallness of every derivative norm. At the obtained solution the exact differential is \(D_cF=B+\mathscr Q(c,\cdot)+\mathscr Q(\cdot,c)\). Its product with \(B^{-1}\) differs from the identity by an operator of norm at most \(2\nu_0q_0r_0\le1/2\); the Neumann series converges, so it is invertible. The pointwise implicit function theorem gives a smooth branch, equal to the continuous fixed-point branch by local uniqueness. One-sided endpoint derivatives follow either by smooth local extension of the finite-dimensional data or from successive differentiation and continuity up to the endpoints. The first derivative is exactly

\[ c'=(D_cF)^{-1}\left[d'-B'c-(\partial_\eta\mathscr Q)(c,c)\right]. \tag{P5.8} \]

For order \(r\), differentiate \(Bc+\mathscr Q(c,c)=d\) using the finite binomial and multinomial product rules. The terms with \(c^{(r)}\) are exactly \(D_cF\,c^{(r)}\). Every other term uses derivatives of \(c\) of order at most \(r-1\) and derivatives of the given smooth data through order \(r\). The inverse bound and induction give finite continuous derivatives of every order on the compact parameter interval. This proves the claimed smoothness without a hidden all-orders smallness assumption. When \(\mathscr Q=0\), the exact solution is \(B^{-1}d\) with no smallness requirement.

The actual support-scale derivative bound is also retained. For a fixed family \(\delta V=v_*\sum c_j(\eta)\beta_j(X/\rho)\),

\[ \partial_X^r\partial_\eta^k\delta V =v_*\rho^{-r}\sum c_j^{(k)}(\eta)\beta_j^{(r)}(X/\rho),\qquad \|\partial_X^r\partial_\eta^k\delta V\|_\infty \le |v_*|\rho^{-r}\sum_j\|\beta_j^{(r)}\|_\infty\|c\|_{C^k}. \tag{P5.9} \]

For fixed-width logarithmic bumps, \(X\partial_X=\partial_{\log X}\) gives the analogous formula with the logarithmic bump derivatives. Each later preservation of a strict inequality must compare this bound with its actual positive margin. This general solve does not certify any unexamined application margin.

In the source's two applications the exponents are explicit. At \(\alpha=1/10\), the blocks have powers \((0,3/5)\) and \((1/2,1/10,-9/10)\). At \(\alpha=-1/2-\lambda\), they have powers \((0,-\lambda)\) and \((1/2,-1/2-\lambda,-3/2-\lambda)\). P4.5 gives the possible \(\lambda^{-1}\) loss in the first block; the second stays separated near zero. The source fixes positive \(\lambda\) before selecting the later radial frequency. The actual comparisons are derived in O, H and Q for the outer and joining constructions, and in V4 for the final shear correction, with positive lambda fixed before the radial frequency.

P6. The exact stress-cone test

The waves used later must have real amplitudes; their squared amplitudes are positive. This restricts the allowable stress direction. Here we prove the exact algebraic test in the original shear and stress coordinates and its connection to the covariance construction. The positive profile \(F\) and the lengths of the coordinate vectors are retained.

For \(a>0\), set \(t_s=-b_s/a\), \(v_s=a(1+t_s^2)\), \(P_c=p_{s,1}+t_sp_{s,2}\), \(J_c=p_{s,2}-t_sp_{s,1}\). These are the original coordinates, with no unit-vector factors suppressed. Define

\[ \mathcal U(P,J)=P+J^2/4-|J|\sqrt{(P-2)/2+J^2/16}. \tag{P6.1} \]

For \(P>2\), the roots in \(v\) of \(2(P-v)^2-(v-2)J^2\) are \(v_\pm=P+J^2/4\pm|J|\sqrt{(P-2)/2+J^2/16}\). To check their location, put \(x=P-2>0\). The inequality \(\sqrt{x/2+J^2/16}\ge|J|/4\) gives \(v_-\le P\); and \((x+J^2/4)^2-J^2(x/2+J^2/16)=x^2>0\) gives \(v_->2\). The quadratic is positive below the smaller root and above the larger root. Since \(v_+\ge P\), on \(2<v<P\) positivity is exactly \(v<v_-\). This also covers \(J=0\), where both roots equal \(P\). Therefore, for \(v_s>2\), the source's admissible condition is exactly

\[ P_c>v_s,\qquad (v_s-2)J_c^2<2(P_c-v_s)^2. \tag{P6.2} \]

Its map to the physical stress is exact:

\[ \mathcal T_{0,\theta}+t_s\mathcal T_{0,z}=F(P_c-v_s),\qquad \mathcal T_{0,z}-t_s\mathcal T_{0,\theta}=FJ_c. \tag{P6.3} \]

Thus, where \(F>0\), P6.2 is precisely the positive stress-cone inequality used in the covariance derivation C1–C9. This proves the coordinate connection to that receiving argument, without asserting that the complete profile meets the inequality.

Finally retain the source's compact-set sufficient condition. For a nonempty compact \(K\subset\{(a,b_s,w):a>0\}\), suppose its listed pointwise quantities satisfy \(a-b_sw>0\) and \(2b_sw+b_s^2/a+(a-2)w^2<2\). Set \(c=1-b_sw/a\), \(j=w+b_s/a\), \(v=a+b_s^2/a\). Expansion gives the exact identity

\[ (v-2)j^2-2c^2=(1+b_s^2/a^2)\left[(a-2)w^2+2b_sw+b_s^2/a-2\right]. \tag{P6.4} \]

Hence choose \(c_K,\gamma_K>0\), \(B_K\ge1\) with \(c\ge c_K\), \(G:=2c^2-(v-2)j^2\ge\gamma_K\), \(v\le B_K\) and \(cv\le B_K\) on \(K\). Let

\[ P_K=\max\{(B_K+2)/c_K,\ 8B_K/\gamma_K\}. \tag{P6.5} \]

For \(p_{s,1}=p\ge P_K\), \(p_{s,2}=wp\), one has \(P_c=pc\ge B_K+2>\max(2,v)\), \(J_c=pj\), and

\[ \frac{2(P_c-v)^2-(v-2)J_c^2}{p^2} =G-4cv/p+2v^2/p^2\ge\gamma_K/2>0. \tag{P6.6} \]

For \(v>2\) the equivalence already proved gives admissibility. For \(v\le2\), the inequality \(\mathcal U(P_c,J_c)>2\) proves the relaxed condition directly. This completes Lemma 4.5, including its original threshold.

The figure uses the exact section \(a=3,b_s=0\) of P6.2. It is a diagram of the proved inequalities, not a numerical sample of the constructed velocity. The second panel records the five-moment correction map; its full bump integrals and support factors are given in P5.1–P5.9.

P7. Five worked exercises

Exercise 1. Identify the exact exterior stress tails. Fix the axial variable and time. Let smooth angular and axial residuals \(R_\theta(r),R_z(r)\) vanish outside \(0<r<R_*\), and suppose they vanish near the axis. Solve

\[ (\partial_r+2/r)T_\theta=-R_\theta,\qquad (\partial_r+1/r)T_z=-R_z \]

with regular axis behavior. Determine exactly when the stresses vanish for \(r\ge R_*\).

Solution. Multiplication by \(r^2\) and \(r\), respectively, gives

\[ \partial_r(r^2T_\theta)=-r^2R_\theta,\qquad \partial_r(rT_z)=-rR_z. \]

Regularity at zero makes both integration constants zero. Therefore

\[ T_\theta(r)=-r^{-2}\int_0^r \rho^2R_\theta(\rho)\,d\rho,\qquad T_z(r)=-r^{-1}\int_0^r \rho R_z(\rho)\,d\rho. \tag{P7.1} \]

They vanish near zero because the residuals do. On the exterior the integrals are the constants

\[ M_\theta^R=\int_0^{R_*}\rho^2R_\theta(\rho)\,d\rho,\qquad M_z^R=\int_0^{R_*}\rho R_z(\rho)\,d\rho. \]

Thus the exterior stresses are exactly \(-M_\theta^Rr^{-2}\) and \(-M_z^Rr^{-1}\). They both vanish there if and only if both weighted moments vanish. A nonnegative, nonzero smooth bump supported in \((R_*/3,2R_*/3)\), used as either residual, has a strictly positive corresponding moment and a nonzero tail. This proves why vanishing exterior residual alone is insufficient. The full construction arranges its total moments to eliminate these actual constants.

Exercise 2. Can a different smooth axis pressure preserve the same exterior stress? Suppose the two exterior profiles and all five moments agree as in P3, but the two axis pressure data differ by \(g\in C^\infty([-1,1])\). If their full stresses agree on a nonempty radial exterior interval for every \(\eta\), prove that \(g=0\).

Solution. P3.2, with \(X>0\) and \(L>0\), gives

\[ (1-\eta^2)g'(\eta)=4A\eta g(\eta),\qquad -1<\eta<1. \]

Direct product differentiation, without division by \(g\), gives

\[ \frac{d}{d\eta}\bigl[(1-\eta^2)^{2A}g(\eta)\bigr] =(1-\eta^2)^{2A-1} \bigl[(1-\eta^2)g'-4A\eta g\bigr]=0. \]

Thus \(g(\eta)=c(1-\eta^2)^{-2A}\) on the connected open interval. Since \(A>0\) and \(g\) is bounded up to \(\eta=1\), the constant \(c\) is zero. Conversely \(g=0\) preserves the stress by P3.

The endpoint hypothesis matters. On the open interval, a nonzero \(c\) would give the physical pressure difference

\[ q^{-2A}g(\eta)=c[q(1-\eta^2)]^{-2A} =c(1-t)^{-2A}, \tag{P7.2} \]

which is spatially constant for each \(t<1\) and therefore changes no pressure gradient. Its profile fails the stipulated bounded endpoint condition. This identifies the exact pressure-gauge freedom and why it is absent from the smooth closed profile class used here.

Exercise 3. Compute the first radial coefficients at a zero-stress axis. Write

\[ \phi(X,\eta)=\phi_0(\eta)+X\phi_1(\eta)+O(X^2),\quad U(X,\eta)=U_0(\eta)+XU_1(\eta)+O(X^2), \]

with \(\phi_0>0\) and \(\Pi(0,\eta)=\Pi_{\rm ax}(\eta)\). Derive the coefficients forced by P1.7. All remainders here are the ordinary local Taylor remainders of smooth functions on a fixed compact parameter interval.

Solution. At the axis,

\[ W_0=1-2D\eta U_0-dU_0',\qquad H_{c,0}=D\eta+dU_0,\qquad l(0,\eta)=1. \]

Both \(XU_X\) and \(X\Pi_X\) vanish there. Hence

\[ \begin{aligned} \phi_1 &=\frac{\phi_0}{4L} \left[ W_0+h(1-2\eta U_0)+(D\eta+dU_0)\frac{\phi_0'}{\phi_0} \right],\\ U_1 &=\frac1{2L}\left[ A(1-2\eta U_0)U_0 +(D\eta+dU_0)U_0' +d\Pi_{\rm ax}'-4A\eta\Pi_{\rm ax} \right]. \end{aligned} \tag{P7.3} \]

The factors \(4L\) and \(2L\) arise from \(X\phi_{XX}+2\phi_X\) and \(XU_{XX}+U_X\), respectively, at zero. The pressure coefficient is also fixed:

\[ \Pi_X(0,\eta)=\phi_0(\eta)^2/\mathsf C^2. \]

These are necessary first-coefficient identities and follow from an actual zero-stress solution. Constructing the convergent axis solution requires the full analytic argument in J0–J6; these two coefficients alone do not establish that existence.

Exercise 4. Retain the support scale in an actual moment correction. For the five coefficients in P5, suppose \(\|c\|_{C^k}\le2\nu_k\|d\|_{C^k}\). Give explicit bounds for the original increments \(u(X/\rho,\eta)\) and \(e(X/\rho,\eta)\), and determine the original change in \(J\) from transformed data \(d_2,d_3\).

Solution. The coefficients may depend on \(\eta\), but \(\rho>0\) is fixed. Repeated differentiation gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \|\partial_X^r\partial_\eta^k u(X/\rho,\eta)\|_\infty &\le 2\nu_k\rho^{-r}\|d\|_{C^k} \sum_{i=1}^2\|\beta_i^{(r)}\|_\infty,\\ \|\partial_X^r\partial_\eta^k e(X/\rho,\eta)\|_\infty &\le 2\nu_k\rho^{-r}\|d\|_{C^k} \sum_{j=1}^3\|\gamma_j^{(r)}\|_\infty. \end{aligned} \tag{P7.4} \]

The correction coefficients are the actual nonlinear solution, so its moment change is the target, including every quadratic contribution. Applying the inverse row map P5.3 yields

\[ \delta J(\eta)=\sqrt2\,\rho^{3/2} \bigl[e_*f_*(\eta)d_2(\eta)+u_c(\eta)d_3(\eta)\bigr]. \tag{P7.5} \]

The second term cannot be discarded when \(u_c\ne0\). A finite positive margin involving \(r\) radial and \(k\) parameter derivatives is preserved by choosing the discrepancy small compared with the right sides of P7.4 and the actual margin. There is no bound uniform in \(\rho\downarrow0\) for fixed nonzero coefficients and \(r>0\); the displayed \(\rho^{-r}\) remains.

Exercise 5. Invert the stress-cone coordinates exactly. For \(a>0,F>0\), recover \(p_s\) and \(\mathcal T_0\) from \(P_c,J_c\). Then describe the section \(a=3,b_s=0\) and its boundary.

Solution. The matrix taking \(p_s\) to \((P_c,J_c)\) is

\[ \begin{pmatrix}1&t_s\\-t_s&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det=1+t_s^2>0. \]

Its exact inverse gives

\[ p_{s,1}=\frac{P_c-t_sJ_c}{1+t_s^2},\qquad p_{s,2}=\frac{t_sP_c+J_c}{1+t_s^2}. \]

Since \(a=v_s/(1+t_s^2)\) and \(-b_s=at_s\), the stress is

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal T_{0,\theta} &=\frac F{1+t_s^2}(P_c-v_s-t_sJ_c),\\ \mathcal T_{0,z} &=\frac F{1+t_s^2}\bigl[t_s(P_c-v_s)+J_c\bigr]. \end{aligned} \tag{P7.6} \]

For the stated section \(t_s=0,v_s=3,P_c=p_{s,1},J_c=p_{s,2}\). The admissible set is exactly

\[ p_{s,1}>3,\qquad |p_{s,2}|<\sqrt2(p_{s,1}-3). \tag{P7.7} \]

Its two boundary rays have \(p_{s,2}=\pm\sqrt2(p_{s,1}-3)\) for \(p_{s,1}\ge3\), with vertex \((3,0)\). The stress components there are \(F(p_{s,1}-3),Fp_{s,2}\). The boundary and vertex are excluded by the strict inequalities. Every compact subset of the open cone has positive minimum values of its two continuous defining gaps. This is the exact margin used when choosing sufficiently small later corrections.

Sources and the next construction

The original OpenAI paper, pages 24–32, 34–35 and 126–128, supplies the source formulas and arguments: the cone comparison on page 32, Lemma 4.7 and the moment identities in Appendix A. The source identity and hash are in SOURCES.json.

The complete editorial calculations are G0–G6 of the profile and moment audit. This lesson retains those proofs and develops their transport, pressure-gauge, support and cone consequences. It makes no novelty claim.

The actual next construction begins with O0–O8, which fixes the outer profile and pressure datum, and H0–H7, which inserts the exact heat exterior and restores the moments. J0–J6, Q0–Q9 and V0–V7 then provide the axis solution, join and actual admissible shear. These proofs supply the existence inputs for the full theorem; N2 continues by developing them as lessons with all their choices and estimates.

Constructing the outer profile and its heat exterior

The five moments from N2.1 give us a way to change a velocity profile while controlling its stress. We now use that method to construct a profile. We choose every radial interval, solve the moment equations, determine the pressure needed at the axis, and prove the strict stress inequalities. We then replace the distant power law by a heat flow and prove that the stress goes smoothly to zero at the outer edge.

This lesson supplies the outer part of the leading-profile construction: a complete reference family and its heat modification. Its temporary inner reference is explicitly given and has integrable boundary traces, but is not a smooth Cartesian axis field. The analytic axis, its exact join, and the shear realization have separate complete proofs linked at the end. They are the subsequent teaching components of N2. The final assembly appears in the energy and comparison lesson.

Read N1 for the original coordinates and N2.1 P0–P6 for the full stress, moments, bump-matrix inverse, nonlinear solve and cone criterion. Those proofs are included in this cumulative reader. Here \(q-z^2q^{2h}=1-t\), \(X=r^2/(2q)\), \(\eta=z/q^D\), \(A=1/2+h\), \(D=1/2-h\). We keep every original physical factor. Scalar changes of variable in integrals are always accompanied by their Jacobians and the factors needed to recover the original quantity.

The source is OpenAI, Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, original paper, pages 129–144, Proposition A.4 through Proposition A.10, equations (A.5)–(A.56). The source version and mathematical locators are in SOURCES.json. The exposition below is a separate derivation and teaching text; it does not rewrite the diplomatic transcription.

Figure. The schedule is a diagram of ordered intervals, not a plot of a sampled velocity or a scale drawing. The four reserved patches lie in the long interval before the pulse. The heat change begins at \(X_K=e^{1/5}X_{\rm tail}\); its three changed moments are restored in the second reserved patch. At \(X_b=e^3X_{\rm tail}\), both stress components vanish, while their quotient has the exact sixth-order factor proved in H6. All interval lengths and full formulas appear below.

How the construction fits together

The construction has three jobs. First, the inner reference and the gradual axial transition produce a positive angular stress. The long interval then makes the accumulated axial moments small relative to the local moment scales. A pulse and two tiny end corrections set both axial moments and the quadratic stress moment to zero. These are exact equations, not numerical approximations.

Second, after the pulse, the angular profile is made independent of \(\eta\). Two more bumps restore its angular integral without changing the total pressure increment. A steep interval reduces its amplitude enough to offset the small parameter \(h\) in the later estimates. A final holding time is chosen by an explicit formula; it makes the subtracted angular moment exactly zero.

Third, the heat integral supplies an actual exterior solution. Replacing the power law changes three moments. The three-bump nonlinear system restores them, preserves the pressure datum and keeps the stress cone strict. Backward integration then proves compact support of the stress and its direction at the outer edge. The sections follow these dependencies, so each use of a small or large parameter comes after the estimates that justify choosing it.

O0. The complete reference schedule and the order of choices

Retain \(A=1/2+h,D=1/2-h,d=1-\eta^2,L=1-2h\eta^2\), \(f=(1+\eta^2)^{-1}\), \(J_0=\log(1+\eta^2)\), \(H=\sqrt{2X}E\), \(l=X\partial_X\log H\). All profiles have \(-1\le\eta\le1\). For each interval the coordinate \(y\) starts at its left endpoint and satisfies \(dX=X\,dy\). Hence prescribing l means solving \((\log E)'=l-1/2\), with the preceding endpoint value of E. Every prime on a radial profile below is a y derivative unless otherwise indicated.

Use the source's smooth step

\[ \sigma(y)=\frac{e^{-1/y^2}}{e^{-1/y^2}+e^{-1/(1-y)^2}}\ (0<y<1),\quad \sigma(y)=0\ (y\le0),\quad \sigma(y)=1\ (y\ge1). \tag{O0.1} \]

It is increasing and smooth, flat at its endpoints. Indeed the logarithmic derivative of the ratio of the second exponential to the first is \(-2(1-y)^{-3}-2y^{-3}<0\); endpoint smoothness follows from \(y^{-n}e^{-1/y^2}\to0\) for every n. Positive correcting bumps are fixed translates or rescalings of \(\sigma'\), with the supports stated below. Their fixed derivative norms are finite.

The parameter order is

\[ M_d,\qquad T_d=e^{M_d}+10,\qquad P_*>e^{T_d},\qquad 0<\lambda\ll1,\qquad 0<h\ll\min\{\lambda,e^{-T_d}\},\qquad X_R. \tag{O0.2} \]

We always take \(h<1/100\). Fixed shape constants, including the interpolation length \(T_f\) and terminal constant \(c_o\), are chosen independently of the later small parameters. Below, \(C_{\rm pre}\) denotes finite constants depending only on those shapes, \(M_d,T_d,P_*\) and a specified finite derivative order, uniformly for sufficiently small \(\lambda\) and then sufficiently small h. No such constant depends on \(X_R\) or the amplitude factor \(\mathsf C\). Constants denoted C before the choice of \(M_d\) depend only on the fixed shapes. Estimates below justify this order rather than assuming its compatibility.

The entire schedule is as follows.

  1. For \(X=X_Re^y\), \(y\le0\), set \(U=4\eta\), \(E=P_*fe^{y/10}\), so \(l=3/5\). This is the temporary inner reference, not a regular physical axis.
  2. For one unit of logarithmic length keep \(U=4\eta\), and set \(l=(3/5)(1-\sigma(y))\).
  3. On \(0\le y\le T_d\), set \(l=0\), \(E=P_1fe^{-y/2}\), and
\[ U=k(y)\eta,\quad k(y)=4[1-\sigma(\log(1+y)/M_d)],\qquad |k'(y)|\le\frac{e_d}{1+y},\quad e_d=4\|\sigma'\|_\infty/M_d. \tag{O0.3} \]

Here \(e^{-1/2}P_*\le P_1\le e^{1/10}P_*\). The function k is zero on the last eleven units, since it is zero for \(y\ge e^{M_d}-1=T_d-11\). 4. With \(U=0\), move l from zero to \(-\lambda\) by \(l=-\lambda\sigma(y)\) on a unit interval. Keep \(l=-\lambda\) for \(T_w=60\log(1/\lambda)\). Reserve, in this latter local coordinate, the four intervals

\[ (T_w-25,T_w-20),\quad(T_w-20,T_w-15),\quad (T_w-14,T_w-9),\quad(T_w-8,T_w-3). \tag{O0.4} \]

For sufficiently small \(\lambda\), all are nonempty, ordered and inside this interval. None of the reference-profile corrections below touches them. On them \(U=0\), \(E\) is the same positive multiple of \(fX^{-1/2-\lambda}\). 5. Let \(X_p\) be the end radius and \(E(X_p,\eta)=e_bf\).
