Joining the analytic axis to the outer field

NS-BLOWUP N2.4. The inner and outer solutions now exist separately. This lesson constructs their actual smooth connection. It activates the stress at the inner edge, preserves its required direction on a first collar, continues through a region of small shear, and restores all five original radial moments before entering the outer field.

The analytic-axis lesson, J0–J8, supplies the actual inner solution with its prescribed pressure and strict endpoint inequality. The outer-profile lesson, O0–H7, supplies the complete outer field and heat exterior. The stress and moment lesson, P0–P7, proves the exact physical operators, exterior-preservation map, bump-matrix inverse and nonlinear correction estimates. All three lessons are included in this cumulative reader.

The matching problem concerns the original fields and their entire radial history. Agreeing on velocity values at one radius is insufficient: the pressure and integrated stress also depend on the five cumulative moments. We compute their exact differences, retain the original scale factors, and solve the five nonlinear equations.

The source is OpenAI, Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, original paper, pages 150–157, equations (B.22)–(B.40), Lemma B.4 through Corollary B.10. This lesson is an independent derivation and teaching text; it does not replace or amend the diplomatic transcription. Source identity and mathematical locators are recorded in SOURCES.json.

Figure. The radial positions show order rather than proportional distance. Every displayed radius, factor and endpoint is the one used below. The two bump families have disjoint supports; Exercise 4 proves the resulting exact separation of the axial equations. The lower panel gives the actual inner pressure difference from Exercise 2. The stress is zero to infinite order at its inner edge while having a nonzero limiting direction.

Why the transition length comes first

The proof has three linked tasks. First, a reference continuation gives uniform parameter bounds for an entire family of narrow transitions. These bounds let us reduce the shear without introducing an inverse power of the small shear factor into the cone estimate. The stress starts with the exact flat factor proved in Q3.

Second, the endpoint bound for \(\log(\mathsf C E)\) fixes a finite transition length before the final amplitude \(\mathsf C\). Increasing that amplitude then moves the matching scale \(X_R\) outward while keeping the earlier transition endpoint fixed. Q7 proves exactly how the five original moments transform; it does not assume their unscaled discrepancies all tend to zero.

Third, the fixed outer data determine the correction tolerance before \(X_R\) is selected. Five fixed bumps solve the actual moment equations inside that tolerance. The common pressure datum and exact moment identities then preserve the entire outer field, including its heat exterior.

Q0. Objects, norms and the reference continuation

The reference field is constructed by integrating prescribed slopes. Its cutoff is radial only, so parameter differentiation does not create inverse cutoff widths. We keep the natural axis solution and its pressure integral identifiable throughout.

Retain \(A=1/2+h\), \(D=1/2-h\), \(d=1-\eta^2\), \(L=1-2h\eta^2\), \(0<h<1/100\), and the parameter interval \(-1\le\eta\le1\). Thus \(1-2h\le L\le1\). The prescribed datum is the actual analytic \(\Pi_0\) of O4. Write the J solution as

\[ U_{\rm nat}=U_*+\Lambda^{-1}\mathfrak u(\Lambda X,\eta), \quad \phi_{\rm nat}=\phi_*\Phi(\Lambda X,\eta), \quad E_{\rm nat}=\frac{\sqrt{2X}}{\mathsf C}\phi_{\rm nat}, \quad \widetilde\zeta_0=\Lambda\zeta_*, \quad \zeta_*=-\frac{LH_*}{H_*^2+\sigma_*^2}. \tag{Q0.1} \]

Here \(U_*=4\eta+j_0\), \(H_*=D\eta+dU_*\), and \(W_*,Z_*,\chi\) are exactly J0.1–J0.4. The original unaccented \(\zeta_*\) and accented \(\widetilde\zeta_0\) follow (B.3). For each fixed integer \(k\), \(\|\cdot\|_k\) is the maximum of parameter derivatives through order \(k\), uniformly on the indicated radial interval. A bound uniform in \(\mathsf C\) is asserted only for \(\mathsf C\ge\mathsf C_0(\Lambda)\). Constants allowed to depend on the already fixed \(\Lambda\) will be indicated by \(K_k(\Lambda)\); they do not depend on subsequent cutoff widths.

Use exactly

\[ X_0=4/\Lambda,\qquad X_b^{\rm loc}=100,\qquad X_i=110, \qquad y=\log(X/X_0),\qquad 4e^{2\bar t}<4.1. \tag{Q0.2} \]

The superscript distinguishes this local radius 100, called \(X_b\) in Appendix B, from the exterior stress endpoint of Appendix A. No radius has been changed. Increase \(\Lambda\) if necessary so \(X_0<100\). Fix a positive \(\bar t\) satisfying Q0.2. With the original smooth step

\[ \sigma(s)=\frac{e^{-1/s^2}}{e^{-1/s^2}+e^{-1/(1-s)^2}}\quad(0<s<1), \qquad \sigma(s)=0\ (s\le0),\quad \sigma(s)=1\ (s\ge1), \tag{Q0.3} \]

choose \(0<t_1\le\bar t\). Let \((U_{\rm r},\phi_{\rm r})\) equal the analytic solution for \(y\le t_1\); on \(t_1<y<2t_1\) define

\[ \partial_yU_{\rm r}=[1-\sigma((y-t_1)/t_1)]\mathcal D_XU_{\rm nat}, \qquad \partial_y\log\phi_{\rm r}=[1-\sigma((y-t_1)/t_1)]\mathcal D_X\log\phi_{\rm nat}. \tag{Q0.4} \]

Integrate from \(y=t_1\), then keep both functions constant for \(y\ge2t_1\). Positivity of \(\phi_{\rm r}\) follows by exponentiation. Flatness of the step at its endpoints makes the fields smooth at both joins. Set \(E_{\rm r}=\sqrt{2X}\phi_{\rm r}/\mathsf C\). Define \(\Pi_{\rm r},Q_{s,\rm r},N_{s,\rm r}\) by the original forward pressure and stress integrals P1.3 and P2.1, with the same \(\Pi_0\).

The J estimates give, for every fixed \(k\),

\[ \|U_{\rm r}-U_*\|_k\le K_k/\Lambda,\quad \|\log\phi_{\rm r}-\log\phi_*\|_k\le K_k,\quad \|\Pi_{\rm r}-\Pi_0\|_k\le K_k(\Lambda)\mathsf C^{-2} \quad(0\le X\le X_i). \tag{Q0.5} \]

For the first two bounds integrate Q0.4 over length at most \(\bar t\): the integrands and all parameter derivatives are bounded respectively by \(K_k/\Lambda\) and \(K_k\), since \(4\le\Lambda X\le4.1\) there. Before that interval J4.4 applies, and after it the fields are constant. The radial average is exactly \(\mathcal A_Xf=\int_0^1f(aX,\eta)\,da\), a contraction in every such norm, so the first bound holds also for \(\mathcal A_XU_{\rm r}-U_*\). Finally,

\[ \Pi_{\rm r}(X,\eta)-\Pi_0(\eta) =\mathsf C^{-2}\int_0^X\phi_{\rm r}(v,\eta)^2\,dv. \tag{Q0.6} \]

The factor \(\sqrt{2X}\) in E is essential to this identity. Product differentiation and Q0.5 bound this integral through every fixed parameter order, including at zero. Exponentiation and reciprocal differentiation show that \(\mathsf C E_{\rm r}\) and \((\mathsf C E_{\rm r})^{-1}\) have bounded \(k\)-norms on \([X_0,X_i]\), with positive lower bounds there, uniformly in \(\mathsf C,t_1\). All these statements use parameter derivatives; high radial cutoff derivatives need not be bounded as \(t_1\) decreases.

Q1. The reference source and strict shear comparison

The reference continuation must retain a strict margin over the threshold two. The angular estimate covers one parameter region; the nonvanishing axial source covers the other. Both comparisons apply to the whole family before a final transition width is selected.

The weighted gradient bounds used in J5 remain valid through the cutoff. To check this directly, put \(q(Y,\eta)=\log\Phi(Y,\eta)\). Differentiating the center \(\log f_0(Y\chi)\) and using \(|H_*\chi'|\le2\|H_*'\|_\infty\chi\), together with J4.4 and positivity, gives

\[ |Yq_Y|+|H_*q_\eta|+|H_*\partial_\eta(Yq_Y)| \le K\chi+K/\Lambda,\qquad 0\le Y\le4.1. \tag{Q1.1} \]

All denominators are bounded below by J4.5. In Q0.4 the cutoff has no parameter dependence. Integrating its parameter derivative, and using the last term of Q1.1 on the interval of length at most \(\bar t\), proves

\[ |\mathcal D_X\log\phi_{\rm r}| +|H_*\partial_\eta(\log\phi_{\rm r}-\log\phi_*)| \le K\chi+K/\Lambda. \tag{Q1.2} \]

The unweighted derivative of \(\log\phi_{\rm r}-\log\phi_*\) is also bounded by Q0.5. Since \(H_{c,\rm r}-H_*=d(U_{\rm r}-U_*)\), Q0.5 and \(|\zeta_*|\le L\sigma_*^{-1}\sqrt\chi\) give

\[ -H_{c,\rm r}(\log\phi_{\rm r})_\eta \ge \Lambda L\chi-K\chi-K_{\sigma_*}\sqrt\chi-K/\Lambda. \tag{Q1.3} \]

Furthermore \(W_{\rm r}-W_*=O(\Lambda^{-1})\), by the actual radial-average formula, and \(|U_{\rm r}|\le4.1\) for large \(\Lambda\). In the exact source

\[ S_{q,\rm r}=-W_{\rm r}l_{\rm r}-h(1-2\eta U_{\rm r}) -H_{c,\rm r}(\log\phi_{\rm r})_\eta,\qquad l_{\rm r}=1+\mathcal D_X\log\phi_{\rm r}, \]

Q1.2 therefore bounds the change caused by \(l_{\rm r}-1\) by \(K\chi+K/\Lambda\). Hence

\[ S_{q,\rm r}\ge\Lambda L\chi-W_*-10h-K\chi-K_{\sigma_*}\sqrt\chi-K/\Lambda \ge .94\Lambda L\chi+2.4. \tag{Q1.4} \]

For the last inequality choose \(\Lambda\) so \(K\chi\le.03\Lambda L\chi\), and use \(K_{\sigma_*}\sqrt\chi\le.03\Lambda L\chi+ K_{\sigma_*}^2/(.12\Lambda(1-2h))\). Then enlarge \(\Lambda\) so the remaining \(1/\Lambda\) terms are smaller than .3. The original bounds \(-W_*>2.8\) and \(10h\le.1\) supply the constant 2.4, with strict spare room by making the last error smaller. No division by \(\chi\) occurs. This estimate is uniform over a fixed small reference-width family.

On the natural interval, J5.7–J5.8 give \(\mathcal D_X\log\phi_{\rm nat}=-p_1/2<0\). Multiplication by the nonnegative cutoff and then setting the slope to zero proves \(l_{\rm r}\le1\).

For the axial source, retain every term of P1.1. Q0.5, \(\mathcal D_XU_{\rm r}=O(\Lambda^{-1})\), and Q0.6 yield

\[ \|S_{n,\rm r}-Z_*\|_k\le K_k/\Lambda+K_k(\Lambda)\mathsf C^{-2}. \tag{Q1.5} \]

The two pressure derivatives are included: \(\Pi_{\rm r}-\Pi_0\) is Q0.6 and \(\mathcal D_X\Pi_{\rm r}=E_{\rm r}^2/2\). Choose \(\Lambda\), then \(\mathsf C\), so the right side for \(k=0\), after division by L, is below \(\delta_*/4\). On \(\chi\le.99\), \(|Z_*|>\delta_*\) by J0.4. The equation and its exact solution are

\[ \partial_y n_{s,\rm r}+n_{s,\rm r}=S_{n,\rm r}/L,\qquad n_{s,\rm r}(y)=e^{-y}n_{s,\rm r}(0)+ \int_0^y e^{-(y-v)}\,\frac{S_{n,\rm r}(v)}L\,dv. \tag{Q1.6} \]

The analytic initial value differs from \(Z_*/L\) by \(O(\Lambda^{-1})\). Both terms in this convex average have the sign of \(Z_*\) and absolute value at least \(\delta_*/2\), after the same choice. Therefore \(|n_{s,\rm r}|\ge\delta_*/2\) on that parameter region throughout the continuation.

The positive stress integral gives \(p_{1,\rm r}>0\), and its equation is

\[ \partial_y p_{1,\rm r}=\frac{XS_{q,\rm r}}L-l_{\rm r}p_{1,\rm r}. \tag{Q1.7} \]

Using \(l_{\rm r}\le1\), Q1.4 and \(X=X_0e^y\) in the integrating-factor inequality gives both exact lower comparisons

\[ \begin{split} p_{1,\rm r}(y)&\ge p_{1,\rm r}(0)e^{-y} +1.88\chi(e^y-e^{-y}),\\ p_{1,\rm r}(X)&\ge p_{1,\rm r}(X_0)\frac{X_0}X +1.2\left(X-\frac{X_0^2}X\right). \end{split} \tag{Q1.8} \]

The coefficient 1.88 is \(.94\Lambda X_0/2\); the coefficient 1.2 uses \(L\le1\) and \(2.4/2\). On \(\chi>.99\), J6 gives \(p_{1,\rm r}(0)>2.3\). Replacing it by 2.3 in the first comparison gives \(1.88\chi e^y+(2.3-1.88\chi)e^{-y}\), whose derivative is positive for \(y\ge0\), because \(1.88\chi>2.3/2\). Thus \(p_{1,\rm r}>2.3\) there. The second comparison is greater than 3 for \(100\le X\le110\), since \(X_0\le4\) and \(1.2(100-16/100)>3\).

The reference pressure and field bounds, or their exact moment formulas, also give a finite upper bound \(M_0(\Lambda)\) for \(p_{1,\rm r}\), independently of subsequent \(\mathsf C,t_1\). Let \(E_{\max}(\Lambda)\) bound \(\mathsf C E_{\rm r}\). On \(\chi\le.99\),

\[ \frac{p_{2,\rm r}^2}{p_{1,\rm r}} =\frac{X^2 n_{s,\rm r}^2}{E_{\rm r}^2p_{1,\rm r}} \ge \frac{\mathsf C^2X_0^2\delta_*^2} {4E_{\max}(\Lambda)^2M_0(\Lambda)}. \tag{Q1.9} \]

Increase \(\mathsf C\) so this is at least \(5/2\). On the other region \(p_{1,\rm r}>2.3\). Consequently

\[ v_{\rm r}:=p_{1,\rm r}+\frac{p_{2,\rm r}^2}{p_{1,\rm r}}>2+.2 \quad\hbox{on }[X_0,X_i]\times[-1,1]. \tag{Q1.10} \]

Each fixed parameter derivative of \(p_{1,\rm r},n_{s,\rm r}\) is uniformly bounded: the moment formulas P2.5 use Q0.5–Q0.6, one additional parameter derivative, positive denominators and integrals on a fixed interval. For \(Q_{s,\rm r}\), its common amplitude factor cancels exactly between numerator and denominator. For \(N_{s,\rm r}\), Q1.5–Q1.6 apply. The lower comparison in Q1.8 is uniform and positive. Once a finite \(\mathsf C\) is fixed these bounds therefore give a finite \(V_{\max}\) bounding \(v_{\rm r}\) for every sufficiently small \(t_1\), before any one width is selected. This proves the full reference statement of Lemma B.4.

Q2. Activation and the stress cone without an inverse cutoff loss

The same positive factor multiplies both shear components. Cancel it in their ratio before estimating. This exact cancellation is why making the shear small does not make the cone errors large.

Fix a sufficiently large finite \(\mathsf C\) as above. All constants in this section may depend on it and on \(\Lambda\), but are uniform as \(t_1\) and \(0<\kappa_0<1/2\) decrease. On \(0<y<t_1\), prescribe

\[ e_a=(1-\kappa_0)\sigma(y/t_1),\quad \kappa=1-e_a,\quad a=\kappa p_{1,\rm r},\quad \mathcal D_XU=-\frac{\kappa Xn_{s,\rm r}}2,\quad \partial_y\log\phi=-\frac{\kappa p_{1,\rm r}}2. \tag{Q2.1} \]

Integrate from the actual axis values at \(y=0\); leave the analytic solution unchanged for \(X\le X_0\). Define \(E=\sqrt{2X}\phi/\mathsf C\), and compute pressure and stresses by forward integration with the same \(\Pi_0\).

On this entire first interval the reference is the natural solution. Its zero leading stress gives the exact differences

\[ \partial_y(\log\phi-\log\phi_{\rm r})=\frac{e_ap_{1,\rm r}}2,\qquad \partial_y(U-U_{\rm r})=\frac{e_aXn_{s,\rm r}}2. \tag{Q2.2} \]

The step is increasing, so \(\int_0^ye_a(v)\,dv\le ye_a(y)\). Parameter differentiation commutes with these integrals and never differentiates the cutoff. Thus the field differences and \(\log\phi-\log\phi_{\rm r}\) are \(O_k(ye_a)\). Exponentiating gives \(E_{\rm r}/E=1+O_k(ye_a)\). On this compact annulus the moment integrands are smooth functions of the fields; their differences vanish before \(X_0\). Their integrals obey the same bound, also with one additional parameter derivative. P3.3–P3.6 consequently prove

\[ p_s-p_{s,\rm r}=O_k(ye_a),\qquad E_{\rm r}/E=1+O_k(ye_a). \tag{Q2.3} \]

These are estimates on values and parameter derivatives, not bounds on radial cutoff derivatives.

Since \(p_{2,\rm r}=Xn_{s,\rm r}/E_{\rm r}\), the actual shear is exactly \(\mathfrak s=\kappa(p_{1,\rm r},p_{2,\rm r}E_{\rm r}/E)\). Divide its two components before estimating: because \(\kappa>0\),

\[ t_s=-b_s/a=\frac{p_{2,\rm r}}{p_{1,\rm r}}\frac{E_{\rm r}}E,\quad v_s=\kappa v_{\rm r}+O(ye_a),\quad P_c=v_{\rm r}+O(ye_a),\quad J_c=O(ye_a). \tag{Q2.4} \]

The bounded reciprocal of \(p_{1,\rm r}\) follows from Q1.8. Every error constant is independent of \(\kappa_0^{-1}\): the common \(\kappa\) cancels exactly in \(t_s\), while \(0<\kappa\le1\) multiplies the remaining error in \(v_s\).

Choose one constant \(K\) bounding the four errors, and use \(v_{\rm r}>2+.2\), \(v_{\rm r}\le V_{\max}\). Taking \(t_1\) small enough yields positive constants \(c_1,c_2\), independent of its final smaller value, with

\[ P_c-v_s\ge c_1e_a,\quad P_c>2+c_2,\quad \frac{(v_s-2)_+J_c^2}{(P_c-v_s)^2} \le\frac{(V_{\max}+1)K^2}{c_1^2}y^2<2. \tag{Q2.5} \]

For example require the error in the first difference to be at most \(e_a\), the error in \(P_c\) to be at most .1, and the final displayed upper bound to be less than 2. These are finitely many width bounds on already fixed constants. P6.1–P6.2 prove the admissible cone where \(v_s>2\); where \(v_s\le2\), the fact that \(\mathcal U(P_c,J_c)>2\) proves the strict relaxed condition. Continuity from \(v_s(0,\eta)=v_{\rm r}(0,\eta)>2+.2\), uniformly on the compact parameter interval, supplies a positive first collar with \(v_s>2+.1\).

Q3. Flat stress factor and limiting direction at the inner edge

A stress that vanishes at an endpoint can still have a definite smooth direction there. We prove this by dividing by its actual flat scalar factor, computing the resulting smooth vector, and proving that vector is nonzero.

For \(y\ge0\) near zero write, exactly,

\[ e_a(y)=e^{-t_1^2/y^2}g_a(y),\qquad g_a(y)=\frac{1-\kappa_0} {e^{-t_1^2/y^2}+e^{-1/(1-y/t_1)^2}},\qquad g_a(0)=(1-\kappa_0)e>0. \tag{Q3.1} \]

The exponential extends smoothly by zero at zero, so \(g_a\) is smooth and positive on a closed small collar. For a nonnegative integer \(m\) and a smooth \(b\), the substitution in H6.1–H6.2, now with \(c=t_1^2\), gives the full formula

\[ \begin{split} \frac1{e_a(y)}\int_0^y e_a(v)v^m b(v,\eta)\,dv ={}&\frac{y^{m+3}}{2g_a(y)} \int_0^\infty e^{-t_1^2w}(1+y^2w)^{-(m+3)/2}\\ &\qquad\cdot g_a\!\left(\frac{y}{\sqrt{1+y^2w}}\right) b\!\left(\frac{y}{\sqrt{1+y^2w}},\eta\right)\,dw . \end{split} \tag{Q3.2} \]

Every fixed mixed derivative of the integral is dominated by \(e^{-t_1^2w}\) times a polynomial in \(w\); the chosen \(t_1>0\) is fixed here. Hence the right side is \(y^{m+3}\) times a smooth function through zero. This retains the integration factor \(1/2\), rather than only recording a vanishing order.

Apply \(m=0\) to Q2.2. Field and logarithmic differences belong to \(e_ay^3C^\infty\). Products and smooth compositions preserve this class: write, for instance, \(\exp(e_ay^3b)-1=e_ay^3b\int_0^1\exp(se_ay^3b)\,ds\). Reciprocals are handled by \((f+g)^{-1}-f^{-1}=-g/[f(f+g)]\), where the fields have nonzero denominators. Each moment and pressure difference is one further forward integral of such a difference, with smooth radial weights \(dX=X_0e^y\,dy\) and \(1/X\) on this collar. Applying Q3.2 with \(m=3\) gives \(e_ay^6C^\infty\).

Substituting these exact classes in P3.4 gives \(p_s-p_{s,\rm r}\in e_ay^3C^\infty\). The shear formula in Q2.4 then proves

\[ \mathcal T_0=F(p_s-\mathfrak s)=e_a B_0(y,\eta),\qquad B_0\in C^\infty,\qquad B_0(0,\eta)=F(X_0,\eta)p_{s,\rm r}(X_0,\eta)\ne0. \tag{Q3.3} \]

Here \(F=\phi/\mathsf C\) is positive, \(p_{1,\rm r}>0\), and no division by a vanishing field was used. At the endpoint \(t_s=p_{2,\rm r}/p_{1,\rm r}\), so exactly

\[ B_0\cdot(-t_s,1)=0,\qquad B_0\cdot(1,t_s)=F(X_0,\eta)v_{\rm r}(X_0,\eta)>0. \tag{Q3.4} \]

It follows that \(2[B_0\cdot(1,t_s)]^2-(v_s-2)[B_0\cdot(-t_s,1)]^2\) has a positive minimum at the endpoint. Smoothness and compactness preserve that minimum, and \(|B_0|>0\), on a smaller collar. Thus \(B_0/|B_0|\) is the smooth limiting unit stress direction.

Differentiating Q3.1 any fixed number of times introduces only finitely many inverse powers of \(y\). Since \(X_0>0\), \(\partial_X=X^{-1}\partial_y\) has smooth bounded coefficients here. For every fixed radial/parameter multi-index \(I\),

\[ |\mathcal T_0|\ge c e^{-t_1^2/y^2},\qquad |\partial^I\mathcal T_0|\le C_Ie^{-t_1^2/y^2}y^{-N_I}. \tag{Q3.5} \]

The upper bounds tend to zero to every order. The stress therefore extends smoothly by zero to \(X\le X_0\), while its direction extends by Q3.4. This proves the full inner endpoint assertions (B.30)–(B.31).

Q4. Continuation with small shear to the radius 110

The explicit integrated prescriptions continue the field. The small parameters are chosen in order from bounds already available for the reference family. A first-crossing argument then preserves the angular margin on the final constant-slope interval.

After \(y=t_1\), keep Q2.1 with \(\kappa=\kappa_0\) up to \(X=100\). These are explicit integrals of the already constructed reference coefficients, so they define smooth \(U,\log\phi\) and positive E. On the reference cutoff, the reference logarithmic slopes are bounded independently of its width; their integrals over length \(t_1\) are \(O_k(t_1)\). After that cutoff both reference fields are constant. Integrating the actual slopes over the fixed remaining interval gives \(O_k(\kappa_0)\). Together with Q2.2 this proves

\[ \|U-U_{\rm r}\|_k+\|\log\phi-\log\phi_{\rm r}\|_k +\|p_s-p_{s,\rm r}\|_k \le K_k(\mathsf C,\Lambda)(t_1+\kappa_0) \quad(X_0\le X\le100). \tag{Q4.1} \]

For the last term use the exact five moment differences and P3.4 with one extra parameter derivative. Positivity and a lower bound for E follow first from the bound on the logarithm. No radial derivative of a narrow cutoff is used in this comparison.

The same common-\(\kappa\) cancellation as in Q2.4 gives

\[ P_c=v_{\rm r}+O(t_1+\kappa_0),\qquad v_s=\kappa_0v_{\rm r}+O(t_1+\kappa_0) \quad(t_1\le y\le\log(100/X_0)). \tag{Q4.2} \]

Choose \(\kappa_0\) so \(\kappa_0V_{\max}<1/4\), \(\kappa_0\sup p_{1,\rm r}<.8\), and all the errors contributed by \(\kappa_0\) in Q4.2 are below \(\min(.05,1/8)\). Then choose \(t_1>0\) so its errors satisfy the same bounds as well as Q2.5. This gives \(P_c>2+.1\) and \(v_s<1\) after the first activation interval. Since \(\mathcal U(P_c,J_c)>2\), the strict relaxed condition holds irrespective of the size of \(J_c\). The entire reference family, rather than a previously selected member, supplied the constants, so there is no circular dependence on the choice of \(t_1\).

At \(X=100\) multiply the axial prescription by a smooth \(\beta\) decreasing from 1 to 0 on a short logarithmic interval; keep \(a=\kappa_0p_{1,\rm r}\) there. The reference coefficients have been defined up to 110. For final transition lengths with sum \(\omega_{\rm fin}\), integration gives the same comparisons as Q4.1, with an additional \(K_k\omega_{\rm fin}\). On the axial cutoff,

\[ t_s=\beta\frac{p_{2,\rm r}}{p_{1,\rm r}}\frac{E_{\rm r}}E,\qquad P_c=p_{1,\rm r}+\beta\frac{p_{2,\rm r}^2}{p_{1,\rm r}} +O(t_1+\kappa_0+\omega_{\rm fin}). \tag{Q4.3} \]

Since \(p_{1,\rm r}>3\), \(0\le\beta\le1\), and \(\kappa_0V_{\max}<1/4\), decreasing the chosen parameters makes \(P_c>2\) and \(v_s<1\) on this cutoff. At its end \(\mathcal D_XU=0\). On the next short interval interpolate \(a\) from \(\kappa_0p_{1,\rm r}\) to .8 by \(a=(1-\theta)\kappa_0p_{1,\rm r}+.8\theta\), where \(\theta\) is a flat-ended smooth step. Keep \(\mathcal D_XU=0\). Then \(0<a\le.8\), \(b_s=0\), \(v_s=a<1\). P3.4 and the short-interval comparison with the value at 100 give \(P_c=p_1>2\) throughout. Both transitions fit strictly before 110 by requiring \(\omega_{\rm fin}<\log(110/100)\).

After the second transition keep \(a=.8\), \(l=.6\), and \(U\) constant in X. The parameter derivative of \(\log\phi\) is then constant in X. At its start it equals

\[ (\log\phi)_\eta=\Lambda\zeta_*+ (\log\Phi(4,\eta))_\eta+r_\eta(\eta),\qquad \|r_\eta\|_k\le K_k(\Lambda)(t_1+\kappa_0+\omega_{\rm fin}). \tag{Q4.4} \]

To prove the stated independence from \(\mathsf C\), differentiate the integrated slopes in Q2.1 and the two final cutoffs. The only varying parameter coefficients are derivatives of \(p_{1,\rm r}\), whose bounds in Q1 are uniform in \(\mathsf C\). The constant .8 has zero parameter derivative. For U the corresponding coefficients are \(n_{s,\rm r}\), also uniformly bounded. Thus \(U-U_*=O_k(\Lambda^{-1})+O_k(\Lambda)(t_1+\kappa_0+\omega_{\rm fin})\) throughout the construction, including its radial average.

As in Q1.3, after increasing \(\Lambda\) as an axis parameter and then decreasing the final widths, the gradient term is bounded below by

\[ -H_c(\log\phi)_\eta \ge\Lambda L\chi-K\chi-K_{\sigma_*}\sqrt\chi-K/\Lambda -K(\Lambda)(t_1+\kappa_0+\omega_{\rm fin})\ge-.1. \tag{Q4.5} \]

The fixed-\(\Lambda\) coefficient of the last error includes multiplication by \(\Lambda\zeta_*\); it is finite and is made small by the later choices. One can simultaneously ensure \(-W\ge2.75\) and \(|U|\le4.1\). The original source then satisfies

\[ S_q=-.6W-h(1-2\eta U)-H_c(\log\phi)_\eta \ge .6(2.75)-.1-.1>1. \tag{Q4.6} \]

Starting from \(p_1>2\), a first downward crossing of 2 on this interval would have \(\partial_y p_1=XS_q/L-.6p_1>X-1.2>0\). At a first crossing from above its left derivative must be nonpositive, a contradiction. Consequently \(p_1>2\) through \(X_i=110\). This completes the actual continuation of Proposition B.5, including positivity, the inner admissible collar, the later strict relaxed cone and the specified final slopes.

Q5. One analytic collar and amplitude-independent endpoint bounds

The inner parameter-analytic rectangle is protected by the direction of the radial integrals. Separately, bounds for the endpoint values use integrated cutoff values, so the transition length can be selected before the amplitude.

Choose \(0<t_c<t_1\) inside the admissible collar of Q2–Q3, with \(4e^{t_c}<4.1\). The J solution has a joint complex neighborhood of its compact radial/parameter rectangle; shrink the parameter neighborhood once so that \(\Phi\) has no zeros and L has no zeros. In the first collar the reference is the natural solution. Its \(p_{1,\rm r},n_{s,\rm r}\) and all their radial derivatives are holomorphic in that same smaller parameter neighborhood, using either J5.7 or the original forward integrals. Q2.1 then integrates holomorphic coefficients multiplied by radial-only cutoffs. Its exponential for \(\phi\) is nonzero. Differentiating these formulas radially changes cutoff derivatives but neither introduces a new parameter singularity nor changes the parameter domain.

The exact expressions

\[ \frac E{\sqrt{2X}}=\frac{\phi}{\mathsf C},\qquad \frac{V_0}X=\frac{2\eta U-2D\eta\mathcal A_XU-d\partial_\eta\mathcal A_XU}{L}, \qquad \Pi=\Pi_0+\mathsf C^{-2}\int_0^X\phi(v,\eta)^2\,dv \tag{Q5.1} \]

are therefore smooth in \((X,\eta)\) through \(X=0\) and holomorphic in \(\eta\) on a common neighborhood for \(0\le X\le X_0e^{t_c}\). Each fixed radial derivative has finite bounds on a smaller common neighborhood. Subsequent modifications will lie strictly to its right. Since all the integrals in Q5.1 are forward integrals, later modifications leave this rectangle unchanged. The size of \(t_c\) and the radial derivative bounds need not be uniform as the final amplitude grows or the transition widths decrease. This proves precisely Corollary B.6.

For the endpoint quantities

\[ \ell_i(\eta)=\log(\mathsf C E(X_i,\eta)),\qquad G_i(\eta)=U(X_i,\eta),\qquad L_0=\log(X_i/X_0), \tag{Q5.2} \]

let \(M_k,N_k\) be the uniform bounds for \(p_{1,\rm r},n_{s,\rm r}\) from Q1. Before the final interpolation, \(a=\kappa p_{1,\rm r}\); during it a is a convex combination of \(\kappa_0p_{1,\rm r}\) and .8; afterwards it is .8. Thus \(\|a\|_k\le M_k+.8\). Integrating \(\partial_y\log\phi=-a/2\) gives the explicit finite bound

\[ \|\ell_i\|_k\le \tfrac12|\log(2X_i)|+ \sup_{\mathsf C\ge\mathsf C_0(\Lambda)} \|\log\phi_*+\log\Phi(4,\cdot)\|_k +\tfrac12(M_k+.8)L_0=:\mathcal B_k. \tag{Q5.3} \]

The supremum is finite by J4.4 and positivity. It depends on \(\Lambda\) and the prior axis data, but not on subsequent \(\mathsf C\) or smaller widths.

For U, the first activation contributes at most \(X_0e^{\bar t}N_kt_1/2\) to its endpoint \(k\)-norm. On the remainder, including its final cutoff, the integrand has magnitude at most \(\kappa_0X|n_{s,\rm r}|/2\); using \(dX=X\,dy\) bounds its integral by \(\kappa_0X_iN_k/2\). It is zero after the axial cutoff. Therefore

\[ \|G_i-U_*\|_k \le\frac{C_k^{\rm nat}}{\Lambda} +\frac{N_k}{2}(X_0e^{\bar t}t_1+X_i\kappa_0) \le\frac{C_k^{\rm nat}}{\Lambda} +C_k^{\rm join}(\Lambda)(t_1+\kappa_0+\omega_{\rm fin}). \tag{Q5.4} \]

The natural constant is independent of large \(\Lambda,\mathsf C\) by J4.4, after the axis shape data have been fixed. The joining constant is independent of subsequent \(\mathsf C\) and widths. No inverse cutoff width occurs because only integrated cutoff values, not radial derivatives, were used. This proves Lemma B.7 with its full stated uniformity.

Q6. Transition length chosen before the amplitude

The interpolation changes the logarithm of the angular field. Its two endpoint parameter gradients have a common lower bound, and its radial slope remains in a fixed interval. The original source equation therefore keeps the required sign throughout the transition.

Keep \(f(\eta)=(1+\eta^2)^{-1}\). Choose a positive finite \(T_{\rm sh}\) satisfying

\[ T_{\rm sh}\ge20\|\sigma'\|_\infty (\mathcal B_0+\|\log f\|_\infty). \tag{Q6.1} \]

The right side is already fixed before the final amplitude. For \(y_i=\log(X/X_i)\ge0\), prescribe

\[ \log E=-\log\mathsf C+\frac{y_i}{10} +[1-\sigma(y_i/T_{\rm sh})]\ell_i +\sigma(y_i/T_{\rm sh})\log f,\qquad U=G_i. \tag{Q6.2} \]

At \(X_i\) this matches the existing constant slopes to every radial order; the step is flat at zero. E is positive by construction. Its exact slope is

\[ l=\frac35+\frac{\sigma'(y_i/T_{\rm sh})}{T_{\rm sh}} (\log f-\ell_i)\in[.55,.65], \quad a=2-2l\in[.7,.9],\quad b_s=0. \tag{Q6.3} \]

Q5.3 supplies the stated interval without any growth of \(T_{\rm sh}\) with \(\mathsf C\).

The angular source remains positive on this potentially long interval. Q4.4 and J5.2 imply

\[ -H_c\ell_i'\ge\Lambda L\chi-K\chi-K_{\sigma_*}\sqrt\chi -K/\Lambda-o(1), \tag{Q6.4} \]

where \(o(1)\) is bounded by a fixed-\(\Lambda\) constant times \(t_1+\kappa_0+\omega_{\rm fin}\). The full radial history of U stays close to \(U_*\), so this also bounds \(W-W_*\) through its actual radial average. The other endpoint gradient has the exact expression

\[ -H_c(\log f)'=\frac{2\eta H_c}{1+\eta^2} \ge-\frac{j_0^2}{2D}-\|G_i-U_*\|_0. \tag{Q6.5} \]

Indeed \(\eta H_*=(D+4d)\eta^2+dj_0\eta \ge D\eta^2-j_0|\eta|\ge-j_0^2/(4D)\), and \(2|\eta|d/(1+\eta^2)\le1\). This verifies the bound at both parameter endpoints as well as near the zero of \(H_*\).

Young's inequality as in Q1 makes the right side of Q6.4 at least \(-.1\) for large \(\Lambda\) and the later small widths. Q6.5 is at least \(-.1\) for \(j_0\le.05\), large \(\Lambda\) and the same sufficiently small widths. Since the cutoff in Q6.2 is independent of \(\eta\), its parameter gradient is the convex combination of these two gradients. Also \(-W\ge2.75\) and \(|U|\le4.1\) persist. Hence the exact source satisfies

\[ S_q=-Wl-h(1-2\eta U)-H_c(\log E)_\eta \ge2.75(.55)-.1-.1>1. \tag{Q6.6} \]

At a putative first downward crossing \(p_1=2\), the original equation gives \(\partial_{y_i}p_1=XS_q/L-lp_1>X-1.3>0\), impossible for \(X\ge110\). Thus \(p_1>2\), \(v_s=a\le.9<2\), and \(P_c=p_1>2\): the strict relaxed cone persists.

At \(X_{\rm sep}=X_ie^{T_{\rm sh}}\) the field becomes exactly

\[ E=\mathsf C^{-1}f(X/X_i)^{1/10} =P_*f(X/X_R)^{1/10},\qquad X_R=X_i(\mathsf C P_*)^{10},\qquad U=G_i. \tag{Q6.7} \]

The equality retains the amplitude and every power. The step is flat at its upper endpoint, so the match is smooth. Before axial restoration the same source bound and crossing argument continue to apply to this constant-slope interval. The endpoint \(X_{\rm sep}\) is fixed before \(\mathsf C\), whereas \(X_R\) grows with it; this is the scale separation required for the moment estimates below.

Q7. All five moment errors with their original scale factors

The original moments have different powers of the radial scale. We display the invertible comparison map and carry each factor through the stress formulas. The short inner segment then has explicit small contributions in the units needed for the correction solve.

Introduce \(x=X/X_R\) only with the exact comparison

\[ \begin{gathered} M=X_R\widehat M,\quad I=X_R^{3/2}\widehat I,\quad J=X_R^{3/2}\widehat J,\quad S=X_R\widehat S,\quad C_p=\widehat C_p,\\ \widehat H(x,\eta)=\sqrt{2x}\,E(X_Rx,\eta),\qquad H(X_Rx,\eta)=\sqrt{X_R}\widehat H(x,\eta),\\ \widehat C_p(x,\eta)=\int_0^x\frac{E(X_Rv,\eta)^2}{2v}\,dv,\qquad \Pi(X_Rx,\eta)=\Pi_0(\eta)+\widehat C_p(x,\eta). \end{gathered} \tag{Q7.1} \]

The other hatted moments are the integrals in \(dv\) of \(U,\widehat H,U\widehat H,U^2-E^2/2\), evaluated at \(X_Rv\). Changing variables in the original moments proves every factor in Q7.1. Substitution in P2.5 gives the exact original functions at \(X_Rx\):

\[ \begin{split} W&=1-\frac{2D\eta\widehat M+d\widehat M_\eta}{x},\\ Q_s&=-W+ \frac{(1-h)\widehat I-D\eta\widehat I_\eta-d\widehat J_\eta +2(h-D)\eta\widehat J}{x\widehat H},\\ N_s&=-WU+ \frac{D(\widehat M-\eta\widehat M_\eta)+4h\eta\widehat S-d\widehat S_\eta}{x} +4A\eta\Pi-d\Pi_\eta. \end{split} \tag{Q7.2} \]

These formulas remove \(X_R\) from the coefficient map, but not from the physical moments or from \(p_s=(X_Rx/L)(Q_s,N_s/E)\). Those factors remain in use.

The short inner portion ends at

\[ x_{\rm sep}=\frac{X_{\rm sep}}{X_R} =\frac{e^{T_{\rm sh}}}{(\mathsf C P_*)^{10}}. \tag{Q7.3} \]

Q0, Q5 and Q6 bound U and \(\mathsf C E\) on \(0\le X\le X_{\rm sep}\) in each fixed parameter norm, independently of later large \(\mathsf C\) and the allowed smaller widths. Near zero \(\mathsf C E=\sqrt{2X}\phi_{\rm nat}\). Therefore at \(x=x_{\rm sep}\),

\[ \|\widehat M\|_k+\|\widehat S\|_k\le K_k(\Lambda)x_{\rm sep},\qquad \|\widehat I\|_k+\|\widehat J\|_k \le K_k(\Lambda)\mathsf C^{-1}x_{\rm sep}^{3/2},\qquad \|\widehat C_p\|_k\le K_k(\Lambda)\mathsf C^{-2}. \tag{Q7.4} \]

For the first bounds use the bounded U and \(E=O(\mathsf C^{-1})\) in the exact integrands. For I and J integrate the retained factor \(\sqrt{2x}\) against this E bound. For pressure, change back to X: on \([0,X_0]\) its integrand is \(\mathsf C^{-2}\phi_{\rm nat}^2\); on \([X_0,X_{\rm sep}]\) it is bounded by \(K_k(\Lambda)\mathsf C^{-2}/X\), whose integral is finite because \(X_0>0\) and \(X_{\rm sep}\) is fixed. Product differentiation supplies the same estimates through every chosen finite order. No singular \(1/x\) majorant was integrated to zero.

The ideal inner part of the actual outer family has \(U_0=4\eta\), \(E_0=P_*fx^{1/10}\). Its exact moments are

\[ \begin{split} \widehat M_0&=4\eta x,& \widehat I_0&=\frac{5\sqrt2}{8}P_*fx^{8/5},& \widehat J_0&=4\eta\widehat I_0,\\ \widehat S_0&=16\eta^2x-\frac5{12}P_*^2f^2x^{6/5},& \widehat C_{p,0}&=\frac52P_*^2f^2x^{1/5}. \end{split} \tag{Q7.5} \]

In particular, at the endpoint, \(\widehat C_{p,0}(x_{\rm sep})=(5/2)f^2e^{T_{\rm sh}/5}\mathsf C^{-2}\). Every term of Q7.5, with every fixed parameter derivative, tends to zero there as \(\mathsf C\) grows. Q7.4–Q7.5 consequently make the actual differences of all five hatted moments as small as any preassigned positive tolerance, uniformly over the later width choices. Through Q7.1 this is a proved statement about the original moments, not their replacement by different objects.

After \(x_{\rm sep}\), E is exactly \(E_0\). Put \(g(\eta)=G_i-4\eta\). Choose \(\mathsf C\) so \(x_{\rm sep}<e^{-8}\), and on \(-8<\log x<-7\) restore the axial field by

\[ U=4\eta+\rho(x)g,\qquad \rho(x)=1-\sigma(\log x+8). \tag{Q7.6} \]

Take \(\rho=1\) before that interval and \(\rho=0\) after it. The error integrands after \(x_{\rm sep}\), before any angular bumps, are exactly

\[ \Delta U=\rho g,\quad \Delta\widehat H=0,\quad \Delta(U\widehat H)=\sqrt2P_*fx^{3/5}\rho g,\quad \Delta(U^2-E^2/2)=8\eta\rho g+\rho^2g^2,\quad \Delta(E^2/(2x))=0. \tag{Q7.7} \]

Their weights \(1,x^{3/5}\) are integrable at zero. Integrating to \(e^{-5}\), and differentiating in \(\eta\), bounds the five moment discrepancies by

\[ K_k^{\rm out}\|g\|_{k+1}+o_{\mathsf C}(1) \tag{Q7.8} \]

provided \(\|g\|_{k+1}\le1\); the extra derivative is retained for Q7.2. Here \(K_k^{\rm out}\) depends only on the fixed outer data and the fixed restoration cutoff. The error \(o_{\mathsf C}(1)\) is the sum of the explicit bounds in Q7.4–Q7.5, with fixed axis data. On \([e^{-8},e^{-5}]\), the same bound controls the fields, their logarithmic radial derivatives and the input moment histories. This follows by differentiating the fixed \(\rho\) in Q7.6; its derivative norms do not involve the small activation widths.

Q8. A fixed cone tolerance and the exact five-bump solution

The correction is a finite nonlinear construction on a fixed radial patch. Its tolerance is selected using the outer field. The cone calculation retains the factor \(X_R\), while the exact row map proves that the solved equations cancel the original moments.

Let \(\mathcal R=[e^{-8},e^{-5}]\times[-1,1]\). The ideal functions \(E_0>0\) and \(Q_{s,0}>1\) have positive minima there by O5.2; \(N_{s,0}\) is bounded by Q7.2 with Q7.5 and the fixed \(\Pi_0\). Define the actual finite constants

\[ Q_{\min}=\min_{\mathcal R}Q_{s,0}>0,\qquad e_*=\min_{\mathcal R}E_0>0,\qquad w_*=1+\max_{\mathcal R}\left|\frac{N_{s,0}}{E_0Q_{s,0}}\right|. \tag{Q8.1} \]

The reference shear is \(a=.8,b_s=0\). Apply the explicit difference and reciprocal formulas P3.3–P3.5 to Q7.2 on the fixed rectangle. They give finite Lipschitz constants for \(Q_s,N_s\) in a prescribed \(C_\eta^k\) norm, using one additional parameter derivative of the field and moment inputs. The same product and reciprocal formulas applied to \(a=1-2xE_x/E\), \(b_s=2xU_x/E\) control the shears from the fields and their first logarithmic radial derivatives. A sufficiently small positive input tolerance, depending only on these fixed outer data, therefore ensures

\[ Q_s\ge Q_{\min}/2,\quad E\ge e_*/2,\quad |a-.8|\le.1,\quad \left|\frac{N_s}{EQ_s}\right|\le w_*, \qquad |b_s|\le\frac{.1}{1+w_*}. \tag{Q8.2} \]

The last bound retains the original decimal .1 in (B.36), page 156; this factor gives the quantitative cone margin in the next calculation.

The original cone coordinates then obey

\[ \begin{split} v_s=a+\frac{b_s^2}{a}&\le.9+\frac{.01}{.7}<1,\\ G:=Q_s-\frac{b_sN_s}{aE} &\ge\left(1-\frac{.1w_*}{.7(1+w_*)}\right)Q_s \ge\frac67Q_s\ge\frac{3Q_{\min}}7,\\ P_c&=\frac{X_Rx}{L}G. \end{split} \tag{Q8.3} \]

Thus \(X_R>14e^8/(3Q_{\min})\) makes \(P_c>2\) throughout \(\mathcal R\), since \(L\le1\). This proves the strict relaxed cone without making the tolerance shrink with \(X_R\).

For an actual moment correction, set \(a_0=e^{-6}\), \(b_0=e^{-5}\), \(c_j=a_0+j(b_0-a_0)/6\) for \(j=1,\ldots,5\), and \(\omega=(b_0-a_0)/20\). Use the explicit fixed positive bumps

\[ \beta_j(x)= \begin{cases} \exp[-1/(1-((x-c_j)/\omega)^2)],&|x-c_j|<\omega,\\ 0,&|x-c_j|\ge\omega. \end{cases} \tag{Q8.4} \]

Their supports are ordered, disjoint and strictly inside \((e^{-6},e^{-5})\). Put \(u=c_1^{\,\rm amp}(\eta)\beta_1+c_2^{\,\rm amp}(\eta)\beta_2\) and \(e=\sum_{j=3}^5c_j^{\,\rm amp}(\eta)\beta_j\). Here the superscript distinguishes the five coefficient functions from the fixed centers. The unperturbed fields on this patch already equal \(U_0=4\eta,E_0=P_*fx^{1/10}\). Replace them by \(U_0+u,E_0+e\).

The increments of the original five moments, over this whole patch, are exactly

\[ \begin{split} \delta M&=X_R\int u\,dx,& \delta I&=\sqrt2X_R^{3/2}\int\sqrt x\,e\,dx,\\ \delta J&=\sqrt2X_R^{3/2}\int\sqrt x\,(4\eta e+E_0u+ue)\,dx,\\ \delta S&=X_R\int(8\eta u+u^2-E_0e-e^2/2)\,dx,& \delta C_p&=\int(E_0e/x+e^2/(2x))\,dx. \end{split} \tag{Q8.5} \]

Let \(\Delta\mathbf m\) denote the original moment discrepancy accumulated before these bumps. Apply the exact invertible row map

\[ \mathscr L_\eta(\delta\mathbf m)= \left( \frac{\delta M}{X_R}, \frac{\delta J-4\eta\delta I}{\sqrt2X_R^{3/2}P_*f}, \frac{\delta I}{\sqrt2X_R^{3/2}}, -\frac{\delta S-8\eta\delta M}{X_RP_*f}, \frac{\delta C_p}{P_*f} \right). \tag{Q8.6} \]

Its inverse is P5.3 with \(\rho=X_R,u_c=4\eta,e_*=P_*,f_*=f\). Thus solving for target \(d_{\rm tar}=-\mathscr L_\eta(\Delta\mathbf m)\) is exactly equivalent to cancelling all original moments.

The transformed linear coefficient matrix has the two actual blocks

\[ B_U= \begin{pmatrix}\int\beta_1&\int\beta_2\\ \int x^{3/5}\beta_1&\int x^{3/5}\beta_2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad (B_E)_{ij}=\int x^{\alpha_i}\beta_{j+2}(x)\,dx, \quad(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)=(1/2,1/10,-9/10). \tag{Q8.7} \]

P4 proves invertibility for these ordered nonnegative bumps and distinct powers. The factors \(P_*f\) in Q8.6 are positive and their parameter derivatives and inverses are bounded by the outer data. The exact nonlinear part, with no dropped term, is

\[ \mathscr Q_\eta(c,c)= \left(0,\frac{\int\sqrt x\,ue\,dx}{P_*f},0, \frac{-\int u^2\,dx+\frac12\int e^2\,dx}{P_*f}, \frac{\int e^2/(2x)\,dx}{P_*f}\right). \tag{Q8.8} \]

For \(m=k+1\), let \(\nu_m\) be the operator norm of \(B^{-1}\) and \(q_m\) the bilinear norm of this quadratic map in \(C_\eta^m\), including the finite product-rule factors. Both are finite and independent of \(X_R,\mathsf C\). For

\[ 8\nu_m^2q_m\|d_{\rm tar}\|_m\le1, \qquad c_{n+1}=B^{-1}\bigl(d_{\rm tar}-\mathscr Q_\eta(c_n,c_n)\bigr),\quad c_0=0, \tag{Q8.9} \]

the estimates P5.6–P5.7 show that the iteration stays in the radius \(2\nu_m\|d_{\rm tar}\|_m\) ball and contracts by at most \(1/2\). It therefore converges to an actual solution of all five equations, with that norm bound. P5.8 supplies an invertible derivative in c and proves that this solution is smooth in \(\eta\), with finite derivatives of every fixed higher order. Only the selected finite norm must be small.

The same coefficient bound controls u, e, their first logarithmic radial derivatives and their partial moment integrals throughout the patch: each is a fixed finite sum or integral of the fixed bumps, with finite coefficient norms. Let \(K_{\rm patch}\) be the maximum of these finitely many operator bounds and their product-rule constants on the chosen small coefficient ball. Shrink the fixed discrepancy tolerance so that \(2K_{\rm patch}\nu_m\|d_{\rm tar}\|_m\) is below half the input tolerance of Q8.2, and so that Q8.9 holds. Require the preexisting error in Q7.8 to be below the other half. Both requirements involve only fixed outer-data constants. They guarantee Q8.2 throughout the restoration and every partial moment correction, not merely at its final endpoint.

At the right endpoint the five moment differences vanish identically as functions of \(\eta\). The bumps have compact interior supports, so the fields already agree with the ideal fields on a neighborhood of that endpoint. Continue with the actual outer family of O and H. The same \(\Pi_0\), the vanishing five moments, and P3.1–P3.4 prove exact equality thereafter of

\[ \Pi,\ V_0,\ Q_s,\ N_s,\ p_s,\ a,\ b_s,\ \mathcal T_0 \tag{Q8.10} \]

with their actual outer-profile values, including all their derivatives. In particular the heat exterior, exact zero outer stress, smooth terminal direction and all total-moment conditions survive. This completes Proposition B.8 by an actual nonlinear moment solve.

Q9. Compatible choices and the precise completed component

The earlier estimates now give one compatible sequence of finite choices. Smallness is required in finitely many parameter norms needed by the construction. Smoothness supplies every other fixed derivative after those choices have been made.

Fix in advance the finite parameter derivative orders needed for the inequalities and finite moment solve, including the additional derivative in Q7.2. Keep the outer shape choices \(M_d,T_d,P_*,\lambda,h\) of O and H. Their constructed family has the same analytic \(\Pi_0\) for every sufficiently large \(X_R\); the heat compensation has zero pressure increment and preserves that datum.

First fix the restoration and bump functions Q7.6 and Q8.4. The compact ideal rectangle in Q8.1 then fixes the positive cone and moment-solve tolerances independently of \(X_R\). Choose \(j_0>0\), at most .05, so the contribution of the constant \(U_*-4\eta=j_0\) to Q7.8 is smaller than a chosen fraction of that tolerance. Then choose \(\delta_*,\sigma_*\) as in J0, and \(\Lambda\) large enough for J, Q1, the gradient absorptions, and \(C_k^{\rm nat}/\Lambda\) in Q5.4 to satisfy their finite inequalities. These constants are determined after \(j_0\), so small \(\sigma_*\) causes no circular choice.

The uniform reference bounds and Q5.3 now fix all required \(\mathcal B_k\), hence a positive \(T_{\rm sh}\) and \(X_{\rm sep}\), before the amplitude. Choose a finite \(\mathsf C\) large enough for the analytic construction, Q1.5 and Q1.9, and for all the following:

\[ \begin{gathered} X_R=X_i(\mathsf C P_*)^{10}> \max\left(X_R^{\rm outer},\,\frac{14e^8}{3Q_{\min}}\right),\qquad x_{\rm sep}<e^{-8},\\ \text{the finite Q7.4–Q7.5 moment errors are below the fixed tolerance.} \end{gathered} \tag{Q9.1} \]

Here \(X_R^{\rm outer}\) is the finite threshold already obtained for the actual O–H family. The quantities required to decay in Q9.1 are explicit positive powers of \(\mathsf C^{-1}\), with constants fixed before \(\mathsf C\), so such a finite choice exists. The initial-segment bounds hold uniformly over the allowed subsequent width family by Q5.3–Q5.4; selecting smaller widths does not undo Q9.1.

With this fixed \(\mathsf C,\Lambda\), choose \(\kappa_0\), then \(t_1\), then the finite final transition widths as in Q2 and Q4. Make their additional contribution in Q5.4, Q4.4 and Q7.8 as small as the remaining fractions of the fixed tolerances require. Positivity and the reference comparisons hold for the entire smaller-width family, so decreasing a width preserves the earlier estimates. The strict inequalities before the matching patch use finite constants that may depend on \(\mathsf C,\Lambda\); their widths are chosen after those constants. The matching tolerance uses only the fixed outer data and therefore does not conflict with this order. Finally solve Q8.9. Higher derivatives exist by smoothness and the finite-dimensional inverse argument, without infinitely many simultaneous smallness requirements.

This realizes the original order (B.40):

\[ \begin{aligned} M_d,T_d,P_*,\lambda,h &\ \longrightarrow\ \text{fixed matching tolerance},j_0\\ &\ \longrightarrow\ \delta_*,\sigma_*,\Lambda\\ &\ \longrightarrow\ (\mathcal B_k),T_{\rm sh}\\ &\ \longrightarrow\ \mathsf C,X_R\\ &\ \longrightarrow\ \kappa_0,t_1,\text{final widths}. \end{aligned} \tag{Q9.2} \]

The radial frequency for the later shear modification has not yet been chosen.

The constructed profile is smooth through the Cartesian axis by J4 and unchanged on its reserved analytic rectangle. E is positive for \(X>0\). The leading stress is zero through \(X_0\), has the exact inner flat factor and smooth nonzero limiting direction of Q3, and satisfies the admissible cone on a positive inner collar. It satisfies the strict relaxed cone thereafter through the matching point \(\log(X/X_R)=-5\). All five original radial moments, the pressure and all exterior fields match exactly there, so the already established outer-profile and heat-exterior properties remain true. The stress is nonzero between its two endpoints: throughout a strict relaxed region \(v_s<\mathcal U(P_c,J_c)\le P_c\), so its parallel component is \(F(P_c-v_s)>0\); the inner and outer collars have their proved positive direction bounds. These statements establish Lemma B.4, Proposition B.5, Corollary B.6, Lemma B.7, Proposition B.8 and Corollary B.10, with the parameter ordering of Remark B.9.

Q10. Five worked exercises

Exercise 1. Compute the coefficient after division by the flat factor

Give the exact endpoint value of the smooth coefficient in Q3.2. Apply it to both field differences in Q2.2, retaining the transition width.

Solution. Put \(c=t_1^2>0\). For every fixed nonnegative integer \(m\) and smooth \(b\), Q3.2 writes

\[ \frac{\int_0^y e_a(v)v^m b(v,\eta)\,dv}{e_a(y)y^{m+3}} =\frac1{2g_a(y)}\int_0^\infty e^{-cw}(1+y^2w)^{-(m+3)/2} g_a\!\left(\frac y{\sqrt{1+y^2w}}\right) b\!\left(\frac y{\sqrt{1+y^2w}},\eta\right)\,dw. \tag{Q10.1} \]

For each fixed mixed derivative, the integrand is bounded by \(e^{-cw}\) times a polynomial in \(w\), on a sufficiently small closed collar. This is integrable because the chosen \(c\) is positive. Differentiation under the integral proves a smooth extension to zero. Since \(g_a(0)>0\) and \(\int_0^\infty e^{-cw}\,dw=1/c\), its endpoint value is exactly

\[ \left.\frac{\int_0^y e_a(v)v^m b(v,\eta)\,dv} {e_a(y)y^{m+3}}\right|_{y=0} =\frac{b(0,\eta)}{2t_1^2}. \tag{Q10.2} \]

The quotient notation at zero denotes this proved smooth extension.

Write \(p_e=p_{1,\rm r}(X_0,\eta)\) and \(n_e=n_{s,\rm r}(X_0,\eta)\). In the first activation interval the reference is the natural axis solution. Applying Q10.2 with \(m=0\) to the two exact integrals Q2.2 gives

\[ \begin{split} \log\phi-\log\phi_{\rm r}&=e_a y^3 A_\phi(y,\eta), &A_\phi(0,\eta)&=\frac{p_e}{4t_1^2},\\ U-U_{\rm r}&=e_a y^3 A_U(y,\eta), &A_U(0,\eta)&=\frac{X_0n_e}{4t_1^2}. \end{split}\tag{Q10.3} \]

Both coefficients are smooth through zero, including all fixed mixed derivatives. The original \(X_0\) comes from \(X=X_0e^y\) in the axial integrand. The angular coefficient is strictly positive because \(p_e>0\). These formulas retain the width dependence rather than claiming uniform radial bounds as \(t_1\) shrinks.

Exercise 2. Find the leading differences of all five original moments

Compare the activated field with the reference on its first collar. Compute the exact coefficients of the differences of \(M,I,J,S,C_p\) after division by \(e_a y^6\).

Solution. All moment differences vanish before \(X_0\). At the endpoint set

\[ U_e=U_{\rm r}(X_0,\eta),\quad E_e=E_{\rm r}(X_0,\eta),\quad H_e=\sqrt{2X_0}\,E_e=\frac{2X_0\phi_{\rm r}(X_0,\eta)}{\mathsf C}. \tag{Q10.4} \]

Each quantity is the actual endpoint value, not its leading approximation at the axis. For fixed \(X\), \(E/E_{\rm r}=H/H_{\rm r}=\exp(\log\phi-\log\phi_{\rm r})\). Q10.3 and the exact integral formula for the exponential give

\[ \left.\frac{\Delta E}{e_a y^3}\right|_0 =\frac{E_ep_e}{4c},\qquad \left.\frac{\Delta H}{e_a y^3}\right|_0 =\frac{H_ep_e}{4c},\qquad c=t_1^2. \tag{Q10.5} \]

Products of two field differences have zero coefficient at this order. Thus the endpoint coefficients of the original moment integrands are

\[ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{integrand difference}& \left.\text{integrand difference}/(e_a y^3)\right|_0\\ \hline \Delta U&X_0n_e/(4c)\\ \Delta H&H_ep_e/(4c)\\ \Delta(UH)&H_e(U_ep_e+X_0n_e)/(4c)\\ \Delta(U^2-E^2/2)&(2U_eX_0n_e-E_e^2p_e)/(4c) \end{array} \tag{Q10.6} \]

The first four moments use \(dX=X_0e^y\,dy\), so their coefficients acquire another factor \(X_0/(2c)\) under the integration rule Q10.2 with \(m=3\). For the fifth moment,

\[ \Delta C_p =\int_0^y\frac{E(v,\eta)^2-E_{\rm r}(v,\eta)^2}{2}\,dv. \]

Here \(dX/X=dy\); there is no additional \(X_0\) factor. The coefficient of its integrand divided by \(e_a y^3\) is \(E_e^2p_e/(4c)\). We therefore obtain the full vector

\[ \left. \frac{(\Delta M,\Delta I,\Delta J,\Delta S,\Delta C_p)}{e_a y^6} \right|_0 =\frac1{8t_1^4} \begin{pmatrix} X_0^2n_e\\ X_0H_ep_e\\ X_0H_e(U_ep_e+X_0n_e)\\ X_0(2U_eX_0n_e-E_e^2p_e)\\ E_e^2p_e \end{pmatrix}^{\!T}. \tag{Q10.7} \]

The displayed row and column notation specifies the same five ordered components. Every quotient has a smooth extension: its integrand lies in \(e_a y^3C^\infty\), and Q10.1 proves the next integration step in all fixed derivatives. The common datum \(\Pi_0\) gives \(\Delta\Pi=\Delta C_p\). In particular,

\[ \Delta\Pi=e_a y^6 B_\Pi(y,\eta),\qquad B_\Pi(0,\eta)=\frac{E_e^2p_e}{8t_1^4}>0. \tag{Q10.8} \]

This positive difference is local to the first activation collar. The later five-bump correction cancels the complete accumulated pressure moment at the matching point; no intermediate equality of pressure was assumed.

Exercise 3. Restore the original scale in the moment-error estimates

Determine the amplitude powers in Q7.4–Q7.5 and in the corresponding original moment discrepancies. Show how a finite amplitude achieves the fixed tolerance.

Solution. With all preceding shape data fixed, put

\[ \alpha=X_iP_*^{10},\qquad d_{\rm sep}=e^{T_{\rm sh}}P_*^{-10}. \]

These are the exact constants in

\[ X_R=\alpha\mathsf C^{10},\qquad x_{\rm sep}=d_{\rm sep}\mathsf C^{-10},\qquad X_Rx_{\rm sep}=X_ie^{T_{\rm sh}}. \tag{Q10.9} \]

Let \(\Delta\widehat{\mathbf m}\) compare the actual and ideal moments at this endpoint. Q7.4 gives orders \(\mathsf C^{-10}\) for \(\widehat M,\widehat S\), \(\mathsf C^{-16}\) for \(\widehat I,\widehat J\), and \(\mathsf C^{-2}\) for \(\widehat C_p\). For the ideal moments Q7.5 gives the same orders, with the angular term of \(\widehat S_0\) carrying the still smaller factor \(\mathsf C^{-12}\). In particular its pressure term is exactly

\[ \widehat C_{p,0}(x_{\rm sep}) =\frac52 f^2 e^{T_{\rm sh}/5}\mathsf C^{-2}. \tag{Q10.10} \]

Triangle inequalities and the finite product-rule sums prove, in every selected parameter norm, finite bounds

\[ \begin{split} \|\Delta\widehat M\|_k+\|\Delta\widehat S\|_k&\le K_{MS,k}\mathsf C^{-10},\\ \|\Delta\widehat I\|_k+\|\Delta\widehat J\|_k&\le K_{IJ,k}\mathsf C^{-16},\\ \|\Delta\widehat C_p\|_k&\le K_{p,k}\mathsf C^{-2}. \end{split}\tag{Q10.11} \]

The constants retain the fixed \(d_{\rm sep},P_*,f,X_i\), the original inner-profile bounds and all their required derivatives. They are independent of subsequent amplitude and smaller transition widths. For a desired total error \(\varepsilon>0\), the finite choice

\[ \mathsf C\ge \max\left\{ 1,\left(\frac{3K_{MS,k}}\varepsilon\right)^{1/10}, \left(\frac{3K_{IJ,k}}\varepsilon\right)^{1/16}, \left(\frac{3K_{p,k}}\varepsilon\right)^{1/2} \right\} \tag{Q10.12} \]

makes the sum of the five displayed norms at most \(\varepsilon\). Take the maximum with the other finite thresholds in Q9.1.

Restoring the original quantities by Q7.1 gives

\[ \begin{split} \|\Delta M\|_k+\|\Delta S\|_k&\le\alpha K_{MS,k},\\ \|\Delta I\|_k+\|\Delta J\|_k&\le\alpha^{3/2}K_{IJ,k}\mathsf C^{-1},\\ \|\Delta C_p\|_k&\le K_{p,k}\mathsf C^{-2}. \end{split}\tag{Q10.13} \]

The argument therefore does not claim that the unscaled \(M,S\) discrepancies tend to zero. The exact invertible row map Q8.6 uses their retained \(X_R\) factors and converts the proved small quantities into the actual five-equation target. Its inverse then cancels the original discrepancies exactly. The remaining axial restoration error is controlled separately by \(G_i-4\eta\), with the order of choices in Q9.

Exercise 4. Use the disjoint supports in the exact nonlinear correction

Show that the two axial bump coefficients can be solved exactly before the three angular coefficients. Retain the full nonlinear terms and prove an actual reduced solve.

Solution. Use the fixed bumps Q8.4 and write their coefficient vectors as

\[ \mathbf a=(a_1,a_2),\qquad \mathbf b=(b_1,b_2,b_3),\qquad u=a_1\beta_1+a_2\beta_2,\quad e=\sum_{j=1}^3b_j\beta_{j+2}. \]

All five supports are disjoint. Consequently \(ue=0\) pointwise, and there are no cross terms in either square. Set

\[ A_i=\int\beta_i^2\,dx,\qquad B_j=\int\beta_{j+2}^2\,dx,\qquad D_j=\int x^{-1}\beta_{j+2}^2\,dx. \tag{Q10.14} \]

These constants are finite and positive, since the fixed supports lie inside \((e^{-6},e^{-5})\). The full quadratic remainder Q8.8 becomes exactly

\[ \left(0,0,0, \frac{-\sum_{i=1}^2A_i a_i^2+\frac12\sum_{j=1}^3B_j b_j^2}{P_*f}, \frac{\sum_{j=1}^3D_j b_j^2}{2P_*f}\right). \tag{Q10.15} \]

For the original transformed target \(d=(d_1,\ldots,d_5)=-\mathscr L_\eta(\Delta\mathbf m)\), the first two equations therefore give

\[ \mathbf a=B_U^{-1}(d_1,d_2)^T \tag{Q10.16} \]

exactly. Define

\[ \mathbf r=\left(d_3,\ d_4+\frac{\sum_iA_i a_i^2}{P_*f},\ d_5\right)^T,\qquad q_E(\mathbf b,\mathbf b)= \left(0,\frac{\sum_jB_jb_j^2}{2P_*f}, \frac{\sum_jD_jb_j^2}{2P_*f}\right)^T. \tag{Q10.17} \]

The remaining three equations are precisely \(B_E\mathbf b+q_E(\mathbf b,\mathbf b)=\mathbf r\). No original moment or quadratic term has been discarded.

For a selected \(C_\eta^m\) norm, let \(\nu_U,\nu_E\) be the norms of the two actual inverse matrices, let \(q_E^*\) bound the displayed bilinear map, and let \(\gamma_m\) bound \(\mathbf a\mapsto\sum_iA_i a_i^2/(P_*f)\) by \(\gamma_m\|\mathbf a\|_m^2\). The product rule and the fixed positive \(P_*f\) make these constants finite and independent of \(X_R,\mathsf C\). Fix the target tolerance \(\varepsilon\) small enough that

\[ \gamma_m\nu_U^2\varepsilon\le1,\qquad 16\nu_E^2q_E^*\varepsilon\le1. \tag{Q10.18} \]

Q7–Q9 achieve this fixed tolerance, together with the earlier cone tolerance, by their already proved finite choices. Then \(\|\mathbf a\|_m\le\nu_U\varepsilon\) and \(\|\mathbf r\|_m\le2\varepsilon\). On the radius \(2\nu_E\|\mathbf r\|_m\) ball, the iteration

\[ \mathbf b_{n+1}=B_E^{-1}\bigl(\mathbf r-q_E(\mathbf b_n,\mathbf b_n)\bigr), \qquad\mathbf b_0=0 \tag{Q10.19} \]

stays in that ball and has Lipschitz constant at most \(4\nu_E^2q_E^*\|\mathbf r\|_m\le1/2\). Indeed its quadratic contribution to the radius is at most half the linear radius, by the same inequality. The complete-space contraction argument supplies the actual angular coefficients. They obey \(\|\mathbf b\|_m\le4\nu_E\varepsilon\); decreasing the fixed tolerance also meets the partial-patch bounds used in Q8.

The derivative in \(\mathbf b\) is \(B_E+2q_E(\mathbf b,\cdot)\), whose inverse follows from a norm-convergent geometric series after multiplication by \(B_E^{-1}\). Smooth dependence on \(\eta\) follows by differentiating these three finite equations and using that inverse at each fixed order. Substitution in Q8.5–Q8.6 proves exact cancellation of all five original moments. The axial coefficients are independent of the angular targets \(d_3,d_4,d_5\); their exact dependence is Q10.16. This is a property of the specified disjoint supports, not an approximation that neglects a mixed term.

Exercise 5. Determine which analyticity survives stress activation

Prove that the angular profile has the same full radial Taylor data as the natural solution at \(X_0\), yet is not real analytic in \(X\) there. Reconcile this with the common parameter-analytic collar and its exact physical coordinates.

Solution. On \(X\le X_0\), the actual and natural profiles agree. On the first activation interval, Q10.3 gives

\[ \log\phi-\log\phi_{\rm nat}=e_a y^3A_\phi,\qquad A_\phi(0,\eta)=p_e/(4t_1^2)>0. \tag{Q10.20} \]

Since \(e_a\) vanishes to infinite order and \(X=X_0e^y\) is an analytic invertible coordinate near \(y=0\), the difference and every fixed mixed derivative vanish at \(X_0\). Exponentiation proves the same equality of all derivatives for \(\phi\) and \(E\).

For every fixed real \(\eta\), Q2.2 also gives

\[ \log\phi-\log\phi_{\rm nat} =\frac12\int_0^y e_a(v)p_{1,\rm r}(X_0e^v,\eta)\,dv>0 \quad(0<y<t_1). \tag{Q10.21} \]

Every integrand is positive there. The natural profile is analytic in \(X\) on a neighborhood of \(X_0\), supplied by J. If the activated \(\phi\) were analytic there as well, the equality of all Taylor coefficients would force equality on a neighborhood, contradicting Q10.21. Thus \(\phi\), and also \(E=\sqrt{2X}\phi/\mathsf C\), are smooth but not real analytic in \(X\) at \(X_0\). This statement concerns the constructed leading profile.

For parameter analyticity, Q2.1 integrates holomorphic parameter coefficients against radial-only cutoffs. Exponentiation, the nonvanishing denominators and the forward integrals Q5.1 preserve one common parameter neighborhood. Every fixed radial derivative remains holomorphic there: differentiating the cutoff changes a finite radial coefficient without changing that parameter domain. These are the exact maps that produce the regularity stated in Corollary B.6.

For the original viscosity \(\nu>0\), the physical comparison is

\[ X_\nu=\frac{r_\nu^2}{2\nu q_\nu},\qquad \eta_\nu=\frac{z_\nu}{\sqrt\nu\,q_\nu^D},\qquad q_\nu-\frac{z_\nu^2}{\nu}q_\nu^{2h}=1-t. \tag{Q10.22} \]

It follows from \(x_\nu=\sqrt\nu\,x\), with the original time and parameter data retained. For fixed \(z_\nu,t<1\), the activation edge and protected collar have the exact radii

\[ r_{\nu,0}=\sqrt{2\nu q_\nu X_0},\qquad 0\le r_\nu\le\sqrt{2\nu q_\nu X_0e^{t_c}}. \tag{Q10.23} \]

The radial coordinate map is analytically invertible near the positive edge radius, so the failure of radial analyticity persists under this map. The collar remains smooth and parameter analytic as proved. Every subsequent modification is supported strictly outside it. The forward integrals for pressure and radial velocity use only smaller radii, so those later modifications leave all collar fields and derivatives exactly unchanged. The final matching equations separately preserve the exterior by Q8.10.

What the connected field supplies next

The actual connection now preserves the analytic inner rectangle, activates a smooth nonzero stress with its exact limiting direction, continues in the strict relaxed cone, and joins the entire outer field with exactly the same pressure and all five original moments. The finite choices and all original radial factors are part of the proof.

The next construction is the admissible-shear realization V0–V7. It preserves the protected collars and exact moments while enforcing the stronger shear condition throughout the intervening annulus. The admissible-shear lesson, V0–V8, gives the construction and its exercises. The base construction Z0–Z8 then treats the higher-order physical residual.

The final theorem lesson, EC0–EC5, uses these constructions to prove Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 10.6.

Realizing the admissible shear and completing the leading profile

NS-BLOWUP N2.5. The joined field now has the required axis, pressure and exterior. A part of its connecting interval still has shear below the threshold required by the later viscous waves. We construct one smooth field that satisfies the stronger cone everywhere, then prove all six conclusions of the leading-profile theorem.

The construction changes radial derivatives by an amount of order one while changing field values by an amount of order \(N^{-1}\). Here \(N\) is one sufficiently large, finite integer. A periodic family of admissible shears has exactly the original mean. Its periodic primitives produce the actual field. Five subsequent corrections restore the original cumulative moments exactly, so the axis and exterior retain their entire previous constructions.

The stress and moment lesson, P0–P7, supplies the full operators and nonlinear moment inverse. The outer lesson, O0–H7, supplies the four reserved patches, heat field and outer stress factor. The axis lesson, J0–J8, and joining lesson, Q0–Q10, supply the regular axis, exact connection and inner stress factor. All four are included in the cumulative reader.

The source is OpenAI, Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, Theorem 4.6, pages 32–34, the cone formulas on pages 31 and 38, and Appendix C, pages 157–165, (C.1)–(C.19). This is independent teaching and editorial mathematics; the diplomatic transcription continues to reproduce what OpenAI wrote. SOURCES.json records the source identity and mathematical locators.

Figure. The upper panels show the exact averaging map and actual field formulas. The radial diagram records order, with both endpoint collars protected. The lower panel displays the leading endpoint pressure-moment change proved in Exercise 2 and cancelled by the exact correction in Exercise 3. It shows no sampled fluid flow.

Why a small field change can supply the required shear

The shear uses a radial derivative; the five moments use field values. Evaluating a periodic primitive at \(N\log X\) and dividing its amplitude by \(N\) makes the field difference small while leaving the derivative of its fast phase at order one. The two shear components must be integrated with their exact different factors. In particular, changing the angular field exponentially produces an exponential denominator in the axial shear.

The periodic family must have the exact prescribed mean and depend smoothly on both profile coordinates, even where the axial stress coefficient vanishes. V1–V2 prove those properties. V3 constructs the finite-frequency field and controls every quantity needed by the cone. V4 cancels the five nonlinear moment differences. V5–V7 then carry the two endpoint factorizations through all six conclusions of Theorem 4.6.

The exercises give exact formulas at zero axial stress, sharper moment and correction estimates, explicit endpoint derivative powers and the original physical phase at every viscosity. These are proved consequences of the same construction. They do not allege an error in the source's sufficient bounds.

V0. The actual input and the interval of modification

Keep the actual joined input fixed. The radial interval below contains every place that still needs the stronger cone, and the following moment patch is already reserved by the outer construction.

Fix the entire profile constructed in Q, including its finite parameters, common axis pressure and exact exterior matching. Keep

\[ A=1/2+h,\quad D=1/2-h,\quad d=1-\eta^2,\quad L=1-2h\eta^2, \quad 0<h<1/100,\quad -1\le\eta\le1. \tag{V0.1} \]

Its inner stress endpoint is \(X_a=X_0=4/\Lambda\); its outer stress endpoint \(X_b\) is the endpoint of the actual H exterior. These are not the local continuation radius 100. The original functions are

\[ \begin{gathered} F=E/\sqrt{2X},\quad H=\sqrt{2X}E,\quad a=1-2X\partial_X\log E,\quad b_s=2XU_X/E,\\ p_s=\frac X L(Q_s,N_s/E),\quad \mathcal T_0=F[p_s-(a,-b_s)]. \end{gathered} \tag{V0.2} \]

All five cumulative integrals \(\mathbf m=(M,I,J,S,C_p)\), their integration constants and \(\Pi=\Pi_0+C_p\) remain those of P2. The input has \(a>0\), the strict relaxed cone on \((X_a,X_b)\), an admissible inner collar and the admissible outer portion beginning in the intermediate power-law interval. These properties were derived in Q9, O8 and H5, rather than assumed for a nonexistent profile.

Choose \(X_{\rm an}\) strictly inside the analytic admissible inner collar of Q5. Then choose \(X_-\) beyond \(X_{\rm an}\), still inside that collar, and \(X_+\) inside the admissible intermediate power-law interval, before the first reserved patch. This is possible by the positive lengths established in Q5 and O0.4. Set \(\mathcal I=[X_-,X_+]\). The compact interval contains every point where the input need not be admissible; the input is admissible near both endpoints. Retain shorter endpoint collars outside its support. The first reserved patch will restore moments; the third and fourth remain available for later positive-order and mean corrections. The second was already used for the heat compensation, which will be preserved exactly.

For any \(a>0,b\in\mathbb R,p\in\mathbb R^2\), keep the original gap map

\[ \begin{gathered} v=a+b^2/a,\quad c=p_1-(b/a)p_2,\quad j=p_2+(b/a)p_1,\\ \Psi(a,b,p)=(a,v-2,c-v,2(c-v)^2-(v-2)j^2). \end{gathered} \tag{V0.3} \]

It is smooth on its stated domain. P6 proves that positivity of all four components is exactly the admissible cone. With \(t_s=-b_s/a\), its c and j are \(P_c(t_s)\) and \(J_c(t_s)\), where

\[ P_c(t)=p_{s,1}+p_{s,2}t,\qquad J_c(t)=p_{s,2}-p_{s,1}t. \tag{V0.4} \]

V1. A smooth variance family, including zero axial stress

Vary the ratio of the two shear components while keeping its average fixed. The exponential distribution makes the stress projection remain above two. Its variance can reach every finite positive target, including when the axial stress coefficient is zero.

On the compact rectangle \(\mathcal I\times[-1,1]\), choose \(0<d_0<\tfrac12\min(P_c(t_s)-2)\). This minimum is positive by the already constructed strict relaxed cone. With the separate auxiliary angle \(\theta'\), define

\[ M_e(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{z\sin\theta'}\,d\theta',\qquad t(\theta';\mu)=t_s+d_0\frac{e^{\mu p\sin\theta'}/M_e(\mu p)-1}{p}, \quad p=p_{s,2},\quad \mu\ge0. \tag{V1.1} \]

This auxiliary average is not the physical angular or wave-torus average. Differentiation under the integral on compact z intervals proves smoothness, and \(M_e>0\). The change \(\theta'\mapsto\theta'+\pi\) proves evenness. The numerator in the quotient vanishes at p=0. Writing it as \(p\int_0^1\partial_pG(up)du\) proves a joint smooth extension in \((\theta',\mu,p)\), with value \(t=t_s+d_0\mu\sin\theta'\) at zero. Direct integration gives

\[ \langle t\rangle=t_s,\qquad P_c(t)=P_c(t_s)+d_0[e^{\mu p\sin\theta'}/M_e(\mu p)-1]>P_c(t_s)-d_0>2, \tag{V1.2} \]

and the exact variance

\[ V(\mu,p)=\langle(t-t_s)^2\rangle =\frac{d_0^2}{p^2}\left[\frac{M_e(2\mu p)}{M_e(\mu p)^2}-1\right], \qquad V(\mu,0)=d_0^2\mu^2/2. \tag{V1.3} \]

The integral of the squared smoothly extended quotient is also a direct proof of smoothness at p=0.

For \(g=\log M_e\), differentiating the quotient for \(g'\) gives exactly the variance of \(\sin\theta'\) under density \(e^{z\sin\theta'}/(2\pi M_e(z))\). It is strictly positive: the density is positive everywhere and \(\sin\theta'\) is not constant on any full-measure set. Thus \(g''>0\). For p nonzero and \(\mu>0\),

\[ \partial_\mu[g(2\mu p)-2g(\mu p)] =2p[g'(2\mu p)-g'(\mu p)]>0. \tag{V1.4} \]

For negative p both factors in brackets and outside are negative; for positive p both are positive. This proves strict increase of V for \(\mu>0\); the p=0 formula does so there as well.

The unbounded range can be proved with explicit analytic estimates. For \(|u|\le\pi\), \(1-u^2/2\le\cos u\le1-2u^2/\pi^2\). The lower bound follows by integrating \(1-\cos u\le u^2/2\); the upper follows from \(\sin(|u|/2)\ge |u|/\pi\), the chord inequality for the concave sine on \([0,\pi/2]\), in \(1-\cos u=2\sin^2(u/2)\). Centering the angle at its maximum and integrating over \(|u|\le z^{-1/2}\) for the lower bound, and over the whole real Gaussian for the upper, yields for \(z\ge1\)

\[ \frac{e^{-1/2}}\pi\frac{e^z}{\sqrt z} \le M_e(z)\le\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2\sqrt2}\frac{e^z}{\sqrt z}. \tag{V1.5} \]

Evenness supplies the same bounds for negative z with \(|z|\). Consequently the ratio in V1.3 is bounded below by a positive constant times \(\sqrt{|\mu p|}\) when \(|\mu p|\ge1\). For each fixed nonzero p this tends to infinity as \(\mu\to\infty\); for p=0 use V1.3. Given any finite target, continuity gives for each p an open neighborhood and one finite \(\mu_p\) exceeding the target there. A finite subcover of the compact p range and monotonicity give one finite \(\mu_{\max}\) such that

\[ V(\mu_{\max},p)>3/a_{\min},\qquad a_{\min}=\min_{\mathcal I\times[-1,1]}a>0. \tag{V1.6} \]

No uniform large-z estimate near p=0 was assumed in this compactness step.

The original upper cone bound is

\[ \mathcal U(P,J)=P+J^2/4-|J|\sqrt{(P-2)/2+J^2/16}. \tag{V1.7} \]

P6 proves \(2<\mathcal U(P,J)\le P\) for P>2, including J=0. Continuity suffices here; no derivative of \(|J|\) is taken. The entire compact family in V1.1 with \(0\le\mu\le\mu_{\max}\) has P>2 by V1.2. Choose \(0<\delta_L<1\) below the minimum of \(\mathcal U-2\) on that family and below the positive minimum of \(v_s-2\) on fixed smaller radial boundary neighborhoods. The order is \(d_0,\mu_{\max},\delta_L\).

V2. The variance choice and the exact prescribed mean

Choose the variance only where the original shear is too small. Then change the speed with which the loop is traversed. The exact Jacobian gives both required component averages.

Using the smooth step of O0.1, take \(\zeta_L(w)=1-\sigma((w-2-\delta_L/8)/(\delta_L/8))\). It lies in [0,1], is one below \(2+\delta_L/8\) and zero above \(2+\delta_L/4\). Set exactly

\[ v_*=2+\delta_L/2,\qquad \rho=\zeta_L(v_s)^2(v_*-v_s),\qquad v=v_s+\rho. \tag{V2.1} \]

Define \(\rho=0\) where the cutoff vanishes. On its possible nonzero support, \(v_*-v_s\ge\delta_L/4\); hence \(\sqrt\rho=\zeta_L(v_s)\sqrt{v_*-v_s}\), extended by zero, is smooth. Since \(v_s=a+b_s^2/a>0\) and \(v_*<5/2\), one has \(0\le\rho<3\). There is a unique \(0\le\mu<\mu_{\max}\) solving

\[ V(\mu,p)=\rho/a. \tag{V2.2} \]

Existence follows from V1.6 and the intermediate value theorem; strict monotonicity proves uniqueness.

Here is the smooth dependence at zero, which the ordinary derivative of V alone would not justify. Taylor expansion under the defining integral gives \(M_e(z)=1+z^2/4+O(z^4)\). Thus

\[ \frac{M_e(2z)}{M_e(z)^2}-1=z^2F_e(z),\quad F_e(0)=1/2, \qquad V(\mu,p)=d_0^2\mu^2F_e(\mu p), \tag{V2.3} \]

where \(F_e\) is smooth and even near zero. This is an exact factorization, obtained by the twice-integrated Taylor remainder; the displayed value follows from the second derivative. In a fixed neighborhood it is positive. Therefore the signed square root \(d_0\mu\sqrt{F_e(\mu p)}\) is smooth, odd in \(\mu\), and has derivative \(d_0/\sqrt2\) at zero. Its implicit equation with smooth right side \(\sqrt\rho/\sqrt a\) gives a unique smooth \(\mu\) through zero. Away from zero use the strictly positive derivative V1.4. Local solutions agree by uniqueness, including at \(\eta=\pm1\), by smooth local extension or one-sided implicit differentiation. No cusp in \(\sqrt\rho\) is introduced.

If \(v_s\le2+\delta_L/8\), then v=v_*>2. In the transition zone, \(2<v_s\le v\le v_*\). Off the cutoff, v=v_s>2 and \(\mu=0\). Thus where the loop changes, \(2<v\le2+\delta_L/2<\mathcal U(P_c(t),J_c(t))\). Where it does not change, the original relaxed inequality and v_s>2 give the same conclusion. Every vector \(v(1,t)/(1+t^2)\) is therefore admissible.

To obtain the original average, define the lift

\[ \varphi(\theta')=\int_0^{\theta'}\frac{a(1+t(s)^2)}{2\pi v}\,ds, \qquad (a_L,-b_L)(\varphi)=\frac{v(1,t(\theta'))}{1+t(\theta')^2}. \tag{V2.4} \]

V1.2–V1.3 and V2.2 give \(a\langle1+t^2\rangle=a(1+t_s^2)+aV=v_s+\rho=v\). Consequently the lift increases by exactly one as \(\theta'\) increases by \(2\pi\). Its derivative is bounded below by a positive constant on the compact family, so it has a smooth parameter-dependent inverse. For completeness, the derivative of the inverse is \((\partial_{\theta'}\varphi)^{-1}\), while any parameter derivative is \(-\varphi_{\rm parameter}/\varphi_{\theta'}\); iterating these identities proves all mixed derivative bounds. The exact two averages are

\[ \int_0^1a_L\,d\varphi=a,\qquad \int_0^1(-b_L)\,d\varphi=a\langle t\rangle=at_s=-b_s. \tag{V2.5} \]

They follow by substituting the full Jacobian in V2.4. On the radial boundary neighborhoods \(\zeta_L=0\), so \(\mu=0,t=t_s,v=v_s\), the lift is \(\theta'/(2\pi)\), and the loop equals the original shear. Positivity of all four components of \(\Psi(a_L,b_L,p_s)\) and compactness yield a common minimum \(\kappa_L>0\). The fixed neighborhoods yield \(\delta_\partial>0\). This establishes every assertion of Lemma C.1, with the exact period-one mean and boundary equalities.

V3. The actual radial modulation and its moment estimates

Integrate the two mean-zero shear differences in the periodic variable, then insert their primitives into the original fields. Differentiate the actual formulas before estimating; this retains the factors needed by the cone.

For any smooth period-one zero-mean f, the unique zero-mean primitive is

\[ (\mathcal P f)(\varphi)=\int_0^\varphi f(s)ds- \int_0^1\int_0^u f(s)ds\,du. \tag{V3.1} \]

Its periodicity follows from \(\int_0^1f=0\), its derivative is f, and its mean is zero by construction. A constant is the only difference between primitives, proving uniqueness. Every fixed parameter derivative commutes with these bounded integrals. Define

\[ \partial_\varphi\mathcal A=-\tfrac12(a_L-a),\qquad \partial_\varphi\mathcal B=\tfrac12E(b_L-b_s),\qquad \langle\mathcal A\rangle_\varphi=\langle\mathcal B\rangle_\varphi=0. \tag{V3.2} \]

V2.5 proves compatibility. Both primitives vanish identically on the radial boundary neighborhoods, so extension by zero is smooth. For an integer N≥1 prescribe the actual fields

\[ E_N=E\exp[\mathcal A(X,\eta,N\log X)/N],\qquad U_N=U+\mathcal B(X,\eta,N\log X)/N. \tag{V3.3} \]

Positivity of E_N and exact agreement outside \(\mathcal I\) follow immediately. Let \(\mathcal D_X=X\partial_X\) hold the independent \(\varphi\) fixed. Differentiation after substitution is \(\mathcal D_X+N\partial_\varphi\). Thus the original shears, with every amplitude factor, are exactly

\[ a_N=a_L-\frac{2\mathcal D_X\mathcal A}N,\qquad b_N=e^{-\mathcal A/N}\left(b_L+\frac{2\mathcal D_X\mathcal B}{NE}\right), \qquad \varphi=N\log X. \tag{V3.4} \]

In the second formula the numerator is \(2\mathcal D_XU+2\partial_\varphi\mathcal B+2\mathcal D_X\mathcal B/N=Eb_L+2\mathcal D_X\mathcal B/N\), and the denominator is \(Ee^{\mathcal A/N}\). This proves the exponential factor as well as both signs.

All coefficients and derivatives are bounded on the fixed compact radial range from \(X_-\) through the first reserved patch, with E and X bounded below. The phase is independent of \(\eta\). The identity \(e^z-1=z\int_0^1e^{sz}ds\), followed by parameter differentiation, proves for each fixed m

\[ \|E_N-E\|_{C^m_\eta}+\|U_N-U\|_{C^m_\eta} +\|a_N-a_L\|_{C^m_\eta}+\|b_N-b_L\|_{C^m_\eta} \le C_m/N. \tag{V3.5} \]

The norms include a radial supremum, and loop values are evaluated at the actual phase. Constants depend on the fixed loop and profile, never on N. Each radial differentiation of the composed primitives contributes at most one N, while the original perturbation has factor N^{-1}. Repeated product and chain differentiation therefore gives

\[ \|\partial_X^r\partial_\eta^m(E_N-E,U_N-U)\|_\infty \le C_{r,m}N^{r-1}\quad(r\ge1). \tag{V3.6} \]

Terms differentiating the exponential k times carry N^{-k} and at most N^r, with k≥1; hence they obey the same bound for N≥1. This is not smallness of radial derivatives.

Compute the actual moments from E_N,U_N, keeping the same \(\Pi_0\). For any field increments e,u, their integrand changes are exactly

\[ u,\quad \sqrt{2X}e,\quad \sqrt{2X}(Ue+Eu+ue),\quad 2Uu+u^2-Ee-e^2/2,\quad Ee/X+e^2/(2X), \tag{V3.7} \]

in the original order (M,I,J,S,C_p). All changes vanish before \(X_-\), so their denominators are bounded away from zero wherever integrated. V3.5 and product differentiation give \(O_m(N^{-1})\) bounds for all five partial integrals, uniformly through the correction interval. The same holds for \(\Pi_N-\Pi=C_{p,N}-C_p\). P2.5 and P3.4 then give

\[ \|\mathbf m_N-\mathbf m\|_{C^m_\eta} +\|\Pi_N-\Pi\|_{C^m_\eta}\le C_m/N,\qquad \|p_{s,N}-p_s\|_{C^m_\eta}\le C'_m/N. \tag{V3.8} \]

For the last estimate use the first bound through order m+1, positive E_N, and the full multiplier X/L. The multiplier is fixed, although possibly large. None of these formulas differentiates the oscillating fields radially.

There is a compact neighborhood of the loop values with a positive lower bound for a; the smooth gap map has a finite Lipschitz constant there. V3.4–V3.8 therefore preserve every gap by at least \(\kappa_L/2\) on \(\mathcal I\) for sufficiently large N. Between \(X_+\) and the reserved patch, fields and shears equal the input, while p_s differs by \(O(N^{-1})\). The input gap has a positive minimum on this compact interval, so the same choice, enlarged if necessary, preserves it. All frequency lower bounds are finite and are chosen after the entire input profile.

V4. Restoring the five original moments on the first reserved patch

The moment mismatch reaches a patch on which the fields still have their exact original power law. The full nonlinear five-moment map is invertible there, and its small solution preserves the cone throughout the patch.

Let the first patch be \((R_-,R_+)\), with its actual radii from O0.4. There the unchanged input is

\[ U=0,\qquad E=K(\eta)X^{-1/2-\lambda},\qquad K(\eta)=c_{\rm patch}(1+\eta^2)^{-1}>0. \tag{V4.1} \]

Fix five centers \(r_j=R_-+j(R_+-R_-)/6\) and width \(\omega=(R_+-R_-)/20\). Let \(\beta_j(X)=\exp[-1/(1-((X-r_j)/\omega)^2)]\) on \(|X-r_j|<\omega\), and zero otherwise. They are smooth, positive on their interiors, and have ordered disjoint compact supports inside the original patch. Put \(u=c_1\beta_1+c_2\beta_2\), \(e=\sum_{j=3}^5c_j\beta_j\), and add them to the fields after modulation.

At the patch entrance the fields themselves are exactly V4.1; the accumulated moment discrepancy is \(O_m(N^{-1})\). The correction map, in row order (M,J,I,S,C_p), has the full increments

\[ \left( \int u,\ \int\sqrt{2X}(Eu+ue),\ \int\sqrt{2X}e, \ \int(u^2-Ee-e^2/2),\ \int(Ee/X+e^2/(2X)) \right). \tag{V4.2} \]
