Every integral here is in dX over the patch. At zero coefficients its matrix B is block diagonal. Its U rows have weights \(1,\sqrt2KX^{-\lambda}\); its E rows have weights \(\sqrt2X^{1/2},-KX^{-1/2-\lambda},KX^{-3/2-\lambda}\). Removing these nonzero row factors for the purpose of the determinant, while retaining them in B and its inverse, gives the exact power lists

\[ (0,-\lambda),\qquad(1/2,-1/2-\lambda,-3/2-\lambda). \tag{V4.3} \]

The fixed positive \(\lambda\) makes both lists distinct. P4's determinant-integral proof applies to the specified bumps, so B is invertible on the closed parameter interval. Its inverse and every fixed parameter derivative are bounded. Its constants may depend on \(\lambda\), K and the original patch radii; no uniformity as \(\lambda\downarrow0\) is asserted or needed.

The exact quadratic remainder is

\[ \mathscr Q(c,c)=\left(0,\int\sqrt{2X}ue,0, \int(u^2-e^2/2),\int e^2/(2X)\right). \tag{V4.4} \]

Take target d to be minus the preexisting moment discrepancy in that same row order. With \(\nu_m\) the multiplication norm of B^{-1} and q_m the quadratic bilinear norm, including product-rule constants, the iteration

\[ c_{n+1}=B^{-1}(d-\mathscr Q(c_n,c_n)),\quad c_0=0, \qquad 8\nu_m^2q_m\|d\|_{C^m_\eta}\le1 \tag{V4.5} \]

is a contraction by P5.6–P5.8, provided also the same condition in C^0. Choose N so those finitely many inequalities hold. It yields smooth coefficients with the selected finite norm \(O_m(N^{-1})\), solving the original five equations exactly. All further fixed parameter derivatives exist by the invertible finite-dimensional derivative. They are also \(O_m(N^{-1})\) as N grows: differentiation of the equation gives B times the highest derivative plus terms containing c or a lower derivative of c, while every derivative of d is \(O_m(N^{-1})\) by V3.8. The inverse derivative is uniformly bounded for the small C^0 branch; induction proves the assertion. This requires no simultaneous smallness threshold for every m.

The fixed bumps bound the corrections and their first radial derivatives by a finite multiple of the selected coefficient norm. Partial moment increments obey the same bound, using V4.2 with the upper integration endpoint inside the patch. P3 therefore retains the \(O(N^{-1})\) p_s bound throughout that patch. Comparing these three finite bounds with the positive input E and the four positive input gap minima on its closed rectangle gives a further finite lower bound for N that preserves positivity and the cone everywhere, including within each bump. This comparison uses actual partial integrals, not only their endpoint values.

Let \(X_{\rm rep}=R_+\). The bumps vanish on neighborhoods of both boundaries. At its right endpoint,

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf m}(X_{\rm rep},\eta)=\mathbf m(X_{\rm rep},\eta),\qquad (\widetilde E,\widetilde U)=(E,U)\quad(X\ge X_{\rm rep}). \tag{V4.6} \]

The forward integrals propagate equality of all five moments, and the common \(\Pi_0\) gives equality of the complete pressure. P3 proves equality of \(V_0,Q_s,N_s,p_s\) and every parameter derivative there; field equality gives all radial derivatives and shears. This preserves the previously performed terminal compensation, heat exterior and outer endpoint. At the inner endpoint both modifications are supported later, and the same forward integration preserves the analytic rectangle and inner collar exactly. The two unused reserved patches are also unchanged. Fix one integer N satisfying the finite requirements before any physical q or later iteration stage is chosen. This proves Proposition C.2.

V5. Nonzero stress and the direction on the closed annulus

The stress vanishes at both radial edges. Divide by each proved scalar flat factor to extend its direction smoothly, then use the interior cone to obtain a uniform margin on the closed annulus.

Use E,U,Π now for the corrected fields. The leading stress vanishes on \([0,X_a]\) by J and Q3, and on \([X_b,\infty)\) by H4. These intervals are exactly preserved by V4.6 and the unchanged inner construction. In the open annulus admissibility gives \(P_c>v_s\), so \(\mathcal T_{0,\theta}+t_s\mathcal T_{0,z}=F(P_c-v_s)>0\). Thus the stress cannot vanish anywhere there.

Define \(n=\mathcal T_0/|\mathcal T_0|\) in the interior. At the inner edge Q3 supplies the exact factor

\[ \mathcal T_0=e^{-t_1^2/y_a^2}g_a(y_a)B_0(y_a,\eta),\quad y_a=\log(X/X_a),\quad g_a(0)>0,\quad B_0(0,\eta)=F(X_a,\eta)p_s(X_a,\eta)\ne0. \tag{V5.1} \]

Hence n extends smoothly there as \(B_0/|B_0|\). At \(X_a\), zero leading stress gives \(p_s=(a,-b_s)=a(1,t_s)\). The limiting direction is a positive multiple of this vector. Consequently \(n_z-t_sn_\theta=0\) and \(n_\theta+t_sn_z=\sqrt{1+t_s^2}>0\) there.

At the outer edge the exact H6 factors give

\[ \mathcal T_0=e^{-4/y_b^2}y_b^{-3}(b_\theta(y_b,\eta),y_b^6b_z(y_b,\eta)), \quad y_b=\log(X_b/X),\quad b_\theta(0,\eta)>0, \tag{V5.2} \]

and therefore

\[ n=\frac{(b_\theta,y_b^6b_z)}{\sqrt{b_\theta^2+y_b^{12}b_z^2}} \longrightarrow(1,0). \tag{V5.3} \]

This is smooth up to the closed edge, including \(\eta=\pm1\), and b_s=0 there because U=0 in the whole outer collar. F remains positive at both edges. At the inner edge a>0 and \(v_s-2>.2\) by J6; at the outer edge H5 gives \(a=v_s\ge2+h\). Interior admissibility and compactness now give positive lower bounds for F,a,v_s−2 on the full closed annulus.

In the interior, division by the actual nonzero stress gives

\[ u_n:=n_\theta+t_sn_z=\frac{P_c-v_s}{|p_s-(a,-b_s)|}>0, \qquad n_z-t_sn_\theta=\frac{J_c}{|p_s-(a,-b_s)|}. \tag{V5.4} \]

The quantity \(r_n=2-(v_s-2)(n_z-t_sn_\theta)^2/u_n^2\) is positive by the cone test. Both u_n and r_n extend continuously to the edges by V5.1–V5.3, with positive u_n and r_n=2 there. Let their minima on the closed rectangle be u_>0 and r_>0. Choose

\[ 0<\kappa=\tfrac12\min\{1,u_*,r_*\}<2. \tag{V5.5} \]

Then everywhere on that rectangle

\[ n_\theta+t_sn_z\ge\kappa,\qquad (v_s-2)(n_z-t_sn_\theta)^2 \le(2-\kappa)(n_\theta+t_sn_z)^2. \tag{V5.6} \]

This proves the precise directional margin of Theorem 4.6(iii), including both specified endpoint directions. A uniform raw stress-gap minimum at the zero-stress endpoints was not assumed.

V6. The common flat weight and all fixed derivatives

The common weight contains both endpoint exponentials. Near either edge the other factor is bounded above and below; on the remaining interior interval the fixed smooth field has ordinary compact bounds.

Use exactly the original weight and endpoint distances

\[ \delta=\min\{1,y_a,y_b\},\qquad \zeta(X)=\exp[-t_1^2/y_a^2-4/y_b^2]\quad(X_a<X<X_b), \tag{V6.1} \]

extended by zero outside the annulus. The two positive logarithmic distances have sum \(\log(X_b/X_a)>0\). Near either endpoint the other distance is bounded below; its exponential is a smooth positive factor bounded above and below. Derivatives of the vanishing factor are its exponential times finite sums of inverse powers of the vanishing distance, because \(y_{a,X}=1/X\) and \(y_{b,X}=-1/X\) have bounded derivatives on the fixed annulus. The exponential dominates each inverse power as its distance tends to zero. This proves smoothness and flatness of ζ at both edges.

V5.1 with Q3 gives a positive constant times \(e^{-t_1^2/y_a^2}\) as a stress lower bound near the inner edge and the same exponential times finite inverse powers as each derivative upper bound. V5.2 and H6 give \(ce^{-4/y_b^2}y_b^{-3}\) as the outer lower bound and its exponential times finite inverse powers for every derivative. On a collar with y_b≤1 the lower polynomial factor is at least one. Dividing each estimate by the bounded positive factor from the opposite endpoint proves the required comparison with ζ. On the remaining closed interior interval both ζ and |T_0| have positive minima; every fixed derivative is bounded because the frequency N has already been fixed. Taking the minimum of the three positive lower constants and, for each derivative, the maximum of the three upper constants yields

\[ |\mathcal T_0|\ge c\zeta,\qquad |\partial_X^{\alpha_1}\partial_\eta^{\alpha_2}\mathcal T_0| \le C_\alpha\zeta\delta^{-m_\alpha} \quad(X_a<X<X_b,\ -1\le\eta\le1). \tag{V6.2} \]

The lower c is independent of α. Each m_α is a finite nonnegative integer; enlarge it if necessary to cover both endpoint powers. These estimates also prove smooth extension of the stress by zero. All constants depend on fixed profile choices and derivative orders, and none on physical q or later bands and correction stages.

V7. Every conclusion of the leading-profile theorem

The exact moment identities preserve pressure and the heat exterior. Together with the protected axis, stress direction and flat weight, they give every assertion of the leading-profile theorem.

The common analytic axis rectangle and smooth Cartesian axis follow from J4 and Q5; V3–V4 leave them unchanged. On every finite closed radial interval, the constructed fields and all fixed mixed derivatives are finite: the only rapid radial frequency is the one fixed finite N, the later corrections have fixed smooth compact supports, and the heat factor is smooth for its full nonnegative argument range by K0/H0. No analyticity of that heat factor at zero is assumed. Positivity of E on X>0 implies positivity of \(\phi=\mathsf C E/\sqrt{2X}\); at zero it follows from J. The quantities F,U,V_0/X and Π extend smoothly through the axis by Q5.1.

The original pressure identity is preserved exactly. The input pressure was canonical, and both the joining and the shear correction restored C_p with the same axis datum. Therefore

\[ \Pi_0=-\int_0^\infty\frac{E(x,\eta)^2}{2x}\,dx,\qquad \Pi(X,\eta)=\Pi_0+\int_0^X\frac{E(x,\eta)^2}{2x}\,dx =-\int_X^\infty\frac{E(x,\eta)^2}{2x}\,dx. \tag{V7.1} \]

These integrals converge: near zero E=\(\sqrt{2X}F\) with smooth F, and at infinity the unchanged heat exterior decays like \(X^{-A}\), with A>0 and bounded heat factor. Differentiating gives \(\Pi_X=E^2/(2X)=F^2\), including its smooth limit at zero. P1's exact tangential residual identities apply to these actual fields; the physical leading stress is \(q^{-A-1/2}\mathcal T_0\). The full momentum residual still includes the axial-viscosity and radial remainder terms of P1.5–P1.6: completing the leading profile does not solve the entire equation. On \(0<X\le X_a\) the original equations (4.13) hold because that analytic solution is unchanged. This proves parts (i)–(ii); V5 proves (iii) and V6 proves (iv).

For part (v), all original convergent total moments remain exactly

\[ M(\infty,\eta)=J(\infty,\eta)=S(\infty,\eta)=0,\qquad \int_0^\infty(H-H_{\rm pow})\,dX=0, \quad H_{\rm pow}=\sqrt{2X}\,c_\infty X^{-A}. \tag{V7.2} \]

They were established in O/H, transferred through the exact Q join, and preserved by V4.6. In particular the convergence of the subtracted angular moment and its exact value are retained, not replaced by an un-subtracted divergent integral. The original heat exterior is

\[ U=V_0=0,\qquad E=c_\infty X^{-A}\mathcal H(2d/X),\qquad \mathcal H(Z)=\frac1{\Gamma(1+h)}\int_0^\infty e^{-v}v^h(1+Zv)^{-h}dv \quad(X\ge X_b). \tag{V7.3} \]

K0/H0 supply its positive smooth heat solution, including Z=0. In original physical coordinates s=r²/2, its swirl is exactly \(c_\infty s^{-A}\mathcal H(2\tau/s)\); the argument equals \(4\tau/r^2\). For the earlier radius \(X_v=X_{\rm end}\) at the end of the pulse, the input has U=M=0 by O1 and O0.6. The correction patch lies before that radius and restores M exactly, so these equalities hold for all X≥X_v. P0's radial-average formula gives V_0=0 there, proving the whole outer-collar assertion.

For part (vi), retain exactly the third and fourth intervals of O0.4, in their original radii, as \(\mathcal I_{\rm pos},\mathcal I_{\rm mean}\). They are ordered, disjoint, lie in \((X_a,X_v)\), and were untouched by the Q join, the heat compensation on the second patch, and the V4 correction on the first. They therefore retain

\[ U=0,\qquad E=c_{\rm patch}(1+\eta^2)^{-1}X^{-1/2-\lambda},\qquad \sup\mathcal I_{\rm pos}<\inf\mathcal I_{\rm mean}. \tag{V7.4} \]

The positive c_patch is independent of X and η, as required. These are the actual intervals receiving the later corrections, not newly chosen substitutes.

Finally, for each original viscosity \(\nu>0\), the exact H7 map retains \(u_\nu(x_\nu,t)=\sqrt\nu u(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t)\), \(p_\nu=\nu p\) and \(T_\nu=\nu T\) at that same mapped point. Its coordinates satisfy

\[ q_\nu-(z_\nu^2/\nu)q_\nu^{2h}=1-t,\qquad X_\nu=r_\nu^2/(2\nu q_\nu),\qquad \eta_\nu=z_\nu/(\sqrt\nu q_\nu^D). \tag{V7.5} \]

All original viscosity factors remain in the physical equations; the spatial derivative contributes \(\nu^{-1/2}\), so divergence of the physical stress has the same \(\sqrt\nu\) factor as the other momentum terms. The positive scalar stress factor preserves its direction. This is the proved comparison with the source's displayed coefficient-one construction, not a change of the target viscosity.

V8. Five worked exercises

Exercise 1. Write the complete loop map at zero axial stress

At a fixed profile point with \(p_{s,2}=0\), compute the variance parameter, the loop and its lifted circle coordinate. Check its period, inverse and both component means without dividing by \(p_{s,2}\).

Solution. Retain \(a>0,t_s,v_s=a(1+t_s^2)\), the actual cutoff value \(\rho\), and \(v=v_s+\rho\) from V2. The removable value in V1 gives

\[ \mu=\frac{\sqrt{2\rho/a}}{d_0},\qquad w=d_0\mu=\sqrt{2\rho/a},\qquad t(\theta')=t_s+w\sin\theta'. \tag{V8.1} \]

The square root is smooth as a function of the profile coordinates by the specific squared cutoff in V2.1. Thus these formulas include \(\rho=0\). Integrating \(1+t^2\) exactly gives

\[ \varphi(\theta')=\frac{\theta'}{2\pi} +\frac{a}{2\pi v} \left[2t_sw(1-\cos\theta')-\frac{w^2}{4}\sin(2\theta')\right]. \tag{V8.2} \]

The coefficient of \(\theta'\) is exactly \(1/(2\pi)\), since \(a(1+t_s^2+w^2/2)=v_s+\rho=v\). In particular, \(\varphi(0)=0\) and \(\varphi(\theta'+2\pi)=\varphi(\theta')+1\). Differentiating retains the positive Jacobian

\[ \frac{d\varphi}{d\theta'}=\frac{a[1+(t_s+w\sin\theta')^2]}{2\pi v}>0,\qquad \frac{d\theta'}{d\varphi}= \frac{2\pi v}{a[1+(t_s+w\sin\theta')^2]}. \tag{V8.3} \]

On the fixed compact family both derivatives have finite positive bounds. The lift is strictly increasing and has the stated degree one, so it is a bijection of the circles. The local inverse derivative in V8.3 and its parameter derivatives give its smooth inverse globally by uniqueness.

With \(\theta'=\theta'(\varphi)\), the loop is exactly

\[ (a_L,-b_L)= \frac{v}{1+(t_s+w\sin\theta')^2}(1,t_s+w\sin\theta'). \tag{V8.4} \]

Multiplying by the full Jacobian gives the first component average \(a\), and the second \(a t_s=-b_s\), since the integral of \(\sin\theta'\) is zero. If \(\rho=0\), the lift is \(\theta'/(2\pi)\) and the loop is the original shear. All factors \(a,v,d_0\) remain identified. The parameter \(d_0\) cancels from the zero-axial-stress loop itself, while it still determines \(\mu\) and the common compact family used in V1.

Exercise 2. Compute the leading changes of all five endpoint moments

Improve the moment estimates using the zero means of \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\). Give the actual leading coefficient at \(X_+\) in the original order \((M,I,J,S,C_p)\), including every radial weight. State what can and cannot be improved in the integrated stress estimate.

Solution. All profiles and the loop are now fixed; only the positive integer \(N\) varies. Constants below may depend on these fixed objects and on the specified derivative orders. For a smooth period-one function \(f(X,\eta,\varphi)\) with zero periodic mean and compact radial support inside \((X_-,X_+)\), write \(f_N(X,\eta)=f(X,\eta,N\log X)\). Let \(\mathcal P\) be V3.1, and let \(\mathcal D_X=X\partial_X\) hold the independent phase fixed. Direct differentiation gives the exact formula

\[ \begin{split} \int_{X_-}^{x} f_N(X,\eta)\,dX &=\frac{x}{N}(\mathcal P f)(x,\eta,N\log x)\\ &\quad-\frac1N\int_{X_-}^{x} \big[(1+\mathcal D_X)\mathcal P f\big](X,\eta,N\log X)\,dX . \end{split} \tag{V8.5} \]

The lower boundary term is zero because \(f\), and therefore its periodic primitive, vanishes on a radial neighborhood of \(X_-\). The formula is also valid at either endpoint by continuity. It proves a uniform \(O_m(N^{-1})\) bound for partial integrals in every fixed \(C^m_\eta\) norm.

At \(x=X_+\) the upper boundary term vanishes too. The operator \(\mathcal K=(1+\mathcal D_X)\mathcal P\) preserves zero periodic mean and compact radial support: differentiation and the bounded phase integrals commute. Repeated use of V8.5 therefore gives, for every integer \(k\ge1\),

\[ \int_{X_-}^{X_+} f_N\,dX =\frac{(-1)^k}{N^k} \int_{X_-}^{X_+}(\mathcal K^k f)(X,\eta,N\log X)\,dX,\qquad \left\|\int_{X_-}^{X_+}f_N\,dX\right\|_{C^m_\eta} \le \frac{C_{k,m}}{N^k}. \tag{V8.6} \]

Every integrand on the right is a fixed smooth function on a compact set, so its integral and each of its finitely many parameter derivatives are bounded. This proves the estimate directly, with no cancellation assumption at a sampled phase.

Put \(A_N=\mathcal A(X,\eta,N\log X)\), \(B_N=\mathcal B(X,\eta,N\log X)\). The original increments are \(u=B_N/N\) and \(e=E(e^{A_N/N}-1)\). Taylor's integral identity

\[ e^z=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2} +\frac{z^3}{2}\int_0^1(1-s)^2e^{sz}\,ds \tag{V8.7} \]

holds for every real \(z\). Boundedness of \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) and their fixed parameter derivatives makes the remainders below \(O_m(N^{-3})\), uniformly in \(X\). Substituting into all five original moment integrands yields

\[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{moment}&N^{-1}\text{ coefficient}&N^{-2}\text{ coefficient}\\ \hline M&B_N&0\\ I&H A_N& H A_N^2/2\\ J&H(UA_N+B_N)&H(UA_N^2/2+A_NB_N)\\ S&2UB_N-E^2 A_N&B_N^2-E^2 A_N^2\\ C_p&E^2 A_N/X&E^2 A_N^2/X \end{array} \tag{V8.8} \]

Here \(H=\sqrt{2X}E\), and every coefficient is integrated with the original \(dX\). For the last two rows one can check the factors directly from

\[ \Delta S'=2Uu+u^2-\frac{E^2}{2}(e^{2A_N/N}-1),\qquad \Delta C_p'=\frac{E^2}{2X}(e^{2A_N/N}-1). \tag{V8.9} \]

Primes in this display mean derivatives in \(X\). Both first-order rows in V8.8 have zero periodic mean, as do all the other first-order rows. Formula V8.5 bounds their partial integrals by \(O_m(N^{-1})\), and the extra prefactor gives \(O_m(N^{-2})\). The quadratic terms and their partial integrals are already \(O_m(N^{-2})\). Thus the actual stronger partial-moment and pressure estimates are

\[ \sup_{x\in[X_-,X_+]} \|\mathbf m_N(x,\cdot)-\mathbf m(x,\cdot)\|_{C^m_\eta} +\sup_{x\in[X_-,X_+]} \|\Pi_N(x,\cdot)-\Pi(x,\cdot)\|_{C^m_\eta} \le C_mN^{-2}. \tag{V8.10} \]

At the upper endpoint use V8.6 with \(k=2\) on the first-order coefficients. On each second-order coefficient subtract its periodic mean; V8.6 with \(k=1\) bounds the remaining integral. Consequently

\[ \mathbf m_N(X_+,\eta)-\mathbf m(X_+,\eta) =N^{-2}\mathbf D(\eta)+O_{C^m_\eta}(N^{-3}), \tag{V8.11} \]

where the entire original coefficient vector is

\[ \mathbf D=\int_{X_-}^{X_+} \begin{pmatrix} 0\\ H\langle\mathcal A^2\rangle_\varphi/2\\ H\big(U\langle\mathcal A^2\rangle_\varphi/2+ \langle\mathcal A\mathcal B\rangle_\varphi\big)\\ \langle\mathcal B^2\rangle_\varphi-E^2\langle\mathcal A^2\rangle_\varphi\\ (E^2/X)\langle\mathcal A^2\rangle_\varphi \end{pmatrix}\,dX . \tag{V8.12} \]

The original \(M\) discrepancy is even smaller: it is \(N^{-1}\int B_N\,dX\), so V8.6 bounds it by every prescribed inverse power of \(N\). This statement concerns its endpoint value; the partial integral can have a nonzero \(N^{-2}\) boundary term in V8.5.

For each fixed \(\eta\), \(D_{C_p}\ge0\), with equality exactly when \(\mathcal A(X,\eta,\varphi)=0\) for every \(X,\varphi\). Indeed \(E^2/X>0\); a continuous square with zero weighted integral must vanish everywhere. If \(\rho>0\) at some radial point for that \(\eta\), the variance gives a nonconstant continuous \(t\) there. The function \(v/(1+t^2)\) cannot then be constant, since a nonconstant continuous real function cannot have constant square. Thus \(a_L-a\) is not identically zero in phase, \(\mathcal A\) is not identically zero, and by continuity \(D_{C_p}>0\). For that fixed parameter the uncorrected endpoint pressure difference is positive for all sufficiently large \(N\), by V8.11. V4 cancels it exactly afterward.

The bound for \(p_{s,N}-p_s\) on the modulation interval remains \(O_m(N^{-1})\): its original formulas also contain the field values \(E_N,U_N\), whose changes have that order. Between \(X_+\) and the correction patch those fields agree exactly with the input, so the improved moment estimate through order \(m+1\) gives \(O_m(N^{-2})\) for \(p_{s,N}-p_s\) there. No small radial-derivative bound has been asserted.

Exercise 3. Propagate the sharper moment estimate through the exact correction

Find the leading coefficient of the actual five bump amplitudes and prove their stronger size estimate. Preserve the row order of the correction map and every quadratic term.

Solution. Let \(\mathscr R\) denote the exact permutation

\[ \mathscr R(x_M,x_I,x_J,x_S,x_{C_p})^T =(x_M,x_J,x_I,x_S,x_{C_p})^T. \tag{V8.13} \]

No moment changes between the end of modulation and the first patch, so V8.11 makes the actual correction target

\[ d_N=-N^{-2}\mathscr R\mathbf D+O_{C^m_\eta}(N^{-3}). \tag{V8.14} \]

The fixed original matrix \(B\) in V4.2–V4.3 includes its factors \(\sqrt2,K(\eta)\) and both patch radii. The actual equation is

\[ Bc_N+\mathscr Q(c_N,c_N)=d_N. \tag{V8.15} \]

Choose \(N\) above the finite smallness thresholds for \(C^0\) and the required \(C^m\) norm in V4.5. The same contraction then gives \(\|c_N\|_{C^m_\eta}\le2\nu_m\|d_N\|_{C^m_\eta}=O_m(N^{-2})\). For any further fixed derivative order, differentiating V8.15 gives the invertible linear operator \(B+2\mathscr Q(c_N,\cdot)\) on its highest derivative. Its inverse stays bounded on the small \(C^0\) branch; all lower derivative terms contain a derivative of \(c_N\) or of \(d_N\). Induction gives \(O_m(N^{-2})\) for every fixed \(m\), with constants and sufficiently large \(N\) allowed to depend on \(m\).

Substitute the established bound into the exact quadratic term: \(\mathscr Q(c_N,c_N)=O_{C^m_\eta}(N^{-4})\). Multiplication by the original \(B^{-1}\) in V8.15 gives

\[ c_N=-N^{-2}B^{-1}\mathscr R\mathbf D+ O_{C^m_\eta}(N^{-3}). \tag{V8.16} \]

All five bump coefficients occur here in their original units. The distinct powers in V4.3 and their actual factors remain in the matrix; no bound uniform as \(\lambda\) tends to zero is used.

For the specified disjoint supports, define

\[ A_i=\int\beta_i^2\,dX\quad(i=1,2),\qquad B_j=\int\beta_{j+2}^2\,dX,\qquad D_j=\int\frac{\beta_{j+2}^2}{X}\,dX\quad(j=1,2,3). \tag{V8.17} \]

All these integrals are finite and positive. With \(c_N=(a_1,a_2,b_1,b_2,b_3)^T\), the retained quadratic vector is exactly

\[ \mathscr Q(c_N,c_N)= \begin{pmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0\\ \sum_{i=1}^2 A_i a_i^2-\frac12\sum_{j=1}^3 B_j b_j^2\\ \frac12\sum_{j=1}^3 D_j b_j^2 \end{pmatrix}. \tag{V8.18} \]

The second component vanishes because \(ue=0\) pointwise; the square terms have the displayed signs from V4.2. This is the exact nonlinear map used in V8.15, not a linearized replacement.

Since the bumps are fixed, the field correction and every fixed radial and parameter derivative are \(O_m(N^{-2})\), with the derivative order included in the constant. Its partial moment increments have the same order by V4.2. Thus the cone estimates on the correction patch can use \(N^{-2}\) in place of the sufficient \(N^{-1}\) bound. The modulation interval still requires the \(N^{-1}\) field and shear comparisons. After the patch all five moments, the pressure and the entire exterior agree exactly, for the fixed selected \(N\), as proved in V4.6.

Exercise 4. Give explicit endpoint powers and a smooth stress amplitude

In V6.2, give a single explicit exponent for a fixed number of radial derivatives. Then prove that the scalar amplitude \(|\mathcal T_0|^{1/2}\), extended by zero, is smooth at both edges.

Solution. Put \(r=\alpha_1,m=\alpha_2\). On the inner collar the stress is \(e^{-t_1^2/y_a^2}g_aB_0\), with \(g_aB_0\) smooth and nonzero at the edge. On the outer collar it is \(e^{-4/y_b^2}y_b^{-3}(b_\theta,y_b^6b_z)\), with the vector in parentheses smooth and nonzero at the edge. Shrink the fixed collars so these nonvanishing properties hold throughout them.

Each \(y\)-derivative of \(e^{-c/y^2}\) contributes a polynomial in \(y^{-1}\) whose greatest power increases by at most three: the exponential derivative is \(2cy^{-3}e^{-c/y^2}\), while differentiating a previous inverse power increases its degree by one. Induction therefore bounds its \(j\)-th derivative by \(C_j e^{-c/y^2}y^{-3j}\) for \(0<y\le1\). The derivatives of \(y_a,y_b\) with respect to \(X\) are bounded on the fixed positive annulus. The full product and chain rules, retaining the outer factor \(y_b^{-3}\), give

\[ \left|\partial_X^r\partial_\eta^m\mathcal T_0\right| \le C_{r,m}\zeta\,\delta^{-(3r+3)}. \tag{V8.19} \]

Parameter derivatives fall only on smooth coefficient functions; the endpoint distances and their exponentials are independent of \(\eta\). The opposite endpoint exponential is bounded above and below on each chosen collar. On the remaining compact interval the same estimate follows by increasing \(C_{r,m}\), since \(\zeta,\delta>0\). Thus \(m_\alpha=3\alpha_1+3\) is an explicit admissible integer, independent of \(\alpha_2\).

For completeness the original weight has the exact logarithmic derivative

\[ \frac{\zeta_X}{\zeta} =\frac1X\left(\frac{2t_1^2}{y_a^3}-\frac8{y_b^3}\right). \tag{V8.20} \]

The second sign comes from \(y_{b,X}=-1/X\). This identity also directly verifies the power three at each differentiated endpoint.

Define \(\gamma=|\mathcal T_0|^{1/2}\) inside the annulus. Its exact collar formulas are

\[ \begin{split} \gamma&=e^{-t_1^2/(2y_a^2)}\,g_a^{1/2}|B_0|^{1/2} &&\text{on the inner collar},\\ \gamma&=e^{-2/y_b^2}y_b^{-3/2} (b_\theta^2+y_b^{12}b_z^2)^{1/4} &&\text{on the outer collar}. \end{split} \tag{V8.21} \]

Every coefficient after the displayed scalar powers is smooth and positive, with bounded fixed mixed derivatives on its collar. The fractional factor \(y_b^{-3/2}\) is kept explicitly. Its \(j\)-th derivative is a constant times \(y_b^{-3/2-j}\); the exponential supplies decay exceeding every such power. The product rule gives

\[ \gamma\ge\sqrt c\,\zeta^{1/2},\qquad |\partial_X^r\partial_\eta^m\gamma| \le C_{r,m}\zeta^{1/2}\delta^{-(3r+2)}. \tag{V8.22} \]

The lower bound is the square root of V6.2. For the upper bound the outer exponent \(3r+3/2\) is bounded by the displayed integer \(3r+2\) when \(\delta\le1\); the inner exponent is \(3r\). The interior is compact and \(\gamma>0\) there. Every derivative tends to zero at either edge, so extension by zero is smooth with all radial and mixed derivatives zero. This gives a precise smooth scalar magnitude for later amplitude constructions; it does not supply their separate wave equations or covariance identities.

Exercise 5. Recover the exact radial phase and supports at viscosity \(\nu\)

Express the actual fast phase in the original physical variables. Compute its radial, axial and time derivatives, and give its exact radial period ratio. Locate the modulation and moment correction supports.

Solution. Keep \(\nu>0\), the original physical coordinates \((r_\nu,z_\nu,t)\) with \(t<1\), and V7.5:

\[ q_\nu-\frac{z_\nu^2}{\nu}q_\nu^{2h}=1-t,\qquad X_\nu=\frac{r_\nu^2}{2\nu q_\nu},\qquad \eta_\nu=\frac{z_\nu}{\sqrt\nu\,q_\nu^D},\qquad L_\nu=1-2h\eta_\nu^2. \tag{V8.23} \]

The coefficient of the \(q_\nu\) derivative in the implicit equation is \(L_\nu\), because \(2D=1-2h\). It is positive on the parameter domain. Differentiating the original equation at fixed other physical coordinates gives

\[ \partial_tq_\nu=-L_\nu^{-1},\qquad \partial_{z_\nu}q_\nu=\frac{2z_\nu q_\nu^{2h}}{\nu L_\nu},\qquad \partial_{r_\nu}q_\nu=0. \tag{V8.24} \]

The actual phase is \(\Phi_\nu=N\log X_\nu\), considered modulo one when evaluating the period-one primitives. Its three derivatives are therefore

\[ \partial_{r_\nu}\Phi_\nu=\frac{2N}{r_\nu},\qquad \partial_{z_\nu}\Phi_\nu=-\frac{2N\eta_\nu}{\sqrt\nu\,L_\nu q_\nu^D},\qquad \partial_t\Phi_\nu=\frac{N}{L_\nu q_\nu}. \tag{V8.25} \]

In the axial identity, the exact comparison \(z_\nu q_\nu^{2h-1}/\nu=\eta_\nu/(\sqrt\nu q_\nu^D)\) uses \(D+2h-1=-D\), retaining the viscosity factor. At fixed \(z_\nu,t\), one complete increase of the phase by one changes \(X_\nu\) by the ratio \(e^{1/N}\) and \(r_\nu\) by the ratio \(e^{1/(2N)}\). Starting at radius \(r_\nu\), the exact radial distance for one phase period is

\[ \Delta r_\nu=r_\nu(e^{1/(2N)}-1). \tag{V8.26} \]

This is the period of the fast phase; the full field also has slowly varying coefficients, so it need not itself repeat after that radial shift.

The primitives vanish outside the original interval \((X_-,X_+)\) and on neighborhoods of both boundaries. Their physical support is accordingly contained in

\[ \sqrt{2\nu q_\nu X_-}<r_\nu<\sqrt{2\nu q_\nu X_+}. \tag{V8.27} \]

The five moment bumps are supported in the distinct later interval

\[ \sqrt{2\nu q_\nu R_-}<r_\nu<\sqrt{2\nu q_\nu R_+}. \tag{V8.28} \]

These formulas retain the fixed original endpoints, every \(\nu,q_\nu\) factor and the protected collars. The selected finite \(N\) is independent of physical \(q_\nu\), viscosity transport and later iteration stages. No infinite-frequency limiting field is used.

What the completed leading profile supplies

The five parts of N2 now construct the actual leading profile from its original moment operators through its axis, outer field, exact connection and admissible shear. V7 verifies every conclusion of Theorem 4.6, with the full source parameters and both preserved endpoint collars. The actual perturbation has one fixed finite radial frequency.

The field still has the axial-viscosity and radial residual terms retained in P1 and J8. The axis-coefficient lesson, global extension and base-field construction treat these terms. The following wave, mean-correction, iteration and terminal-force lessons complete the construction. The summation lesson proves the common summation mechanism.

Authored exposition and figure source: CC0.

Correcting the coefficients on one fixed axis interval

NS-BLOWUP N3.1. The completed leading profile leaves axial-viscosity and radial momentum terms in the full residual. This lesson derives every coefficient equation that treats those terms, constructs the actual first correction, and proves the linear solution step for each later order on the same radial interval.

The leading-profile lessons, ending in V7, supply the actual input, including one common parameter-analytic axis rectangle. The stress and moment lesson, P0–P7, gives the exact physical operators. The axis lesson, J8, computes a nonzero axial residual of the leading field. Exercise 5 below proves exactly how the first correction cancels that residual at the axis, without changing its growing axial velocity trace.

At each positive order the current unknowns satisfy a linear system with six components. One coefficient differentiates in the parameter. That derivative is unbounded on a fixed holomorphic supremum norm, so an ordinary bounded-operator argument would miss the difficulty. We prove a special matrix identity: two adjacent parameter-derivative factors vanish, even when a derivative strikes a variable coefficient. The number of surviving parameter derivatives is therefore at most half the number of integrations. The factorial from the ordered radial integrals then proves convergence for the entire fixed radial interval.

The original source is OpenAI, Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, pages 45–49, (5.1)–(5.8) and Lemma 5.1, together with the physical coordinate formulas on pages 24–26. SOURCES.json gives the bibliography and mathematical locators. This is separate teaching and editorial mathematics; the diplomatic transcription retains OpenAI's text.

Figure. The two coordinate spaces retain the original six unknowns. Their derivative map gives the exact vanishing composition used in D3. The lower panels show the convergence bound and the physical residual cancellation in Exercise 5. Radial positions indicate order, not scale; no numerical solution is plotted.

From the original residual to an actual correction

First retain the physical powers of \(q\), the pressure and both viscosity contributions. The spacing \(2h\) arises from their exact relative powers. Radial incompressibility determines the radial velocity coefficient, including its axis integration constant.

Next write the original equations as a six-component system, listing every nonzero matrix entry. Its diagonal radial singularity has an exact integral inverse. The sparse derivative structure and a shared parameter-domain loss give a convergent series and uniqueness in the stated holomorphic class.

Finally recover smoothness in \(X\), the original radial average, pressure and physical fields. The first correction uses only the already constructed leading profile. Later orders use the same solution operator after the preceding coefficients have been globally extended and their moments corrected; that global step is the next lesson. This local construction alone does not yet supply the full base field.

D0. Original physical coefficients and differential operators

The subscript now records expansion order. Keep the full leading pressure distinct from its axis trace, and include the change of physical power after each axial derivative.

Keep \(A=1/2+h,D=1/2-h,d=1-\eta^2,L=1-2h\eta^2\), with the already fixed \(0<h<1/100\). Use \(z=q^D\eta\), \(1-t=q(1-\eta^2)\), \(X=r^2/(2q)\), and the original amplitude \(\mathsf C\). For \(\lambda_n=2nh\), the physical coefficients are exactly

\[ \begin{gathered} u_{\theta,n}=q^{-A+\lambda_n}E_n =r q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\phi_n/\mathsf C, \qquad E_n=\sqrt{2X}\phi_n/\mathsf C,\\ u_{z,n}=q^{-A+\lambda_n}U_n,\qquad ru_{r,n}=q^{\lambda_n}V_n,\qquad p_n=q^{-2A+\lambda_n}\Pi_n. \end{gathered} \tag{D0.1} \]

Here \(\Pi_0(X,\eta)\) is the full leading pressure; its axis trace is the pressure datum previously denoted \(\Pi_0(\eta)\). The subscript in this section is expansion order. No pressure constant is discarded by this notation.

For a real exponent \(\beta\), retain the original operators

\[ T_\beta f=\frac{-\beta f+D\eta f_\eta+Xf_X}{L},\qquad Z_\beta f=\frac{2\beta\eta f+df_\eta-2\eta Xf_X}{L}, \tag{D0.2} \]

so \(\partial_t(q^\beta f)=q^{\beta-1}T_\beta f\) and \(\partial_z(q^\beta f)=q^{\beta-D}Z_\beta f\). P0.2–P0.3 prove these by differentiation of the actual coordinate map. Write

\[ T_{\beta,n}=T_{\beta+\lambda_n},\qquad Z_{\beta,n}=Z_{\beta+\lambda_n},\qquad Z_{\beta,n}^{[2]}=Z_{\beta+\lambda_n-D}Z_{\beta+\lambda_n}. \tag{D0.3} \]

The composition order in the last expression retains the change in physical power after the first derivative. Negative-index fields are zero.

Incompressibility at order n gives \(q^{\lambda_n-1}[\partial_XV_n+Z_{-A,n}U_n]=0\), because A+D=1. The regular-axis condition fixes V_n(0)=0. Integrating the displayed equation, with \(\int_0^XxU_{n,X}dx=XU_n-\int_0^XU_n dx\), proves

\[ \partial_XV_n=-Z_{-A,n}U_n,\qquad \frac{V_n}{X} =\frac{2\eta U_n-2\eta(D+\lambda_n)\mathcal A_XU_n-d\partial_\eta\mathcal A_XU_n}{L}, \quad \mathcal A_XU_n=\int_0^1U_n(sX,\eta)ds. \tag{D0.4} \]

The integral formula retains its smooth value at X=0 and fixes the integration constant uniquely.

D1. Every term of the coefficient equations

Collect terms only after computing the full cylindrical momentum equation. The angular connection term, radial pressure equation and two different viscous order shifts all remain in the equations below.

Set \(b=-A-1/2\), \(c=-A\). For angular transport, the cylindrical connection term is part of \(u_r(\partial_r+r^{-1})u_\theta\). Substitution of D0.1 yields exactly

\[ u_{r,i}(\partial_r+r^{-1})u_{\theta,j} =\frac r{\mathsf C}q^{b-1+\lambda_i+\lambda_j} V_i(\phi_{j,X}+\phi_j/X). \tag{D1.1} \]

Indeed \((\partial_r+r^{-1})(r\phi_j)=2\phi_j+2X\phi_{j,X}\), and \(r^2=2qX\) gives the stated factor. The angular axial transport is \((r/\mathsf C)q^{b-1+\lambda_i+\lambda_j}U_iZ_{b,j}\phi_j\), because \(-A-D=-1\). The vector radial Laplacian satisfies

\[ (\partial_{rr}+r^{-1}\partial_r-r^{-2})(r\phi(X)) =\frac r q\,2(X\phi_{XX}+2\phi_X). \tag{D1.2} \]

This follows from \(X_r=r/q\) by two ordinary derivatives, including the two cylindrical terms. Two axial derivatives introduce \(q^{-2D}=q^{-1}q^{2h}\), so they move order n−1 to order n. Equating the complete order-n angular residual to zero gives

\[ 2(X\phi_n''+2\phi_n')=T_{b,n}\phi_n +\sum_{i+j=n}\{V_i(\phi_j'+\phi_j/X)+U_iZ_{b,j}\phi_j\} -Z_{b,n-1}^{[2]}\phi_{n-1}. \tag{D1.3} \]

Primes here and in D1.4–D1.6 mean \(\partial_X\) at fixed η.

For the axial component the scalar radial Laplacian is \(2q^{-1}(XU''+U')\). Radial transport contributes \(V_iU_j'\), and axial transport contributes \(U_iZ_{c,j}U_j\), each with factor \(q^{c-1+\lambda_i+\lambda_j}\). The pressure derivative has the same power because \(-2A-D=c-1\). Thus its full equation is

\[ 2(XU_n''+U_n')=T_{c,n}U_n +\sum_{i+j=n}\{V_iU_j'+U_iZ_{c,j}U_j\} +Z_{-2A,n}\Pi_n-Z_{c,n-1}^{[2]}U_{n-1}. \tag{D1.4} \]

For the radial equation multiply the physical momentum equation by r first. The pressure and centrifugal terms at order n are \(q^{-2A+\lambda_n}[2X\Pi_n'-2X\mathsf C^{-2}\sum_{i+j=n}\phi_i\phi_j]\). The time and transport terms have power \(q^{-1+\lambda_k}\), with exact coefficients \(T_{0,k}V_k\), \(V_i(V_j'-V_j/(2X))\) and \(U_iZ_{0,j}V_j\). The vector radial Laplacian of V(X)/r is \(2XV''/(qr)\), so after multiplying by r its contribution is \(-2XV_k''\). The axial-viscosity term at that power is \(-Z_{0,k-1}^{[2]}V_{k-1}\). Since \(-1+\lambda_k=-2A+\lambda_{k+1}\), the result is exactly

\[ \Pi_n'=\mathsf C^{-2}\sum_{i+j=n}\phi_i\phi_j-\frac{\Omega_{n-1}}{2X}, \tag{D1.5} \]

where

\[ \Omega_k=T_{0,k}V_k +\sum_{i+j=k}\{V_i(V_j'-V_j/(2X))+U_iZ_{0,j}V_j\} -2XV_k''-Z_{0,k-1}^{[2]}V_{k-1}. \tag{D1.6} \]

These computations retain all physical powers and all radial and axial viscous terms in original (5.2)–(5.6).

The quotient in D1.5 is regular, with an explicit full formula. Write V_j=Xv_j using D0.4. Direct substitution in D0.2 gives \(T_\beta(Xf)=XT_{\beta-1}f\), \(Z_\beta(Xf)=XZ_{\beta-1}f\). Consequently

\[ \frac{\Omega_k}{X}=T_{-1,k}v_k +\sum_{i+j=k}\{v_i(v_j/2+Xv_j')+U_iZ_{-1,j}v_j\} -4v_k'-2Xv_k''-Z_{-1,k-1}^{[2]}v_{k-1}. \tag{D1.7} \]

Every coefficient is smooth at the axis and holomorphic on a suitable parameter neighborhood whenever the preceding profiles and their needed derivatives are. The factor 1/2 in the quadratic radial term and both radial derivatives remain visible.

D2. The full six-component system

The current order is linear because every middle-index product uses previously constructed coefficients. A radial-average variable makes the system local in the radial coordinate; its defining relation will be recovered exactly.

Fix \(a>0\) with \(X_a<a^2<X_{\rm an}\), inside the common analytic rectangle proved in V7. The radius a is fixed independently of the correction order. In this paragraph use the concise symbols \(\phi=\phi_0,U=U_0,V=V_0\) for the actual leading functions and put

\[ \begin{gathered} \ell=\lambda_n,\quad \beta_n=b+\ell,\quad \gamma_n=c+\ell,\quad \pi_n^{\rm exp}=-2A+\ell,\\ v_0=V_0/X,\quad W=1+Lv_0-2\eta U_0,\quad H_c=D\eta+dU_0,\quad S_\phi=\phi_0+X\phi_{0,X}. \end{gathered} \tag{D2.1} \]

The W here equals the original transport coefficient in P1.1 by D0.4. The superscript on \(\pi_n^{\rm exp}\) distinguishes a scalar exponent from the pressure profile.

At positive order all middle-index terms are already of lower order. Write them, without omission, as

\[ \begin{split} R_{\phi,n}&=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\{V_i(\phi_{n-i}'+\phi_{n-i}/X)+U_iZ_{b,n-i}\phi_{n-i}\} -Z_{b,n-1}^{[2]}\phi_{n-1},\\ R_{U,n}&=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\{V_iU_{n-i}'+U_iZ_{c,n-i}U_{n-i}\} -Z_{c,n-1}^{[2]}U_{n-1},\\ P_n&=\mathsf C^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\phi_i\phi_{n-i}-\Omega_{n-1}/(2X). \end{split} \tag{D2.2} \]

For n=1 these sums are empty. The factors V_i=Xv_i cancel the apparent 1/X in R_φ,n. D1.7 handles the remaining quotient. These are actual finite source expressions, not new free data.

Let \(\xi=\sqrt X\), \(K_n=\mathcal A_XU_n-U_n\), and

\[ \mathbf W_n=(\phi_n,U_n,K_n,\Pi_n,\partial_\xi\phi_n,\partial_\xi U_n)^T, \qquad C_d=\operatorname{diag}(0,0,2,0,3,1). \tag{D2.3} \]

The use of ξ retains X=ξ² and all resulting derivative factors. D0.4 is equivalently

\[ \frac{V_n}{X}=\frac{2\eta(A-\ell)U_n-2\eta(D+\ell)K_n-d\partial_\eta U_n-d\partial_\eta K_n}{L}. \tag{D2.4} \]

The second-order operators are exactly \(2(X\partial_{XX}+2\partial_X)=\tfrac12(\partial_{\xi\xi}+3\xi^{-1}\partial_\xi)\) and \(2(X\partial_{XX}+\partial_X)=\tfrac12(\partial_{\xi\xi}+\xi^{-1}\partial_\xi)\). Also \(\partial_\xi K_n+2K_n/\xi=-\partial_\xi U_n\). Thus the exact system is

\[ \partial_\xi\mathbf W_n+\xi^{-1}C_d\mathbf W_n =A_0\mathbf W_n+A_1\partial_\eta\mathbf W_n+f_n,\qquad \mathbf W_n(0)=0. \tag{D2.5} \]

Here are every nonzero entry of the matrices; all unlisted entries vanish:

\[ \begin{gathered} (A_0)_{15}=1,\quad (A_0)_{26}=1,\quad (A_0)_{36}=-1,\quad (A_0)_{41}=4\xi\phi_0/\mathsf C^2,\\ (A_0)_{51}=2[\beta_n(-1+2\eta U_0)/L+v_0],\\ (A_0)_{52}=2Z_b\phi_0+4\eta(A-\ell)S_\phi/L,\qquad (A_0)_{53}=-4\eta(D+\ell)S_\phi/L,\qquad (A_0)_{55}=\xi W/L,\\ (A_0)_{61}=-8\eta X\phi_0/(L\mathsf C^2),\\ (A_0)_{62}=2[\gamma_n(-1+2\eta U_0)/L+Z_cU_0]+4\eta(A-\ell)XU_{0,X}/L,\\ (A_0)_{63}=-4\eta(D+\ell)XU_{0,X}/L,\qquad (A_0)_{64}=4\pi_n^{\rm exp}\eta/L,\qquad (A_0)_{66}=\xi W/L. \end{gathered} \tag{D2.6} \]

The parameter-derivative matrix is

\[ \begin{gathered} (A_1)_{51}=2H_c/L,\qquad (A_1)_{52}=(A_1)_{53}=-2dS_\phi/L,\\ (A_1)_{62}=2(H_c-dXU_{0,X})/L,\qquad (A_1)_{63}=-2dXU_{0,X}/L,\qquad (A_1)_{64}=2d/L. \end{gathered} \tag{D2.7} \]

The complete source vector is

\[ f_n=(0,0,0,2\xi P_n,2R_{\phi,n},2R_{U,n}-4\eta XP_n/L)^T. \tag{D2.8} \]

To verify these rows, the linear angular equation before the ξ conversion is

\[ \begin{split} 2(X\phi_n''+2\phi_n')={}&[\beta_n(-1+2\eta U_0)/L+v_0]\phi_n +(XW/L)\phi_n'+(H_c/L)\phi_{n,\eta}\\ &+S_\phi(V_n/X)+U_nZ_b\phi_0+R_{\phi,n}. \end{split} \tag{D2.9} \]

Insert D2.4 and multiply by two; \(X\phi_n'=\xi\partial_\xi\phi_n/2\) gives (A_0)55. The axial row has the same derivative coefficients with U_n, together with \(XU_{0,X}(V_n/X)+U_nZ_cU_0+Z_{-2A,n}\Pi_n+R_{U,n}\). Use the already derived pressure row \(\Pi_n'=2\phi_0\phi_n/\mathsf C^2+P_n\) inside \(Z_{-2A,n}\Pi_n=(2\pi_n^{\rm exp}\eta\Pi_n+d\Pi_{n,\eta}-2\eta X\Pi_n')/L\). This supplies (A_0)61, (A_0)64, (A_1)64 and the last term in D2.8. The first four equations then follow from the definitions and the pressure row. This proves the full matrix system, including the terms not printed explicitly in the source.

D3. Exact integral inverse and the sparse derivative structure

Invert the diagonal singular part with its actual zero-axis conditions. Then follow the two coordinate spaces through every factor to prove the vanishing composition before estimating derivatives.

For \(c_i=(C_d)_{ii}\), define

\[ (Gg)_i(\xi,\eta)=\int_0^\xi(s/\xi)^{c_i}g_i(s,\eta)ds =\xi\int_0^1t^{c_i}g_i(t\xi,\eta)dt. \tag{D3.1} \]

For positive ξ, differentiating the first expression gives \((Gg)_i'+c_i(Gg)_i/\xi=g_i\). The second expression extends continuously by zero at ξ=0. Conversely multiplication of a regular solution of that scalar equation by ξ^{c_i}, integration from zero, and its zero axis value recover D3.1. For c_i>0 a nonzero homogeneous integration constant is singular; for c_i=0 it violates the prescribed zero value. Thus G is the exact inverse with these boundary conditions.

Let \(E_4=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)\), \(E_2=\operatorname{span}(e_5,e_6)\). D2.7 proves that A_1 maps E_4 into E_2 and annihilates E_2. Every η derivative of A_1 has the identical support pattern. All G kernels are diagonal and independent of η, so they preserve both spaces. For any such diagonal kernel D_0 and any radii ξ,s,

\[ A_1(\xi)D_0A_1(s)=0,\qquad A_1(\xi)D_0\partial_\eta^jA_1(s)=0\quad(j\ge0). \tag{D3.2} \]

In particular, composing two adjacent factors of the type \(A_1\partial_\eta\) vanishes, including the term where the left derivative strikes the right coefficient. These are exact matrix identities on the original six coordinates.

Put \(\mathcal K=G(A_0+A_1\partial_\eta)\). In the expansion of \(\mathcal K^kG\), there are at most 2^k choices of the two operator types. A nonzero choice cannot contain adjacent parameter-derivative types by D3.2. Hence it has at most

\[ p_k=\lceil k/2\rceil \tag{D3.3} \]

parameter derivatives. This count concerns differential-operator compositions, so it already includes the product-rule terms on variable coefficients. No coefficient is treated as constant in η.

D4. Convergence on the whole fixed radial interval

Allocate the available parameter-domain loss only to the derivatives that survive. Ordered radial integration supplies a full factorial. This proves convergence without a smallness requirement on the chosen radial interval.

For the current order choose a bounded complex neighborhood \(S_\rho=\{\eta:\operatorname{dist}(\eta,[-1,1])<\rho\}\) with no zero of L, on which all current coefficients and sources are bounded and holomorphic, uniformly for \(0\le\xi\le a\). Its radius may depend on n. Such a neighborhood exists for n=1 by V7 and for the induction receiver from the finitely many lower profiles and derivatives that enter D2.2. Take a smaller radius than those available for those finitely many data, so the suprema are finite on its closure. No bound uniform in n is assumed.

For \(0<\rho'<\rho\), set \(\Delta=\rho-\rho'\). Cauchy's integral formula on a disk of radius ε inside the larger domain gives \(\|\partial_\eta f\|_{S_{r-\varepsilon}}\le\varepsilon^{-1}\|f\|_{S_r}\). In a word with p derivatives allocate loss Δ/p to each derivative; coefficient multiplications need no radius loss. For p=0 the derivative factor is one. This bounds the full operator word by a coefficient factor times \((p/\Delta)^p\), without expanding all product-rule terms separately.

Each diagonal integration kernel has norm at most one since c_i≥0 and the nested radii are ordered. Its k+1 integrations range over a simplex of volume \(\xi^{k+1}/(k+1)!\). Choose C_n≥1 bounding the matrices, source and the factor from at most 2^k words. D3.3 then gives the complete estimate

\[ \|\mathcal K^kGf_n\|_{[0,a]\times S_{\rho'}} \le\frac{C_n^{k+1}a^{k+1}}{(k+1)!} \left(\max\{1,p_k/\Delta\}\right)^{p_k}. \tag{D4.1} \]

The convention at p_k=0 is one. The simplex and radius-loss estimates can be applied simultaneously: before taking suprema, each integrand has exactly the same ordered radial variables and parameter-domain losses, and all coefficient bounds are uniform in those radial variables.

The root of the right side tends to zero. For example \((k+1)!\ge((k+1)/e)^{k+1}\), from summing \(\log j\ge\int_{j-1}^j\log x\,dx\) for j≥2, while p_k≤(k+1)/2. The kth root is bounded by a fixed multiple of \((k+1)^{-1/2}\), with fixed a,C_n,Δ. Thus the actual series

\[ \mathbf W_n=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal K^kGf_n \tag{D4.2} \]

converges uniformly on the whole fixed interval and every smaller parameter neighborhood. Uniform convergence preserves holomorphy in η. On a further smaller domain Cauchy's bound also gives convergence of the parameter derivative series, so bounded radial integration passes through the series. Consequently \(\mathbf W_n=G(A_0\mathbf W_n+A_1\partial_\eta\mathbf W_n+f_n)\), and D3.1 proves D2.5. No infinite-frequency or numerical approximation is used.

For uniqueness take two bounded holomorphic solutions on a common parameter neighborhood; their difference H satisfies H=\(\mathcal K^kH\) for every k. The same argument, with k integrations, bounds it by

\[ \|H\|_{[0,a]\times S_{\rho'}} \le\frac{(C_na)^k}{k!} \left(\max\{1,p_k/\Delta\}\right)^{p_k} \|H\|_{[0,a]\times S_\rho}. \tag{D4.3} \]

The right side tends to zero. A common larger domain with finite suprema is obtained by first shrinking the intersection of the two solutions' domains. Hence H=0. This is exactly the stated holomorphic uniqueness class, not a uniqueness assertion for arbitrary smooth parameter dependence.

The chosen a did not enter any smallness condition. Increasing C_n or decreasing the parameter neighborhood still gives convergence by D4.1. Therefore the radial interval stays fixed at every application of this solution operator.

D5. Smoothness, parity and recovery of the original unknowns

Recover radial smoothness through a nonsingular integral identity. Reflection gives the exact parity needed to return from the square-root radial coordinate to the original \(X\).

For continuous g the inverse formula has the nonsingular derivative

\[ \partial_\xi(Gg)_i=g_i(\xi,\eta)-c_i\int_0^1t^{c_i}g_i(t\xi,\eta)dt. \tag{D5.1} \]

It follows either by differentiating the first integral away from zero and passing to zero in the second expression, or by its scalar equation and continuous quotient. Thus continuous g gives one continuous radial derivative. Apply this to \(g=A_0\mathbf W_n+A_1\partial_\eta\mathbf W_n+f_n\); the parameter derivative is continuous on a smaller neighborhood by Cauchy's formula. Once \(\mathbf W_n\) is C^r in ξ, the same formula and product differentiation give C^{r+1} on a smaller parameter domain.

Here is the common-domain conclusion required by the next coefficient construction. At this fixed order n, take the parameter neighborhood \(S_\rho\) on which the input coefficients, source and all their radial derivatives are holomorphic. For n=1 it is supplied by the common analytic rectangle of V7; for the induction it is the intersection of the finitely many neighborhoods of the completed lower coefficients. The source formulas D2.2 use only finitely many derivatives of those fields. On any smaller closed neighborhood, each fixed radial derivative of these data is bounded uniformly on the compact radial interval. The bounds may depend on its derivative order.

Choose once \(0<\rho_2<\rho_1<\rho\). For any prescribed integer r, perform the r applications of D5.1 on the nested neighborhoods with radii \(\rho_1-j(\rho_1-\rho_2)/(r+1)\), \(j=0,\ldots,r\). Each application uses a positive radius difference, so Cauchy's formula controls the one additional parameter derivative. Radial differentiation of the integral in D5.1 introduces the factor \(t^k\) for a k-th radial derivative of its integrand; this is bounded by one on \(0\le t\le1\), so the same differentiated integral formula remains valid at the axis. Induction therefore supplies all radial derivatives through r, continuous and holomorphic on a neighborhood strictly larger than \(S_{\rho_2}\). Every occurrence is a derivative of the one D4.2 solution, by uniqueness, not a new solution chosen with r. Since r was arbitrary, all radial derivatives are holomorphic on this same fixed \(S_{\rho_2}\); their bounds can grow with r. Further parameter derivatives follow from Cauchy's formula on the positive remaining margin. This proves the common parameter neighborhood for all mixed derivatives at this fixed n. Its radius may decrease with n, while the radial interval \([0,a]\) stays unchanged.

For the parity argument extend the original coefficients to negative ξ by X=ξ². Set \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,1,-1,-1)\). Inspection of every entry in D2.6–D2.8 gives

\[ A_j(-\xi)=-SA_j(\xi)S\quad(j=0,1),\qquad f_n(-\xi)=-Sf_n(\xi). \tag{D5.2} \]

For example (A_0)41 is odd, (A_0)15 is even, and A_1 has only last-two-row, first-four-column entries, all even. The lower source profiles are functions of X; f_n's fourth component is odd and its last two are even. The extended G formula in D3.1 and the same absolute estimates construct a unique smooth solution on [-a,a]. Reflection \(\widetilde{\mathbf W}_n(\xi)=S\mathbf W_n(-\xi)\) obeys the same integral equation and axis data by D5.2, so uniqueness gives equality. The first four components are therefore even and the last two odd.

An even smooth function of ξ is smooth as a function of X=ξ² on the half interval. Here is the boundary check with its derivative content. For each integer M, Taylor's formula at zero has only even coefficients through degree 2M, with remainder \(\xi^{2M+2}R_M(\xi)\) whose needed derivatives are bounded. Applying \(\partial_X=(2\xi)^{-1}\partial_\xi\) k times to this remainder gives a finite sum bounded by a constant times \(\xi^{2M+2-2k}\) for M≥k. The polynomial terms give the required limits of each derivative. Taking larger M for each k proves the smooth extension; parameter derivatives and their holomorphy obey the same argument on the smaller neighborhoods already supplied above.

The first two rows recover the derivative coordinates. The third row also recovers the original radial average exactly, rather than a replacement variable. Indeed

\[ \xi^2K_n=-\int_0^\xi s^2\partial_sU_n(s^2,\eta)ds =-\xi^2U_n(\xi^2,\eta)+2\int_0^\xi sU_n(s^2,\eta)ds, \tag{D5.3} \]

where \(\partial_sU_n(s^2,\eta)\) denotes the derivative of the composed function. Changing variables x=s² gives \(K_n=\mathcal A_XU_n-U_n\). Formula D2.4 then reconstructs V_n and D0.4, with V_n(0)=0. The fourth row reconstructs D1.5 with \(\Pi_n(0)=0\); the last two rows, by D2.9 and the pressure substitution, reconstruct D1.3–D1.4. Thus the integral solution solves all original equations, with \(\phi_n(0)=U_n(0)=\Pi_n(0)=0\). Conversely any solution in the source's regular holomorphic class gives this six-component solution and is unique by D4.3.

D6. The actual first correction and the induction receiver

At the first order every source is already an explicit function of the leading profile. The solution series therefore constructs an actual correction. Its complete physical factors are retained when transporting to viscosity \(\nu\).

At n=1 all inputs are already supplied by the verified leading profile. Specifically,

\[ R_{\phi,1}=-Z_{b,0}^{[2]}\phi_0,\qquad R_{U,1}=-Z_{c,0}^{[2]}U_0,\qquad P_1=-\Omega_0/(2X), \tag{D6.1} \]

with the full \(\Omega_0/X\) given by D1.7 using only v_0,U_0 and their derivatives; its negative-index term is zero. Put these actual functions, \(\ell=2h\), and the actual leading coefficients into D2.6–D2.8. The convergent series D4.2 is therefore an explicit exact construction of \((\phi_1,U_1,V_1,\Pi_1)\) on \([0,a^2]\), not an existence statement depending on an unspecified source. Its zero axis values preserve all leading traces. Its original physical fields are D0.1 with \(\lambda_1=2h\), and the preceding identities cancel every order-one residual on this interval.

For higher orders D2.2 displays precisely the finite receiving map from previously completed coefficients. D1.7 proves that its axis source is regular; D4 proves that its size never forces the radial interval to shrink; D5 proves the regularity needed to form the next source. This establishes the full linear solution step of original Lemma 5.1. The actual global extension in Y0–Y7 completes original Lemma 5.2: it extends each current solution, imposes the five actual residual moments and finishes that order before using it at the next. Together these constructions supply the entire global coefficient sequence; its summation into the actual base field is derived in Z0–Z8.

For the original viscosity \(\nu>0\), retain the exact map proved in P1 and H7, with \(r_\nu=\sqrt\nu r,z_\nu=\sqrt\nu z\) and time unchanged. The physical coefficient fields become

\[ \begin{gathered} u_{\theta,n,\nu}=\sqrt\nu q^{-A+\lambda_n}E_n =r_\nu q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\phi_n/\mathsf C,\qquad u_{z,n,\nu}=\sqrt\nu q^{-A+\lambda_n}U_n,\\ r_\nu u_{r,n,\nu}=\nu q^{\lambda_n}V_n,\qquad p_{n,\nu}=\nu q^{-2A+\lambda_n}\Pi_n,\\ X=\frac{r_\nu^2}{2\nu q},\quad \eta=\frac{z_\nu}{\sqrt\nu q^D},\quad q-\frac{z_\nu^2}{\nu}q^{2h}=1-t. \end{gathered} \tag{D6.2} \]

Each full physical momentum term has the same additional factor \(\sqrt\nu\): one spatial derivative contributes \(\nu^{-1/2}\), the pressure has factor ν, and the two derivatives in νΔ cancel their ν^{-1} with the original viscosity. Thus the coefficient cancellations hold at the unchanged target viscosity with every field factor retained.

D7. Five worked exercises

Exercise 1. Prove the exact composition rules for the physical operators

Explain why the two axial derivatives in D0.3 have different subscripts. Prove the corresponding mixed time–axial identity and the rules involving the original radial variable \(X\).

Solution. Let \(f(X,\eta)\) be smooth on the profile rectangle, and let \(\beta\) be a real physical exponent. D0.2 gives

\[ \partial_{zz}(q^\beta f) =q^{\beta-2D}Z_{\beta-D}Z_\beta f,\qquad \partial_t\partial_z(q^\beta f) =q^{\beta-D-1}T_{\beta-D}Z_\beta f. \tag{D7.1} \]

Applying the same identities in the opposite order gives \(\partial_z\partial_t(q^\beta f)=q^{\beta-1-D}Z_{\beta-1}T_\beta f\). The original smooth coordinate map has \(q>0\), \(L>0\), so physical mixed derivatives commute and their common scalar factor is nonzero. Each \((X,\eta)\) with \(X\ge0,|\eta|<1\) is reached by taking any positive \(q\) and setting \(r=\sqrt{2qX},z=q^D\eta,t=1-q(1-\eta^2)\). Thus

\[ T_{\beta-D}Z_\beta f=Z_{\beta-1}T_\beta f. \tag{D7.2} \]

This proves an identity on the original profile domain, not merely on one coordinate trajectory. Continuity gives the one-sided identities at \(\eta=\pm1\) and \(X=0\).

Direct substitution into the full formulas D0.2 gives

\[ \begin{gathered} T_\beta(Xf)=XT_{\beta-1}f,\qquad Z_\beta(Xf)=XZ_{\beta-1}f,\\ \partial_XT_\beta f=T_{\beta-1}\partial_Xf,\qquad \partial_XZ_\beta f=Z_{\beta-1}\partial_Xf. \end{gathered} \tag{D7.3} \]

For instance, \(X\partial_X(Xf)=Xf+X^2f_X\) changes the time coefficient from \(-\beta\) to \(1-\beta\), while \(-2\eta X\partial_X(Xf)\) changes the axial coefficient from \(2\beta\eta\) to \(2(\beta-1)\eta\). Differentiating the original operators gives the last two identities by the same product rule; \(L\) has no \(X\)-dependence.

The order spacing is also exact:

\[ q^{-2D}=q^{-1}q^{2h},\qquad q^{-1+\lambda_k}=q^{-2A+\lambda_{k+1}},\qquad \lambda_k=2kh. \tag{D7.4} \]

The first identity accounts for axial viscosity relative to radial viscosity. The second accounts for the remaining radial momentum terms relative to centrifugal pressure. Neither permits replacing \(Z_{\beta-D}Z_\beta\) by \(Z_\beta^2\).

Exercise 2. Give a finite remainder bound for the convergent integral series

Turn D4.1 into an explicit tail estimate without shrinking \(a\). Retain both parity classes of the summation index.

Solution. Let \(z=C_na>0\), \(\Delta=\rho-\rho'>0\), and retain the actual majorants

\[ t_k=\frac{z^{k+1}}{(k+1)!} \big(\max\{1,p_k/\Delta\}\big)^{p_k},\qquad p_k=\lceil k/2\rceil. \tag{D7.5} \]

For \(m\ge\max\{1,\lceil\Delta\rceil\}\), put \(B_m=(m/\Delta)^m\). Then

\[ t_{2m-1}=\frac{z^{2m}}{(2m)!}B_m,\qquad t_{2m}=\frac{z^{2m+1}}{(2m+1)!}B_m,\qquad \frac{B_{m+1}}{B_m} =\frac{m+1}{\Delta}(1+1/m)^m \le\frac{e(m+1)}{\Delta}. \tag{D7.6} \]

The last bound follows by integrating \(1/(1+s)\le1\) on \([0,1/m]\), giving \(m\log(1+1/m)\le1\). Hence the two exact adjacent-parity comparisons are

\[ \frac{t_{2m+1}}{t_{2m-1}}\le \frac{ez^2}{2\Delta(2m+1)},\qquad \frac{t_{2m+2}}{t_{2m}}\le \frac{ez^2}{2\Delta(2m+3)}. \tag{D7.7} \]

Choose any integer

\[ M\ge \max\left\{1,\lceil\Delta\rceil, \left\lceil\frac{ez^2}{2\Delta}\right\rceil\right\}. \tag{D7.8} \]

Both ratios in D7.7 are then at most \(1/2\) for every \(m\ge M\). Summing each parity class as a geometric majorant proves the actual remainder bound

\[ \left\|\mathbf W_n-\sum_{k=0}^{2M-2}\mathcal K^kGf_n\right\|_{[0,a]\times S_{\rho'}} \le 2\big(t_{2M-1}+t_{2M}\big). \tag{D7.9} \]

All constants in this formula are those from the already established coefficient and source bounds. Increasing \(M\) makes the right side tend to zero by D7.7. The radius \(a\), parameter margin \(\Delta\), source and physical coordinates remain unchanged. This is an analytic error estimate for the actual infinite integral series.

Exercise 3. Compute the first radial coefficients at the axis

Find the exact axis slopes of \(\phi_1,U_1,\Pi_1\), retaining the full original pressure datum. Determine the axis slopes of \(\phi_n,U_n\) at every later positive order.

Solution. For an axis trace \(f(\eta)\), define the restrictions of the original operators by

\[ \mathscr T_\beta f=\frac{-\beta f+D\eta f'}L,\qquad \mathscr Z_\beta f=\frac{2\beta\eta f+df'}L. \tag{D7.10} \]

Here primes mean parameter derivatives. At \(X=0\), the term \(Xf_X\) in D0.2 vanishes for each smooth profile. This remains true after either operator is applied, so taking the axis trace of their composition gives precisely the composition in D7.10.

At each positive order all three prescribed axis traces \(\phi_n,U_n,\Pi_n\) vanish identically in \(\eta\), as do their parameter derivatives. D0.4 then gives \(V_n/X=0\) at the axis. Evaluating D1.3–D1.5 there gives

\[ 4\phi_{n,X}(0,\eta)=R_{\phi,n}(0,\eta),\qquad 2U_{n,X}(0,\eta)=R_{U,n}(0,\eta),\qquad \Pi_{n,X}(0,\eta)=P_n(0,\eta). \tag{D7.11} \]

In the angular current-order terms, \(V_0(\phi_n'+\phi_n/X)\) tends to zero because \(V_0=O(X)\) and \(\phi_n=O(X)\); the term \(V_n\phi_0/X\) tends to zero because \(V_n/X=0\) at the axis. All other current-order terms vanish from their zero traces or explicit \(X\) factors. This verifies the limits rather than cancelling a singular expression formally.

For \(n=1\) use D6.1 and the actual traces \(\phi_*,U_*=4\eta+j_0\):

\[ \phi_{1,X}(0,\eta)=-\frac14\mathscr Z_{b-D}\mathscr Z_b\phi_*, \qquad U_{1,X}(0,\eta)=-\frac12\mathscr Z_{c-D}\mathscr Z_cU_*. \tag{D7.12} \]

In particular the complete \(\Lambda\)-dependent function \(\phi_*\) is retained in the first expression.

To compute the pressure slope, retain \(g(\eta)=U_{0,X}(0,\eta)=-Z_*/(2L)\) from J8.6. The full source \(Z_*\), including the actual axis pressure \(\Pi_0(0,\eta)\), is J0.1. Expanding the exact radial-average formula D0.4 gives

\[ v_*=\left.\frac{V_0}X\right|_0 =\frac{2A\eta U_*-dU_*'}L,\qquad w_*=\left.\partial_X\frac{V_0}X\right|_0 =\frac{(2-D)\eta g-\frac12d g'}L. \tag{D7.13} \]

Indeed \(\mathcal A_XU_0=U_*+gX/2+O(X^2)\), and \(1-D=A\). D1.7 at \(k=0\) now gives the entire finite value

\[ \Pi_{1,X}(0,\eta)= -\frac12\left[ \mathscr T_{-1}v_*+\frac12v_*^2 +U_*\mathscr Z_{-1}v_*-4w_* \right]. \tag{D7.14} \]

The terms with an explicit \(X\) and the negative-index axial-viscosity term vanish at this endpoint. The remaining radial derivative \(-4w_*\), the quadratic factor \(1/2\) and the original pressure inside \(g\) have not been discarded.

For \(n\ge2\), all middle-index terms in \(R_{\phi,n}\) and \(R_{U,n}\) vanish at the axis: every positive-order field has zero trace and \(V_i/X\) has zero trace. The final axial-viscosity terms have the zero trace of the \((n-1)\)-st field and all its parameter derivatives. Therefore

\[ \phi_{n,X}(0,\eta)=U_{n,X}(0,\eta)=0\qquad(n\ge2). \tag{D7.15} \]

This conclusion concerns these two slopes; it does not assert that every pressure slope or higher radial derivative vanishes.

Finally, writing \(\alpha(\eta)=U_{1,X}(0,\eta)\), the exact reconstruction gives

\[ K_1=-\frac{\alpha X}{2}+O(X^2),\qquad V_1=\frac{(2-D-\lambda_1)\eta\alpha-\frac12d\alpha'}L\,X^2+O(X^3). \tag{D7.16} \]

Every fixed parameter derivative has the same remainder order on a smaller common domain, by D5 and Taylor's integral remainder. These formulas describe the actual first correction, not a separately chosen axis polynomial.

Exercise 4. Prove a quantitative source-to-solution map

For the actual fixed matrices \(A_0,A_1\), prove linearity and a finite bound for the solution map on two parameter neighborhoods. State the norms, domains and all radius dependence.

Solution. Use the maximum norm on the original six coordinates and its induced matrix norm. Let \(\mathcal H_\rho\) be the normed space of continuous functions on \([0,a]\times S_\rho\), holomorphic in \(\eta\), with finite supremum norm \(\|\cdot\|_\rho\). We use only bounded holomorphic data; taking uniform limits makes this a Banach space. The actual matrices are bounded on this domain after the prior shrinking in D4. Put

\[ \mathsf M=\max\{1,\|A_0\|_\rho,\|A_1\|_\rho\},\qquad \Delta=\rho-\rho'>0,\qquad \mathfrak S(z,\Delta)= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^k}{(k+1)!} \big(\max\{1,p_k/\Delta\}\big)^{p_k}. \tag{D7.17} \]

The same root estimate as D4, or the two parity estimates in Exercise 2, proves that this series is finite for every finite \(z\ge0\) and every \(\Delta>0\).

The word proof in D3–D4 applies to any \(f\in\mathcal H_\rho\). Separate the source norm from the coefficient norms. There are at most \(2^k\) words, each coefficient multiplication costs at most \(\mathsf M\), and the full simplex has volume \(a^{k+1}/(k+1)!\). Thus

\[ \|\mathcal K^kGf\|_{\rho'} \le\|f\|_\rho\, \frac{a(2\mathsf M a)^k}{(k+1)!} \big(\max\{1,p_k/\Delta\}\big)^{p_k}. \tag{D7.18} \]

Consequently the actual integral solution operator is the bounded linear map

\[ \begin{split} \mathcal S_n:\mathcal H_\rho&\longrightarrow\mathcal H_{\rho'},& \mathcal S_nf&=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal K^kGf,\\ \|\mathcal S_nf\|_{\rho'}&\le a\,\mathfrak S(2\mathsf M a,\Delta)\|f\|_\rho . \end{split} \tag{D7.19} \]

Linearity follows term by term and passes through uniform convergence. On an intermediate parameter neighborhood the series converges with its first parameter derivative on a smaller neighborhood. D3.1 then proves the integral equation, the differential equation and the zero-axis value. The uniqueness argument D4.3 applies to this same bounded holomorphic class.

For two source vectors in the stated space, subtracting the convergent series gives the exact difference map

\[ \mathcal S_nf-\mathcal S_ng=\mathcal S_n(f-g),\qquad \|\mathcal S_nf-\mathcal S_ng\|_{\rho'} \le a\,\mathfrak S(2\mathsf M a,\Delta)\|f-g\|_\rho. \tag{D7.20} \]

The actual smooth source \(f_n\) belongs to the domain; D5 gives the extra smoothness and parity needed to recover its original fields. An arbitrary source in \(\mathcal H_\rho\) need not have that parity, so the map just proved is a six-component solution map, with original-field recovery asserted for the already verified source \(f_n\). The factor \(a\), coefficient norm and full parameter margin remain explicit. No source smallness or radial shrinking is required.

Exercise 5. Show exactly how the first correction removes the axial residual at the axis

Compute \(U_{1,X}(0,0)\) for the actual leading trace, then prove cancellation of the entire axial momentum residual at every point of the physical axis. Retain the original viscosity.

Solution. The actual leading axial trace is \(U_*=4\eta+j_0\), and \(c=-A\). Its first restricted axial derivative is

\[ \mathscr Z_cU_*= \frac{4+2cj_0\eta+(8c-4)\eta^2}{1-2h\eta^2}. \tag{D7.21} \]

At zero the next operator \(\mathscr Z_{c-D}\) acts by parameter differentiation. The derivative of the denominator is zero there, so

\[ (\mathscr Z_{c-D}\mathscr Z_cU_*)(0)=2cj_0=-2Aj_0,\qquad U_{1,X}(0,0)=Aj_0>0. \tag{D7.22} \]

This value follows from the complete coefficient equations and is independent of the later moment extensions, whose supports lie away from this axis interval.

Let \((u_\nu^{(0)},p_\nu^{(0)})\) be the actual leading physical field and \((u_{1,\nu},p_{1,\nu})\) the actual first coefficient from D6.2. Use the original physical \(q_\nu,\eta_\nu\) there. The leading tangential equations cancel time, convection, axial pressure and radial viscosity on the axis interval. Its remaining axial residual at the axis is therefore exactly

\[ \mathcal R_\nu(u_\nu^{(0)},p_\nu^{(0)})\cdot e_z =-\sqrt\nu\,q_\nu^{c-2D} (\mathscr Z_{c-D}\mathscr Z_cU_*)(\eta_\nu), \qquad r_\nu=0. \tag{D7.23} \]

The factor comes from \(\nu\partial_{z_\nu z_\nu} [\sqrt\nu\,q_\nu^cU_*]\): each spatial derivative contributes \(\nu^{-1/2}\), leaving exactly \(\sqrt\nu\). This is the same full axial-viscosity term retained in the original residual.

The first correction has zero axial velocity and pressure traces for every \(\eta\), and \(V_1=O(X^2)\), \(\phi_1=O(X)\). In Cartesian coordinates its horizontal velocity is \(O(r_\nu^3)\) and its axial velocity is \(O(r_\nu^2)\) at fixed \(z_\nu,t\). Thus its time derivatives, axial derivatives and axial pressure derivative vanish on the axis. All extra axial convection terms vanish there too: both fields have zero horizontal velocity on the axis, and the correction's axial trace and axial derivative are zero.

Only its radial viscous term contributes to the axial residual at the axis. Since \(X=r_\nu^2/(2\nu q_\nu)\), direct radial differentiation gives

\[ \left.\nu(\partial_{r_\nu r_\nu} +r_\nu^{-1}\partial_{r_\nu})u_{z,1,\nu}\right|_{r_\nu=0} =2\sqrt\nu\,q_\nu^{c+\lambda_1-1}U_{1,X}(0,\eta_\nu). \tag{D7.24} \]

The displayed axis value is the smooth Cartesian limit. Now \(\lambda_1-1=2h-1=-2D\), and D7.12 gives twice the slope as the negative restricted second axial derivative. Combining D7.23–D7.24 in the momentum residual therefore yields the exact identity

\[ \mathcal R_\nu(u_\nu^{(0)}+u_{1,\nu}, p_\nu^{(0)}+p_{1,\nu})\cdot e_z=0 \qquad(r_\nu=0,\ t<1). \tag{D7.25} \]

This is cancellation for the actual first correction throughout the axis, not only cancellation of a formal coefficient at the origin.

At \(z_\nu=0\), put \(\tau=1-t\). The unchanged leading residual from J8 is \(2Aj_0\sqrt\nu\,\tau^{-A-2D}\). The first correction's original near-axis expansion is

\[ u_{z,1,\nu}(r_\nu,0,t) =\frac{Aj_0}{2\sqrt\nu}\tau^{-A-2D}r_\nu^2+O(r_\nu^4). \tag{D7.26} \]

At each fixed \(t<1,\nu>0\), the radial Laplacian of its displayed quadratic term, multiplied by \(\nu\), is exactly \(2Aj_0\sqrt\nu\,\tau^{-A-2D}\). Its negative sign in the momentum residual cancels the positive leading residual.

The velocity trace itself stays

\[ (u_\nu^{(0)}+u_{1,\nu})\cdot e_z =\sqrt\nu\,q_\nu^{-A}(4\eta_\nu+j_0) \qquad(r_\nu=0). \tag{D7.27} \]

Thus cancellation of the residual does not remove the prescribed growth of the axial trace. D7.15 also shows that later constructed positive orders have zero first radial slope and cannot change this exact axial cancellation. Residuals away from the axis, global moment conditions and the summation into a base field still require their subsequent constructions.

What this fixed-interval solution supplies

D0–D6 prove the complete coefficient equations, all matrix entries, the convergent solution operator, uniqueness, common parameter regularity, parity and recovery of the original fields. They construct the actual first positive-order correction and the full local solution step of Lemma 5.1 on the chosen interval. D7 supplies explicit remainder and stability bounds, exact axis coefficients and the physical residual cancellation.

The next lesson extends each coefficient globally and restores its five original residual moments before it is used at the next order. Those complete derivations are already supplied in the separate extension audit, followed by the actual base-field realization. The global extension lesson proves the extension and moment correction; the base-field lesson constructs their actual sum.

Authored exposition and figure source: CC0.

Extending every coefficient and cancelling its five moments

NS-BLOWUP N3.2. A local coefficient cannot simply be cut off and used at the next order. Radial integration can leave a velocity tail, a pressure constant and two stress tails. This lesson constructs the global coefficients, cancels all five original moments exactly, proves their support and retains the common parameter regularity needed for the next coefficient.

The fixed-interval lesson, D0–D7, supplies the actual inner solution. The completed leading profile, V0–V8, supplies two protected patches, the exact heat exterior and the original flat stress weight. The outer-profile lesson, O0–H7, supplies the smooth cutoff, heat integrals and convergent subtracted moment used below.

The current-order correction is an exact finite linear solve, with no small-discrepancy condition. We prove the two matrix inverses for actual smooth bumps, then prove the radial boundary terms and all integration constants vanish. The exceptional first-order outer stress receives its own endpoint calculation. The final induction constructs every positive-order coefficient; summing them into a base field is the following lesson.

The original source is OpenAI, Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, pages 49–54, (5.9)–(5.22) and the full proof of Lemma 5.2. SOURCES.json records the source identity and mathematical locators. This is separate teaching and editorial mathematics; the diplomatic transcription retains OpenAI's text.

Figure. The diagram retains the original moments, patch order and stress supports. The lower formula is the exact first-order endpoint coefficient proved in Exercise 4. Positions show radial order, not scale; no numerical field is sampled.

Y0. Fixed geometry, data and original moments

Choose the radial geometry once. The five moments have different jobs: they remove radial integration constants and the total tangential residuals. Keep their original weights and pressure derivative until compact pressure has been proved.

Keep all notation and physical fields of D0–D1: \(A=1/2+h,D=1/2-h,d=1-\eta^2,L=1-2h\eta^2\), \(\lambda_n=2nh\), \(R=\sqrt{2X}\), \(r=\sqrt qR\), \(b=-A-1/2,c=-A\), and the original amplitude \(\mathsf C\). Thus \(E_n=R\phi_n/\mathsf C\). The actual leading profile has stress endpoints \(X_a,X_b\), analytic interval \([0,X_{\rm an}]\), and ordered unused patches \(\mathcal I_{\rm pos},\mathcal I_{\rm mean}\) from V7.4. Its leading \(U_0\text{ and }V_0\) vanish after \(X_v<X_b\). Choose, once for all orders,

\[ X_a<X_-<X_{\rm keep}<X_{\rm cut}<a^2<X_{\rm an}<\inf\mathcal I_{\rm pos}, \qquad \max\{X_v,\sup\mathcal I_{\rm mean}\}<X_+<X_b. \tag{Y0.1} \]

The first four radii are inside the positive-length analytic inner collar retained in Q5 and V7; D2 permits this same a. The outer radius can be chosen before the terminal outer collar, because the original schedule places \(X_v\) and both patches strictly before it. The subscripts here label the positive-order construction, not the distinct shear-modification interval in V0. No support radius depends on n.

Let σ be the exact smooth step O0.1 and set

\[ \kappa(X)=1-\sigma\!\left(\frac{X-X_{\rm keep}}{X_{\rm cut}-X_{\rm keep}}\right). \tag{Y0.2} \]

This gives the required values one and zero with smooth flat transitions. At order n the five original moments are

\[ \begin{split} m_{n,1}&=\int_0^\infty RU_n\,dR,\\ m_{n,2}&=\int_0^\infty R^2E_n\,dR,\\ m_{n,3}&=\int_0^\infty\partial_R\Pi_n\,dR,\\ m_{n,4}&=\int_0^\infty R^2\sum_{i+j=n}U_iE_j\,dR,\\ m_{n,5}&=\int_0^\infty\left(R\sum_{i+j=n}U_iU_j-\tfrac12R^2\partial_R\Pi_n\right)dR. \end{split} \tag{Y0.3} \]

Each sum includes both endpoint terms and all middle terms. The pressure derivative, rather than an a priori compact pressure, appears in the last moment. This distinction is retained until compactness has actually been proved.

Y1. Cutoff, five explicit bumps and reconstruction

Cutting off the two freely chosen profiles creates a smooth extension, but it does not yet close the reconstructed radial velocity and pressure. Five disjoint bumps supply the missing degrees of freedom.

Start at n=1 with the actual solution D6.1; for subsequent n use D2.2 with the preceding completed global coefficients. Write its inner solution as \(\phi_n^{\rm in},U_n^{\rm in},V_n^{\rm in},\Pi_n^{\rm in}\). The initial extension is

\[ \widetilde\phi_n=\kappa\phi_n^{\rm in},\qquad \widetilde U_n=\kappa U_n^{\rm in},\qquad \widetilde E_n=R\widetilde\phi_n/\mathsf C, \tag{Y1.1} \]

extended by zero beyond a². Since κ is already zero on a neighborhood of a², all radial derivatives match there.

Choose a closed interval \([R_p,R_q]\) inside \(\{R:R^2/2\in\mathcal I_{\rm pos}\}\). Set \(r_j=R_p+j(R_q-R_p)/6\), \(\omega=(R_q-R_p)/20\), and define

\[ \begin{gathered} w_j(R)=\begin{cases}\exp[-1/(1-((R-r_j)/\omega)^2)],&|R-r_j|<\omega,\\0,&|R-r_j|\ge\omega,\end{cases}\\ I_j=\int_0^\infty w_j(R)dR>0,\qquad b_j=w_j/I_j,\\ (b^U_1,b^U_2)=(b_1,b_2),\qquad(b^E_1,b^E_2,b^E_3)=(b_3,b_4,b_5). \end{gathered} \tag{Y1.2} \]

The spacing is \((R_q-R_p)/6\) and the sum of two widths is \((R_q-R_p)/10\), so the five compact supports are disjoint and ordered. Each is smooth and has exactly integral one; the defining integrals \(I_j\) are retained. For coefficients \(\alpha_{n,j}(\eta)\), \(\beta_{n,j}(\eta)\), put

\[ U_n=\widetilde U_n+\sum_{j=1}^2\alpha_{n,j}b_j^U(R),\qquad E_n=\widetilde E_n+\sum_{j=1}^3\beta_{n,j}b_j^E(R),\qquad \phi_n=\mathsf C E_n/R. \tag{Y1.3} \]

The last quotient is smooth at X=0: every added bump vanishes near that point and the remaining quotient equals \(\widetilde\phi_n\).

Define the other fields by the exact forward integrals

\[ \begin{split} F_n(X,\eta)&=\int_0^XU_n(x,\eta)dx,\\ V_n(X,\eta)&=-\int_0^X(Z_{-A,n}U_n)(x,\eta)dx,\\ \Pi_n(X,\eta)&=\int_0^X\left[\mathsf C^{-2}\sum_{i+j=n}\phi_i\phi_j-\frac{\Omega_{n-1}}{2x}\right](x,\eta)dx. \end{split} \tag{Y1.4} \]

\(F_n\) is the indexed streamfunction coefficient, not the leading angular ratio denoted F in V. The full expression for Ω is D1.6–D1.7; in particular \(\Omega_{n-1}\) contains only already constructed lower orders. D1.7 proves regularity of \(\Omega_{n-1}/x\) at zero. Thus these equations impose original (5.2) and (5.5) globally, with exactly the source's zero axis values.

For \(X\le X_{\rm keep}\) the original inner functions and Y1.3 coincide. Their forward equations and axis values coincide as well, so Y1.4 gives equality of all four inner profiles there. On all of \([0,a^2]\), the cutoff is independent of η and the five bumps vanish. Each fixed radial derivative therefore retains the holomorphic parameter neighborhood obtained in D5; products, finite integrals and the lower source retain it after a finite intersection of neighborhoods. Global correction coefficients need only be smooth in η because they do not enter any of these inner forward integrals.

Y2. The complete affine moment map

At one positive order, the current unknown appears only once in each product. This makes the five equations affine with all earlier orders held fixed. The original patch separates them into two constant invertible matrices.

On the unchanged positive-order patch, V7.4 gives the exact expression

\[ U_0=0,\qquad E_0=e_*f(\eta)R^{-1-2\lambda},\quad e_*=2^{1/2+\lambda}c_{\rm patch}>0,\quad f(\eta)=(1+\eta^2)^{-1},\quad\lambda>0. \tag{Y2.1} \]

The factor \(2^{1/2+\lambda}\) follows from \(X=R^2/2\) in V7.4; λ here is the fixed profile slope, distinct from \(\lambda_n=2nh\). All lower-order terms remain fixed when solving the current five equations.

The pressure equation in Y1.4 gives, with no dropped middle terms,

\[ \partial_R\Pi_n=\frac{2E_0E_n}{R} +\frac1R\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}E_iE_{n-i}-\Omega_{n-1}\right). \tag{Y2.2} \]

Using \(dX=R\,dR\) in the fifth moment gives exactly

\[ m_{n,5}=\int_0^\infty\left(\sum_{i+j=n}U_iU_j-\tfrac12\sum_{i+j=n}E_iE_j+\tfrac12\Omega_{n-1}\right)dX. \tag{Y2.3} \]

For a current perturbation \((\delta U_n,\delta E_n)\) on the patch, the five changes are consequently
