\[ \begin{split} \Delta m_{n,1}&=\int R\,\delta U_n\,dR,\\ \Delta m_{n,2}&=\int R^2\,\delta E_n\,dR,\\ \Delta m_{n,3}&=2e_*f\int R^{-2-2\lambda}\delta E_n\,dR,\\ \Delta m_{n,4}&=e_*f\int R^{1-2\lambda}\delta U_n\,dR,\\ \Delta m_{n,5}&=-e_*f\int R^{-2\lambda}\delta E_n\,dR. \end{split} \tag{Y2.4} \]

For the fourth row \(U_0\delta E_n=0\); for the fifth \(2U_0\delta U_n=0\), whereas the two E endpoints cancel the factor 1/2. No product of two current coefficients occurs: that product has order 2n rather than n. \(\Omega_{n-1}\) is unchanged. This proves affine dependence, for arbitrary finite sizes of the current discrepancies.

Keep the exact constant matrices

\[ \begin{gathered} (B_U)_{ij}=\int_0^\infty R^{p_i}b_j^U(R)dR,\quad(p_1,p_2)=(1,1-2\lambda),\\ (B_E)_{ij}=\int_0^\infty R^{s_i}b_j^E(R)dR,\quad(s_1,s_2,s_3)=(2,-2-2\lambda,-2\lambda). \end{gathered} \tag{Y2.5} \]

Let \(m_{n,j}^0\) denote Y0.3 after setting the five bump coefficients to zero and reconstructing Y1.4. The solution is the explicit pair

\[ \begin{gathered} d_{U,n}=\begin{pmatrix}m_{n,1}^0\\m_{n,4}^0/(e_*f)\end{pmatrix},\qquad d_{E,n}=\begin{pmatrix}m_{n,2}^0\\m_{n,3}^0/(2e_*f)\\-m_{n,5}^0/(e_*f)\end{pmatrix},\\ \alpha_n=-B_U^{-1}d_{U,n},\qquad\beta_n=-B_E^{-1}d_{E,n}. \end{gathered} \tag{Y2.6} \]

These divisions are only the displayed representation of the full rows Y2.4; multiplying back by \(e_*f\), \(2e_*f\) and \(-e_*f\) recovers exactly every original moment, with its sign.

Here is a direct invertibility proof. A nonzero sum of k distinct real powers of R has at most k−1 distinct positive zeros. Substitute \(R=e^t\), divide by the exponential of the least exponent, and differentiate. The derivative has at most k−1 nonzero exponential terms; induction and Rolle's theorem give the assertion, starting with one term. A zero determinant of \((R_j^{s_i})\) at k ordered positive points would contradict that assertion. Hence this determinant never vanishes on the connected region \(R_1<\cdots<R_k\), and its sign is constant there. Multilinearity and Fubini give

\[ \det\left(\int R^{s_i}b_j(R)dR\right) =\int\cdots\int\det(R_j^{s_i})\prod_{j=1}^k b_j(R_j)\,dR_1\cdots dR_k\ne0. \tag{Y2.7} \]

The ordered supports make the integrand have one fixed nonzero sign wherever the bump product is positive. The powers in both lists Y2.5 are distinct because λ>0. Thus both actual matrices are invertible, independently of n and η; their numerical values need not be estimated by sampling. The full moment-map inverse also contains the retained row factors. Since f≥1/2 and \(e_*>0\) is fixed, it and each fixed parameter derivative are bounded on [-1,1]. No bound uniform as λ or \(e_*\) tends to zero is claimed.

The discrepancies are smooth: the current \(U_n,E_n\) have compact support, all prior positive-order factors have the common support proved below, and \(\Omega_0\) has compact support because \(U_0,V_0\) do. The moments contain no current \(V_n\) or its derivatives; \(\Omega_{n-1}\) uses only completed lower orders. Thus each integral defining a discrepancy has a fixed bounded integration region with smooth integrand, regular at zero by D1.7. Differentiation under these integrals is legitimate for every fixed derivative. Equation Y2.6 then gives smooth coefficients and proves

\[ m_{n,j}(\eta)=0\qquad(j=1,\ldots,5,\quad -1\le\eta\le1). \tag{Y2.8} \]

Y3. Exact exterior closure and the reserved mean patch

Use the solved moments to prove compact support. The pressure constant disappears only after the third moment is imposed; its support can extend farther than the velocity correction patch.

For \(X\ge X_+\), the current \(U_n\) and \(E_n\) vanish by construction and

\[ F_n(X,\eta)=\int_0^\infty U_n(x,\eta)dx=m_{n,1}(\eta)=0. \tag{Y3.1} \]

D0.4, with \(\mathcal A_XU_n=F_n/X\), gives \(V_n=0\) there, including all parameter derivatives. The leading \(U_0,V_0\) vanish there by \(X_+>X_v\). Each term of \(\Omega_{n-1}\) contains a V field or its derivative; from D1.6 these are \(T V\), \(V_i(V_j'-V_j/(2X))\), \(U_i ZV_j\), \(-2XV''\) and the lower axial viscous term. All therefore vanish in this exterior. Each product \(\phi_i\phi_j\) of positive total order has at least one positive-order factor, also zero. Equation Y1.4 now yields \(\Pi_{n,X}=0\) there. Finally

\[ \Pi_n(X,\eta)=\Pi_n(0,\eta)+\int_0^\infty\partial_R\Pi_n\,dR=m_{n,3}(\eta)=0 \quad(X\ge X_+). \tag{Y3.2} \]

Both constants of radial integration have been removed by their exact moments, rather than by imposing an additional exterior boundary datum.

At zero,

\[ F_n/X=\int_0^1U_n(sX,\eta)ds,\qquad V_n/X=\frac{2\eta U_n-2\eta(D+\lambda_n)F_n/X-d\partial_\eta(F_n/X)}{L}. \tag{Y3.3} \]

These formulas are smooth through the axis. The resulting original tuple

\[ \mathbf P_n=(\phi_n,U_n,V_n/X,\Pi_n,F_n/X),\qquad \operatorname{supp}_X\mathbf P_n\subset[0,X_+],\qquad \max_{k+\ell\le m}\sup_{X\ge0,|\eta|\le1}|\partial_X^k\partial_\eta^\ell\mathbf P_n|=C_{n,m}<\infty \tag{Y3.4} \]

has finite constants by smoothness and compactness; they may grow with n and m. The construction does not assert convergence of the unrestricted coefficient series.

The current \(E_n,U_n\) already vanish after the positive-order bump patch. Their total axial moment has vanished too, so Y3.1 and Y3.3 show that \(F_n,V_n\) vanish after that patch. In particular

\[ E_n=U_n=F_n=V_n=0\quad\hbox{on }\mathcal I_{\rm mean},\qquad n\ge1. \tag{Y3.5} \]

This does not set \(\Pi_n\) to zero on that earlier patch: \(\Omega_0\) can extend to \(X_v\). Choosing \(X_+\) beyond \(X_v\) was necessary for the pressure-support proof. All original patch and support distinctions are retained.

Y4. Residuals, radial boundary terms and total integrals

Convert the full cylindrical equations to conservative form, keeping every radial boundary term. The five moments then cancel the integrated residuals. At first order the angular viscosity uses a convergent subtracted leading moment.

The actual order-n tangential residuals, retaining every source term, are

\[ \begin{split} \mathfrak r_{\theta,n}={R\over\mathsf C}\bigg[ T_{b,n}\phi_n+\sum_{i+j=n}\{V_i(\phi_j'+\phi_j/X)+U_iZ_{b,j}\phi_j\} -2(X\phi_n''+2\phi_n')-Z_{b,n-1}^{[2]}\phi_{n-1}\bigg],\\ \mathfrak r_{z,n}=T_{c,n}U_n+\sum_{i+j=n}\{V_iU_j'+U_iZ_{c,j}U_j\} +Z_{-2A,n}\Pi_n-2(XU_n''+U_n')-Z_{c,n-1}^{[2]}U_{n-1}. \end{split} \tag{Y4.1} \]

Primes mean \(\partial_X\) at fixed η. These are D1.3–D1.4 with the full residual signs; their physical factors are \(q^{-A-1+\lambda_n}\). They vanish on \([0,X_-]\) by the inner equations and Y1.4. The stress is defined exactly as in original (5.9):

\[ \mathcal T_{n,\theta}=-R^{-2}\int_0^R\rho^2\mathfrak r_{\theta,n}(\rho,\eta)d\rho, \qquad \mathcal T_{n,z}=-R^{-1}\int_0^R\rho\mathfrak r_{z,n}(\rho,\eta)d\rho. \tag{Y4.2} \]

Differentiation gives \((\partial_R+2/R)\mathcal T_{n,\theta}=-\mathfrak r_{\theta,n}\) and \((\partial_R+1/R)\mathcal T_{n,z}=-\mathfrak r_{z,n}\). The physical stress factor is \(q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\), so the radial derivative contributes exactly \(q^{-1/2}\), yielding the required physical residual factor. These higher stresses are signed; no positivity is imposed on them.

To prove their total source integrals vanish, use the exact conservative equations for a smooth axisymmetric divergence-free field:

\[ \begin{split} r^2\mathcal R_\theta={}&\partial_t(r^2u_\theta)+\partial_r(r^2u_ru_\theta)+\partial_z(r^2u_zu_\theta) -\partial_r(r^2\partial_ru_\theta-ru_\theta)-\partial_{zz}(r^2u_\theta),\\ r\mathcal R_z={}&\partial_t(ru_z)+\partial_r(ru_ru_z)+\partial_z(r(u_z^2+p)) -\partial_r(r\partial_ru_z)-\partial_{zz}(ru_z). \end{split} \tag{Y4.3} \]

Expanding the transport derivatives and inserting \(\partial_ru_r+u_r/r+\partial_zu_z=0\) recovers the original angular connection term \(u_ru_\theta/r\) and the axial transport. Expanding the two radial viscous derivatives gives exactly \(r^2(u_{\theta,rr}+u_{\theta,r}/r-u_\theta/r^2)\) and \(r(u_{z,rr}+u_{z,r}/r)\). Thus no cylindrical term is omitted.

At the axis each \(u_{\theta,n}\) is r times a smooth function of r², \(u_{z,n}\) is smooth in r², and \(u_{r,n}\) is r times such a function, by D5 and Y3.3. Hence the radial angular transport boundary is \(O(r^4)\), the axial one \(O(r^2)\), and \(r^2\partial_ru_{\theta,n}-ru_{\theta,n}=O(r^4)\), \(r\partial_ru_{z,n}=O(r^2)\). All vanish at zero. At infinity the positive-order fields and their radial derivatives are compactly supported; the order-n transport products each contain such a factor. All radial boundary terms therefore vanish there as well.

At fixed physical z,t, the substitution \(r=\sqrt q R\) gives the exact undifferentiated moments

\[ \begin{split} \int_0^\infty r^2u_{\theta,n}dr&=q^{3/2-A+\lambda_n}m_{n,2}=0,\\ \int_0^\infty r^2\sum_{i+j=n}u_{z,i}u_{\theta,j}dr&=q^{3/2-2A+\lambda_n}m_{n,4}=0,\\ \int_0^\infty ru_{z,n}dr&=q^{1-A+\lambda_n}m_{n,1}=0,\\ \int_0^\infty r\left(\sum_{i+j=n}u_{z,i}u_{z,j}+p_n\right)dr &=q^{1-2A+\lambda_n}\int_0^\infty R\left(\sum_{i+j=n}U_iU_j+\Pi_n\right)dR =q^{1-2A+\lambda_n}m_{n,5}=0. \end{split} \tag{Y4.4} \]

For the last equality \(\Pi_n\) is now known to be compact and bounded at zero. Integration by parts gives \(\int R\Pi_n dR=[R^2\Pi_n/2]_0^\infty-\frac12\int R^2\partial_R\Pi_n dR\), with both boundary values zero. This use of compact pressure follows Y3, rather than preceding its proof. All product powers depend only on i+j=n. Positive-order integrals and all their fixed physical derivatives have locally bounded compact support for t<1, which justifies their differentiation.

For axial viscosity at n≥2, the analogous order-(n−1) angular and axial moments vanish by Y2.8. At n=1 the leading axial moment vanishes by V7 and P2. The leading angular moment requires its actual subtracted form, proved in H4.6 and preserved by the exact joining and shear moments:

\[ P(r)=c_\infty(r^2/2)^{-A},\qquad \int_0^\infty r^2[u_{\theta,0}(r,z,t)-P(r)]dr =q^{3/2-A}\int_0^\infty[\sqrt{2X}E_0-\sqrt{2X}c_\infty X^{-A}]dX=0. \tag{Y4.5} \]

Near zero the subtracted power has integrable weight \(r^{1-2h}\); the actual field is regular. At infinity H0.2–H0.4 give \(K-P=O(r^{-3-2h})\) for fixed t<1, so its weighted difference is integrable because h>0. On any compact neighborhood of physical (z,t) with t<1, the exterior starts before one finite radius and \(u_{\theta,0}=K(r,t)\) is z-independent beyond it. The same is true of P. Thus the first and second z derivatives of the difference have compact exterior support and are locally bounded at the axis; differentiation under Y4.5 is justified. It proves the vanishing order-one axial-viscosity angular moment without differentiating a divergent un-subtracted integral.

Integrating Y4.3 at order n, the first two moments in Y4.4 cancel the angular time and axial transport terms, and the last two cancel the axial time and flux terms. The preceding paragraph cancels both lower axial-viscosity moments. Removing the nonzero physical factors gives

\[ \int_0^\infty R^2\mathfrak r_{\theta,n}dR=0,\qquad \int_0^\infty R\mathfrak r_{z,n}dR=0. \tag{Y4.6} \]

Explicitly the physical weighted factors are \(q^{1/2-A+\lambda_n}\) and \(q^{-A+\lambda_n}\), respectively. These follow from the residual factor and \(r^2dr=q^{3/2}R^2dR\) or \(r\,dr=qR\,dR\). Time differentiation loses one power of q, axial differentiation loses D, and the order-(n−1) second axial derivative uses \(\lambda_n-\lambda_{n-1}=2h=1-2D\); each term in the respective integrated equation has exactly that same power.

Y5. Full stress support and the exceptional first-order term

The backward stress integral identifies the exact support. All later orders stop before the outer collar. The first order still sees the axial derivative of the leading heat multiplier, so its full flat factor must be calculated.

Equation Y4.6 converts the exact forward integrals into backward ones:

\[ \mathcal T_{n,\theta}=R^{-2}\int_R^\infty\rho^2\mathfrak r_{\theta,n}d\rho, \qquad \mathcal T_{n,z}=R^{-1}\int_R^\infty\rho\mathfrak r_{z,n}d\rho. \tag{Y5.1} \]

For n≥2, every same-order exterior residual term has a positive-order factor, and the axial-viscosity term acts on order n−1≥1. All are zero beyond \(X_+\) by Y3. On the inner interval the residuals vanish and the forward integrals are zero. Consequently

\[ \operatorname{supp}_X\mathcal T_n\subset[X_-,X_+]\quad(n\ge2). \tag{Y5.2} \]

At n=1 the only possible exterior term is the angular \(-\partial_{zz}u_{\theta,0}\); the leading axial field is already zero there. For \(X\ge X_b\), \(u_{\theta,0}=K(r,t)\) is independent of z. Thus

\[ \operatorname{supp}_X\mathcal T_1\subset[X_-,X_b],\qquad \mathcal T_{1,z}=0\quad(X\ge X_+). \tag{Y5.3} \]

Retain the full original terminal multiplier. In \(y=\log(X/X_{\rm tail})\), with \(X_b=e^3X_{\rm tail}\) and \(\delta_b=3-y\), it is

\[ \begin{gathered} f_o(y)=1-\rho_o[1-\sigma((y-1)/2)],\qquad \rho_o=c_oh,\\ 1-f_o=\rho_o e^{-4/\delta_b^2}g(\delta_b),\qquad g(\delta)=\big[e^{-(1-\delta/2)^{-2}}+e^{-4/\delta^2}\big]^{-1},\qquad g(0)=e. \end{gathered} \tag{Y5.4} \]

This is O0 and H6.3, including its denominator and amplitude. On a sufficiently small closed terminal collar, g is positive and smooth, with every fixed derivative bounded. The actual physical field there is

\[ u_{\theta,0}=K(r,t)f_o(y),\quad K=c_\infty(r^2/2)^{-A}\mathcal H(2(1-t)/(r^2/2)),\quad q^AK=c_\infty X^{-A}\mathcal H(2d/X). \tag{Y5.5} \]

The heat factor and all of its needed derivatives are the convergent integrals H0.1–H0.2, including the value at d=0. The factor 2 in its argument is retained.

At fixed physical r,t the coordinate identities P0 give

\[ \begin{gathered} \partial_zy=q^{-D}a_z,\quad a_z=-2\eta/L,\quad \partial_z\eta=q^{-D}d/L,\\ b_z=\frac{-2D\eta a_z+d\partial_\eta a_z}{L},\\ \partial_{zz}(Kf_o)=Kq^{-2D}(a_z^2\partial_{yy}f_o+b_z\partial_yf_o). \end{gathered} \tag{Y5.6} \]

K has no z dependence. Differentiating \(q^{-D}a_z\) gives \(q^{-2D}b_z\), which proves the last formula and retains its exponent derivative. Both \(a_z\) and \(b_z\) and their fixed derivatives are bounded because \(L\ge1-2h>0\). For \(\delta=\delta_b\) and g as in Y5.4 the exact multiplier derivatives are

\[ \begin{split} \partial_y f_o&=\rho_o e^{-4/\delta^2}(8\delta^{-3}g+g'),\\ \partial_{yy}f_o&=\rho_o e^{-4/\delta^2} \big[(24\delta^{-4}-64\delta^{-6})g-16\delta^{-3}g'-g''\big]. \end{split} \tag{Y5.7} \]

Hence the first is bounded by \(C e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^{-3}\) and the second by \(C e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^{-6}\) on a short collar. After multiplying the physical source by \(q^{A+1-\lambda_1}\), the power cancels exactly: \(\lambda_1=2h\) and \(1-\lambda_1-2D=0\). Thus its coefficient is the bounded smooth heat factor from Y5.5 times the two full expressions in Y5.6–Y5.7; no q-dependent constant remains.

For completeness, the radial integration gains exactly the three powers needed at this edge. For any smooth bounded \(B(s,\eta)\) on a small collar and fixed j≥0, the substitution \(s=\delta(1+\delta^2v)^{-1/2}\) gives

\[ \begin{split} \int_0^\delta e^{-4/s^2}s^{-j}B(s,\eta)ds ={}&\tfrac12e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^{3-j} \int_0^\infty e^{-4v}(1+\delta^2v)^{(j-3)/2} B\!\left(\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{1+\delta^2v}},\eta\right)dv. \end{split} \tag{Y5.8} \]

Its Jacobian is \(-\delta^3(1+\delta^2v)^{-3/2}/2\). Each fixed derivative of the final integrand is bounded by \(e^{-4v}\) times a polynomial in v, uniformly on the compact parameter rectangle. Dominated differentiation proves that the last integral is smooth through δ=0, with every fixed derivative finite. This also proves its endpoint value \(B(0,\eta)/4\).

In the backward angular integral Y5.1, \(R=\sqrt{2X_b}e^{-\delta/2}\) and \(dR=-R\,d\delta/2\); all these weights, including the exterior \(R^{-2}\), are smooth and bounded on the fixed collar. Applying Y5.8 to the finite terms of Y5.7, with j≤6, yields the actual smooth representation and bounds

\[ \mathcal T_{1,\theta}=e^{-4/\delta_b^2}\delta_b^{-3}B_1(\delta_b,\eta),\qquad |\mathcal T_1|\le Ce^{-4/\delta_b^2}\delta_b^{-3},\qquad |\partial_X^k\partial_\eta^\ell\mathcal T_1|\le C_{k,\ell}e^{-4/\delta_b^2}\delta_b^{-N_{k,\ell}}. \tag{Y5.9} \]

Here \(B_1\) is smooth; no nonzero endpoint value or sign for it is required. Terms with smaller j acquire the nonnegative powers \(\delta^{6-j}\) in \(B_1\). Each radial derivative of the exponential or the factor \(\delta^{-3}\) introduces only finitely many additional inverse powers; \(\partial_X\delta=-1/X\) and its derivatives are bounded on this collar. Thus every derivative tends to zero at \(X_b\) and the stress extends smoothly by zero there.

Y6. Original flat weight, all fixed derivatives and viscosity

Combine the actual support and endpoint calculation with the same weight used by the leading profile. Restore the original viscosity in both the physical stress and the residual.

Retain V6's actual common weight and the source distance:

\[ \zeta(X)=\exp\!\left[-\frac{t_1^2}{\log(X/X_a)^2}-\frac4{\log(X_b/X)^2}\right],\qquad \delta(X)=\min\{1,\log(X/X_a),\log(X_b/X)\}. \tag{Y6.1} \]

For n≥2, Y5.2 puts every stress and derivative in a fixed compact subinterval of \((X_a,X_b)\), where ζ has a positive minimum. Smoothness then gives Y6.2 below with \(N_{n,k,\ell}=0\). For n=1, the stress is zero on \([0,X_-]\), while near \(X_b\) the inner factor \(\exp(-t_1^2/\log(X/X_a)^2)\) and its reciprocal are smooth and bounded. Equation Y5.9 supplies Y6.2 on that outer collar. On the remaining compact middle interval, smoothness and the positive minimum of ζ supply it as well. Therefore

\[ |\partial_X^k\partial_\eta^\ell\mathcal T_n(X,\eta)| \le C_{n,k,\ell}\zeta(X)\delta(X)^{-N_{n,k,\ell}} \quad(X_a<X<X_b,\ |\eta|\le1), \qquad N_{n,k,\ell}=0\quad(n\ge2). \tag{Y6.2} \]

This proves original (5.13) for every fixed derivative; all constants may depend on n,k,ℓ and the already fixed profile parameters. No simultaneous derivative smallness or uniform bound over all orders has been used.

For the original viscosity ν>0 retain D6.2 and the stress map

\[ x_\nu=\sqrt\nu x,\quad t_\nu=t,\quad u_{n,\nu}(x_\nu,t)=\sqrt\nu u_n(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t),\quad p_{n,\nu}=\nu p_n(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t),\quad T_{n,\nu}=\nu q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\mathcal T_n. \tag{Y6.3} \]

The last expression is evaluated at \(X=r_\nu^2/(2\nu q),\eta=z_\nu/(\sqrt\nu q^D)\), in the original cylindrical components. Spatial differentiation contributes \(\nu^{-1/2}\); hence divergence of this stress and every term of the momentum residual have the same factor \(\sqrt\nu\). Incompressibility is preserved by the same exact derivative map. The five profile moments and all fixed profile bounds above are unchanged statements in their original variables, with these physical factors explicitly restored. This does not change the target viscosity.

Y7. Actual induction and its precise endpoint

Start with the actual first coefficient, complete its global extension, and only then form the source for the next coefficient. The construction uses the same radii, cutoff and bumps at every order.

At n=1, D6 supplies the actual inner solution using only the already constructed leading profile. Equations Y1.1–Y1.4 define its tentative global extension; Y2.6 supplies all five actual smooth correction functions without a small-discrepancy requirement. Y3–Y6 prove its complete support, moments, retained analytic interval and stress bounds, including its exceptional outer heat term.

Suppose the construction has completed the finite orders 1 through n−1. Their full sources in D2.2 are then defined and smooth; D1.7 proves axis regularity, and Y1 preserves their fixed-derivative holomorphic parameter domains on \([0,a^2]\). The D3–D5 series therefore constructs the actual next inner coefficient on that same interval. Apply the explicit Y1 and Y2 formulas to it. Their lower sources are the completed fields, and all integrals are finite by the support argument in Y2–Y3. The constant matrices are the same as before. Y3–Y6 then prove exactly the properties needed at order n. This induction constructs a single sequence at every positive integer order, with one set of radii, one cutoff and one set of bumps.

Every finite order now satisfies original (5.2) and (5.5) globally, the full equations (5.3)–(5.4) on the common inner interval, all five moment identities, the tuple support (5.12), the stress support and derivative estimate (5.13), the profile bounds (5.17), and the reserved-mean-patch equalities (5.18). The coefficient values are given by the convergent integral solution followed by finite explicit integrals and the two fixed matrix inverses. No coefficient or missing source has been assumed into existence.

Y8. Five worked exercises

Exercise 1. Prove determinant signs and explicit lower bounds for the actual bump matrices

Use the five smooth bumps in Y1.2, with their original integrals \(I_j\), to give positive lower bounds for \(|\det B_U|\) and \(\det B_E\). Retain every power of the patch endpoints and the profile slope.

Solution. Put \(H=R_q-R_p>0\) and \(g=H/15\). Consecutive support centers are separated by \(H/6\); the sum of their two widths is \(H/10\). Therefore any points in consecutive bump supports differ by at least \(g\). Every point lies between \(R_p\) and \(R_q\). Each actual density is \(b_j=w_j/I_j\) and has integral one.

For the two axial columns at \(r_1<r_2\), retain the exact determinant

\[ \det\begin{pmatrix} r_1&r_2\\ r_1^{1-2\lambda}&r_2^{1-2\lambda} \end{pmatrix} =r_1r_2(r_2^{-2\lambda}-r_1^{-2\lambda}) =-2\lambda r_1r_2\int_{r_1}^{r_2}s^{-2\lambda-1}\,ds. \tag{Y8.1} \]

The integrand is positive. Since \(\lambda>0\), its value is at least \(R_q^{-2\lambda-1}\), while \(r_1r_2\ge R_p^2\). Integrate the determinant against the two actual bump densities as in Y2.7. Their product integral is one. This proves

\[ \det B_U<0,\qquad |\det B_U|\ge 2\lambda R_p^2R_q^{-2\lambda-1}g>0. \tag{Y8.2} \]

For the three angular columns use points \(r_1<r_2<r_3\) in their ordered supports, and put \(x_j=r_j^2\) only for this determinant calculation. Factoring the indicated powers from each column, without discarding them, gives

\[ \begin{split} \det(r_j^{s_i})_{i,j=1}^3 &=\left(\prod_{j=1}^3r_j^{-2-2\lambda}\right) \det\begin{pmatrix} x_1^{2+\lambda}&x_2^{2+\lambda}&x_3^{2+\lambda}\\ 1&1&1\\ x_1&x_2&x_3 \end{pmatrix}\\ &=\left(\prod_{j=1}^3r_j^{-2-2\lambda}\right) \prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)\,F[x_1,x_2,x_3], \qquad F(x)=x^{2+\lambda}. \end{split} \tag{Y8.3} \]

The cyclic row permutation has positive sign. Subtracting the first column from the other two proves the divided-difference formula displayed here. Its last factor is at least half the minimum of \(F''\) on the interval: if \(c=\min F''\), then \(F-cx^2/2\) is convex, its second divided difference is nonnegative by increasing secant slopes, and that of \(cx^2/2\) is \(c/2\). In this case

\[ F[x_1,x_2,x_3]\ge \tfrac12(2+\lambda)(1+\lambda)R_p^{2\lambda}. \tag{Y8.4} \]

The two consecutive differences in \(x\) are at least \(2R_pg\), and the remaining difference is at least \(4R_pg\). The column factor is at least \(R_q^{-6-6\lambda}\). Integrating Y8.3 against all three actual densities therefore proves

\[ \det B_E\ge 8(2+\lambda)(1+\lambda) R_p^{3+2\lambda}g^3R_q^{-6-6\lambda}>0. \tag{Y8.5} \]

These bounds prove invertibility for the finite-width smooth bumps themselves. They use neither point-mass replacement nor numerical determinant sampling. The factor \(\lambda\) in Y8.2 is retained; no bound uniform as \(\lambda\) tends to zero is asserted.

Exercise 2. Bound the full moment correction in every fixed parameter norm

Prove an explicit \(C^m([-1,1])\) bound for the five actual correction functions. Retain the row factors \(e_*f\), \(2e_*f\), and \(-e_*f\).

Solution. For a vector function \(v\), use \(\|v\|_{C^m}=\max_{0\le j\le m,\,|\eta|\le1}|v^{(j)}(\eta)|_\infty\), and use the induced maximum matrix norm. Since the original \(f=(1+\eta^2)^{-1}\), Y2.6 is exactly

\[ \begin{split} \alpha_n&=-B_U^{-1} \begin{pmatrix}m_{n,1}^0\\(1+\eta^2)m_{n,4}^0/e_*\end{pmatrix},\\ \beta_n&=-B_E^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} m_{n,2}^0\\ (1+\eta^2)m_{n,3}^0/(2e_*)\\ -(1+\eta^2)m_{n,5}^0/e_* \end{pmatrix}. \end{split} \tag{Y8.6} \]

The exact product rule, with terms of negative derivative order omitted, is

\[ \partial_\eta^j[(1+\eta^2)v] =(1+\eta^2)v^{(j)}+2j\eta v^{(j-1)} +j(j-1)v^{(j-2)}. \tag{Y8.7} \]

Thus \(P_m=m^2+m+2\) bounds the multiplier in every derivative through \(m\). Keeping the three rows visible gives

\[ \begin{split} \|\alpha_n\|_{C^m} &\le\|B_U^{-1}\| \max\{\|m_{n,1}^0\|_{C^m},(P_m/e_*)\|m_{n,4}^0\|_{C^m}\},\\ \|\beta_n\|_{C^m} &\le\|B_E^{-1}\| \max\{\|m_{n,2}^0\|_{C^m}, (P_m/(2e_*))\|m_{n,3}^0\|_{C^m}, (P_m/e_*)\|m_{n,5}^0\|_{C^m}\}. \end{split} \tag{Y8.8} \]

These are finite constants for the fixed original patch. The inverse norms can also be bounded explicitly by the adjugate formula, Y8.2 and Y8.5, since every entry of Y2.5 is bounded by the supremum of its retained power on \([R_p,R_q]\).

For example, with the exact bump derivatives

\[ M_{U,k}=\sup_{X\ge0}\sum_{j=1}^2 |\partial_X^k b_j^U(\sqrt{2X})|,\qquad M_{E,k}=\sup_{X\ge0}\sum_{j=1}^3 |\partial_X^k b_j^E(\sqrt{2X})|, \tag{Y8.9} \]

all of which are finite because their supports stay away from the axis, the actual added profiles satisfy

\[ \|\partial_X^k\partial_\eta^\ell(U_n-\widetilde U_n)\|_\infty \le M_{U,k}\|\alpha_n\|_{C^\ell},\qquad \|\partial_X^k\partial_\eta^\ell(E_n-\widetilde E_n)\|_\infty \le M_{E,k}\|\beta_n\|_{C^\ell}. \tag{Y8.10} \]

For \(\phi_n\), replace the angular bump in \(M_{E,k}\) by its full factor \(\mathsf C b_j^E(\sqrt{2X})/\sqrt{2X}\). Its support still stays away from zero. For two discrepancy vectors with the lower profiles fixed, subtract Y8.6: the same bounds hold for their differences. This proves a bounded linear correction map on each stated norm, with the actual row factors and supports. The discrepancies can be arbitrarily large and finite; no smallness is needed at this coefficient order.

Exercise 3. Identify the exterior defects that the five moments remove

Before imposing the moments, calculate the exterior radial velocity and pressure. After the first and third moments are zero, express both total tangential residuals in terms of the remaining moments, and recover their physical stress tails.

Solution. Keep the lower global coefficients fixed, and take a tentative smooth current \(U_n,E_n\) supported to the left of \(X_+\), with \(V_n,\Pi_n\) defined by Y1.4. The lower fields already have the support proved in the induction. The moments \(m_{n,j}\) are those of this tentative extension.

For \(X\ge X_+\), the forward formulas give exactly

\[ F_n=m_{n,1},\qquad V_n=-\frac{2\eta(D+\lambda_n)m_{n,1} +d\,\partial_\eta m_{n,1}}{L},\qquad \Pi_n=m_{n,3}. \tag{Y8.11} \]

Indeed \(U_n=0\), \(\mathcal A_XU_n=m_{n,1}/X\), and D0.4 gives the middle formula. The pressure derivative vanishes there because all its products have a positive-order angular factor and \(\Omega_{n-1}\) contains only the completed lower radial fields. Its axis value is zero, so its exterior constant is the third moment. Consequently the full tuple \(\mathbf P_n\) has zero exterior precisely when \(m_{n,1}=m_{n,3}=0\). Necessity uses \(F_n/X\) and \(\Pi_n\), not a claim that the equation \(V_n=0\) alone forces \(m_{n,1}=0\).

Now impose those two moments, so all current velocity and pressure fields are compactly supported. Define the original operators on functions of \(\eta\) alone,

\[ \mathscr T_\beta v=\frac{-\beta v+D\eta v'}L,\qquad \mathscr Z_\beta v=\frac{2\beta\eta v+dv'}L. \tag{Y8.12} \]

Write \(I_{\theta,n}=\int_0^\infty R^2\mathfrak r_{\theta,n}\,dR\) and \(I_{z,n}=\int_0^\infty R\mathfrak r_{z,n}\,dR\). Apply the exact conservative equations Y4.3 and the undifferentiated moments Y4.4. The lower axial-viscosity moments are zero, including the subtracted first-order angular moment Y4.5. Hence

\[ \begin{split} I_{\theta,n} &=\mathscr T_{3/2-A+\lambda_n}m_{n,2} +\mathscr Z_{3/2-2A+\lambda_n}m_{n,4},\\ I_{z,n} &=\mathscr T_{1-A+\lambda_n}m_{n,1} +\mathscr Z_{1-2A+\lambda_n}m_{n,5} =\mathscr Z_{1-2A+\lambda_n}m_{n,5}. \end{split} \tag{Y8.13} \]

The angular common power is \(q^{1/2-A+\lambda_n}\); the axial common power is \(q^{-A+\lambda_n}\). In the flux terms these follow from \(A+D=1\). The second axial derivative from order \(n-1\) uses \(2h=1-2D\), exactly as in Y4.6.

Let \(X_e=X_+\) for \(n\ge2\), and \(X_e=X_b\) for \(n=1\). Beyond that radius the residual sources vanish, while their forward stress integrals need not. Their full tails are

\[ \mathcal T_{n,\theta}=-\frac{I_{\theta,n}}{R^2}, \qquad \mathcal T_{n,z}=-\frac{I_{z,n}}R \qquad(X\ge X_e). \tag{Y8.14} \]

This follows directly from Y4.2, including its negative sign. In the original viscosity variables \(R=r_\nu/\sqrt{\nu q}\), Y6.3 gives

\[ \begin{split} T_{n,\nu,\theta} &=-\frac{\nu^2 q^{1/2-A+\lambda_n}}{r_\nu^2}I_{\theta,n},\\ T_{n,\nu,z} &=-\frac{\nu^{3/2}q^{-A+\lambda_n}}{r_\nu}I_{z,n}. \end{split} \tag{Y8.15} \]

The first and third moments remove the radial integration defects; the other three make Y8.13 zero and hence remove both stress tails. This proves the exact map from the five original moments to the exterior defects. It does not claim that five zero moments are necessary for the two differential combinations in Y8.13 alone to vanish.

Exercise 4. Compute the actual first-order outer stress coefficient

Find the endpoint value of \(B_1\) in Y5.9, retaining the full heat factor. At \(\eta=0\), determine the sharper leading term that survives when this endpoint value vanishes.

Solution. Set

\[ R_b=\sqrt{2X_b},\qquad R(s)=R_be^{-s/2},\qquad \mathcal E(s,\eta)=c_\infty(X_be^{-s})^{-A} \mathcal H\!\left(\frac{2(1-\eta^2)}{X_be^{-s}}\right),\qquad \mathcal E_b(\eta)=\mathcal E(0,\eta)>0. \tag{Y8.16} \]

These are exactly the heat factors in Y5.5, with every constant and argument retained. Put \(\delta=\log(X_b/X)\). The coefficient of the physical first-order residual on the terminal collar is

\[ \mathfrak r_{\theta,1} =-\mathcal E(\delta,\eta) \big(a_z^2 f_{o,yy}+b_zf_{o,y}\big), \qquad \mathfrak r_{z,1}=0. \tag{Y8.17} \]

The physical power cancels because \(1-\lambda_1-2D=0\). Substituting the exact multiplier derivatives Y5.7 gives the full expression

\[ \begin{split} \mathfrak r_{\theta,1} =\rho_o\mathcal E e^{-4/\delta^2} \big[& 64a_z^2g\,\delta^{-6}-24a_z^2g\,\delta^{-4} +16a_z^2g'\,\delta^{-3}+a_z^2g''\\ &-8b_zg\,\delta^{-3}-b_zg'\big]. \end{split} \tag{Y8.18} \]

Here \(a_z,b_z\) retain their full functions of \(\eta\) from Y5.6. The backward integral is exactly

\[ \mathcal T_{1,\theta}(\delta,\eta) =\frac1{2R(\delta)^2} \int_0^\delta R(s)^3\mathfrak r_{\theta,1}(s,\eta)\,ds. \tag{Y8.19} \]

Apply Y5.8 term by term. The coefficient of \(s^{-6}\) in the integrand, including its factor \(1/2\), is \(32\rho_o R(s)^3\mathcal E(s,\eta)a_z^2g(s)\). Y5.8 divides its endpoint value by \(8\); the outside \(R(\delta)^{-2}\) is retained. Every other term acquires a strictly positive power of \(\delta\) after extracting \(e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^{-3}\). Thus the actual smooth coefficient obeys

\[ \begin{split} B_1(0,\eta) &=4\rho_o R_b\mathcal E_b(\eta)a_z(\eta)^2g(0)\\ &=\frac{16e\rho_o R_b\mathcal E_b(\eta)\eta^2}{L(\eta)^2}. \end{split} \tag{Y8.20} \]

It is positive for every fixed \(\eta\ne0\), including the one-sided parameter endpoints, and zero at \(\eta=0\). No factor from the heat profile or radial measure has been absorbed.

At \(\eta=0\), the exact values are \(a_z=0\), \(b_z=-2\). Y8.18 becomes \(2\rho_o\mathcal E(\delta,0)e^{-4/\delta^2}(8\delta^{-3}g+g')\). The same integral identity, now with \(j=3\) and \(j=0\), proves

\[ \mathcal T_{1,\theta}(\delta,0) =e^{-4/\delta^2}B_{\rm eq}(\delta),\qquad B_{\rm eq}\in C^\infty([0,\delta_0]),\qquad B_{\rm eq}(0)=e\rho_oR_b\mathcal E_b(0)>0. \tag{Y8.21} \]

The \(j=0\) term contributes three additional powers and has zero endpoint coefficient. This explains the exact improvement at the parameter midpoint without discarding the first-order outer term.

Exercise 5. Prove sharp derivative powers and the exact comparison with the leading stress

Give explicit powers in Y6.2 for \(n=1\), and compare the first correction with the original leading angular stress at the outer edge. Prove the resulting endpoint statement for every actual finite coefficient stress sum.

Solution. The representation in Y5.9 is an actual smooth factorization: \(\mathcal T_{1,\theta}=e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^{-3}B_1(\delta,\eta)\). All fixed derivatives of \(B_1\) are bounded on a common closed collar. Since \(\partial_X\delta=-1/X\),

\[ \partial_X e^{-4/\delta^2} =-\frac8{X\delta^3}e^{-4/\delta^2}. \tag{Y8.22} \]

Each radial derivative falling on the exponential therefore costs at most three inverse powers; derivatives of a remaining power cost one, and all derivatives of \(X^{-1}\) and the smooth factors are bounded. Parameter derivatives act only on the smooth coefficient. Induction and the product rule prove

\[ |\partial_X^k\partial_\eta^\ell\mathcal T_1| \le C_{k,\ell}\zeta(X)\delta(X)^{-(3k+3)} \qquad(X_a<X<X_b,\ |\eta|\le1). \tag{Y8.23} \]

Near the outer edge, the inner exponential factor in \(\zeta\) and its reciprocal are bounded. On the remaining compact middle interval use smoothness and a positive minimum of \(\zeta\); near the inner edge the stress is zero. This proves the whole-annulus estimate with the original weight.

For fixed \(\eta\ne0\), the unique most singular derivative term is obtained by putting every radial derivative on the exponential. Every other product-rule term has a smaller inverse power. Hence

\[ \lim_{\delta\downarrow0} \delta^{3k+3}e^{4/\delta^2}\partial_X^k \mathcal T_{1,\theta} =(-8/X_b)^kB_1(0,\eta)\ne0. \tag{Y8.24} \]

Thus the radial exponent \(3k+3\) cannot be reduced uniformly over parameters containing such a point. At \(\eta=0\), Y8.21 instead gives

\[ \lim_{\delta\downarrow0} \delta^{3k}e^{4/\delta^2}\partial_X^k \mathcal T_{1,\theta}(\delta,0) =(-8/X_b)^k e\rho_oR_b\mathcal E_b(0). \tag{Y8.25} \]

This midpoint refinement concerns radial derivatives at that fixed parameter; it does not assert the same power for arbitrary parameter derivatives there.

The complete leading stress, unchanged by the joining and shear moments, satisfies H6.6–H6.8:

\[ \mathcal T_{0,\theta}=e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^{-3}b_\theta,\quad b_\theta(0,\eta)=\frac{16e\rho_o\mathcal E_b(\eta)}{R_b}>0,\quad \mathcal T_{0,z}=e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^3b_z. \tag{Y8.26} \]

Both coefficients are smooth on a closed collar and \(b_\theta\) has a positive lower bound. Therefore the exact quotient of the original stresses extends smoothly, with

\[ \frac{\mathcal T_{1,\theta}}{\mathcal T_{0,\theta}} =\frac{B_1}{b_\theta} \longrightarrow\frac{2X_b\eta^2}{L^2},\qquad \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\delta^{-3} \frac{\mathcal T_{1,\theta}(\delta,0)} {\mathcal T_{0,\theta}(\delta,0)} =\frac{X_b}{8}. \tag{Y8.27} \]

These are exact comparisons; Y8.20 and Y8.26 retain the full factors before taking their quotient. In particular \(\mathcal T_{1,\theta}/\zeta\) is unbounded like \(\delta^{-3}\) at every fixed nonzero \(\eta\), even though its ratio to the leading angular stress has a finite limit. The different weights must not be substituted for each other.

For any fixed \(q>0\) and integer \(N\ge1\), use the actual finite stress

\[ \widehat T^{[N]}=\mathcal T_0+\sum_{n=1}^Nq^{2nh}\mathcal T_n. \tag{Y8.28} \]

On \(X>X_+\), every \(n\ge2\) term is identically zero and \(\mathcal T_{1,z}=0\). Thus throughout the outer collar

\[ \begin{split} \widehat T^{[N]}_\theta &=e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^{-3} (b_\theta+q^{2h}B_1),\\ \widehat T^{[N]}_z &=e^{-4/\delta^2}\delta^3b_z,\\ \left.\frac{b_\theta+q^{2h}B_1}{b_\theta}\right|_{\delta=0} &=1+q^{2h}\frac{2X_b\eta^2}{L^2}>0. \end{split} \tag{Y8.29} \]

For fixed \(q\), compactness gives a common smaller collar where the angular coefficient is positive. The exact direction is

\[ \frac{\widehat T^{[N]}}{|\widehat T^{[N]}|} =\frac{(1,\ \delta^6 b_z/(b_\theta+q^{2h}B_1))} {\sqrt{1+\delta^{12}[b_z/(b_\theta+q^{2h}B_1)]^2}} \longrightarrow(1,0). \tag{Y8.30} \]

It extends smoothly to the endpoint. The original physical stress is \(\nu q^{-A-1/2}\widehat T^{[N]}\), evaluated at the original viscosity coordinates of Y6.3. Its positive scalar factor preserves this direction and retains every physical scale. These finite sums use the already constructed coefficients. Their convergence without cutoffs is not asserted; the subsequent base construction supplies the actual infinite sum.

What the global coefficient construction supplies

Y0–Y7 construct the entire actual coefficient sequence, with one fixed radial geometry, the full original equations on the protected axis interval, all five exact moments, compact coefficient support and the two required stress supports. The first-order outer term is retained with the same flat weight as the leading profile. Y8 proves quantitative matrix bounds, the exact exterior-defect map, sharp first-order edge powers and its smooth comparison with the leading stress.

The next lesson constructs the actual base field from this sequence, using cutoffs of the full vector potentials and both stress components. Its complete proof is supplied in the separate base-field audit, Z0–Z8. The actual base-field lesson, Z0–Z9, gives that construction and its consequences.

Constructing the actual base field

NS-BLOWUP N3.3. The preceding lessons construct every coefficient. This lesson turns that sequence into an actual smooth, divergence-free velocity and its pressure and stress, while keeping the entire coefficient expansion. The remaining augmented momentum residual decays faster than every power of the original scale, with every fixed physical derivative.

The local coefficient lesson, D0–D7, and the global extension lesson, Y0–Y8, supply the actual coefficients. The leading-profile lesson, V0–V8, supplies their leading field and common stress weight. The general summation lesson gives the differential-polynomial argument; here every input is constructed for the actual base, and the full residual is written out.

The source is OpenAI, Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes, pages 55–62, (5.23)–(5.46), Propositions 5.3 and 5.5 and Lemma 5.4. SOURCES.json gives the bibliographical details. This is independent teaching and editorial mathematics; the diplomatic transcription keeps OpenAI's text.

Figure. Here \(\mathcal U_B=(u_B,p_B,T_{\rm phys})\). The displayed operators and factors are the ones proved below. The final panel records the exact axis residual of the actual base, including its first cutoff. This is an operator diagram, with no numerical flow sample.

Z0. Exact Cartesian fields and the derivative loss

Begin with the original physical components. Their exact derivative powers determine how long a finite sum must be before it can control a prescribed residual derivative.

Keep the original \(q,A,D,h,\eta,X,\lambda_n=2nh\), \(R=\sqrt{2X}\) and \(\mathsf C\) from D. Define only the explicit coordinate map \(\xi=(x_1,x_2)/\sqrt q\); then \(X=|\xi|^2/2\) and every original profile below is evaluated at that same X and η. The original velocity coefficients, with every radial and angular factor, are

\[ \begin{split} u_{\theta,n}e_\theta&=q^{-A+\lambda_n}\frac{\phi_n}{\mathsf C}(-\xi_2,\xi_1,0),\\ u_{z,n}e_z&=q^{-A+\lambda_n}U_ne_z,\\ u_{r,n}e_r&=\tfrac12q^{-1/2+\lambda_n}\frac{V_n}{X}(\xi_1,\xi_2,0),\\ p_n&=q^{-2A+\lambda_n}\Pi_n. \end{split} \tag{Z0.1} \]

The factor 1/2 in the radial row follows from \(V_n/R^2=V_n/(2X)\). Y3.3 proves the smooth Cartesian representatives at the axis. On every compact profile range, all fixed mixed derivatives of these representatives are bounded by the already constructed coefficient bounds; their constants can depend on n.

On a function of \((q,\xi,\eta)\), the exact physical differentiation operators are

\[ \begin{gathered} \partial_{x_i}=q^{-1/2}\partial_{\xi_i}\quad(i=1,2),\\ \partial_t=q^{-1}L^{-1}\left(-q\partial_q+\tfrac12\xi\cdot\nabla_\xi+D\eta\partial_\eta\right),\\ \partial_z=q^{-D}L^{-1}\left(2\eta q\partial_q-\eta\xi\cdot\nabla_\xi+d\partial_\eta\right). \end{gathered} \tag{Z0.2} \]

They follow by differentiating \(q(1-\eta^2)=1-t\) and \(q^D\eta=z\), then \(\xi=x_\perp/\sqrt q\). In particular the q and η derivatives are exactly those in P0, and the ξ terms follow from the derivative of \(q^{-1/2}\).

For a profile g(ξ,η), each time application of Z0.2 subtracts one from the q exponent, each axial application subtracts D, and each transverse application subtracts 1/2. Differentiating any coefficient involving L,η,ξ leaves bounded smooth coefficients on a compact profile range, since \(L\ge1-2h>0\). After m derivatives there are finitely many terms; each exponent differentiation contributes a factor β−c with |c|≤m. Induction on m therefore proves

\[ |\partial_{x_\perp}^{\alpha}\partial_z^k\partial_t^\ell(q^\beta g(\xi,\eta))| \le C_m(1+|\beta|)^m\|g\|_{C^m}\, q^{\beta-|\alpha|/2-Dk-\ell},\qquad m=|\alpha|+k+\ell. \tag{Z0.3} \]

Every norm here is on the specified compact profile range. Constants depend on that range and h, but the exponent loss does not depend on β or the coefficient order. Powers of \(\lambda_n\) remain in the finite coefficient constants. No coordinate, factor or field is replaced by its largest-order estimate.

Z1. All terms in the finite augmented residual

A finite sum is an actual smooth field. List its residual directly, including products beyond the truncation and both shifts of radial viscosity; then bound the resulting finite expression.

Use the original finite tuple

\[ \mathcal U^{[N]}=\sum_{n=0}^N(u_n,p_n,q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\mathcal T_n),\qquad \mathcal F_{\rm slow}(u,p,T)=\mathscr R(u,p) +(\partial_r+2/r)T_\theta e_\theta+(\partial_r+1/r)T_ze_z. \tag{Z1.1} \]

Here \(\mathscr R=\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p\) is the source's coefficient-one operator; the exact map back to the original ν is D6.2/Y6.3. All finite velocities are divergence-free by the independently proved order-by-order identity D0.4. Y4.1–Y4.2 cancel the two complete tangential residual coefficients at every retained positive order; the leading ones cancel by P1 and V7. The radial pressure relation D1.5 cancels the retained radial coefficients as well.

The unretained terms can be listed without an appeal to a formal infinite series. Products of two retained fields have \(i,j\le N\); tangential products have total order i+j, and their omitted terms have \(i+j>N\). Tangential axial viscosity acting on a retained order j has order j+1, so only its unretained last index \(j=N\) remains. Time, transverse viscosity and pressure differentiation otherwise retain their index in the tangential equations. In particular the exact tangential components of the remaining augmented residual are

\[ \begin{split} (\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[N]}))_\theta ={}&\frac R{\mathsf C}\sum_{\substack{0\le i,j\le N\\i+j>N}} q^{-A-1+\lambda_{i+j}}\{V_i(\phi_j'+\phi_j/X)+U_iZ_{b,j}\phi_j\} -\frac R{\mathsf C}q^{-A-1+\lambda_{N+1}}Z_{b,N}^{[2]}\phi_N,\\ (\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[N]}))_z ={}&\sum_{\substack{0\le i,j\le N\\i+j>N}} q^{-A-1+\lambda_{i+j}}\{V_iU_j'+U_iZ_{c,j}U_j\} -q^{-A-1+\lambda_{N+1}}Z_{c,N}^{[2]}U_N. \end{split} \tag{Z1.2} \]

Primes mean \(\partial_X\). All operators and profiles are the full ones in D0–D1, and \(\lambda_{i+j}=\lambda_i+\lambda_j\); the index does not denote an unconstructed product profile.

For the radial equation multiplied by r, retain the two distinct physical factors from D1.5–D1.6:

\[ q^{-2A+\lambda_n}\left[2X\Pi_n'-\mathsf C^{-2}2X\sum_{i+j=n}\phi_i\phi_j\right],\qquad q^{-1+\lambda_k}\Omega_k. \tag{Z1.3} \]

The second factor has radial coefficient order k+1 because \(-1+\lambda_k=-2A+\lambda_{k+1}\). Thus radial time and transverse viscosity at retained index j enter order j+1; radial transport products at i+j=k enter order k+1. The radial axial-viscosity term acting on j enters order j+2, because \(-2D+\lambda_j=-2A+\lambda_{j+2}\). This last shift retains the full axial viscosity of \(V_N\): it is not part of the tangential j+1 rule. The pressure/centrifugal difference has order n=i+j in its products. Every coefficient of order at most N cancels by the equations already proved, including all middle terms. All remaining orders are at least N+1 and there are only finitely many of them; radial orders can reach max(2N+1,N+2).

More explicitly the exact remaining radial component, multiplied by r, is

\[ \begin{split} r(\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[N]}))_r ={}&-\frac{2X}{\mathsf C^2}\sum_{\substack{0\le i,j\le N\\i+j>N}}q^{-2A+\lambda_{i+j}}\phi_i\phi_j +q^{-1+\lambda_N}(T_{0,N}V_N-2XV_N'')\\ &+\sum_{\substack{0\le i,j\le N\\i+j+1>N}}q^{-1+\lambda_{i+j}} \{V_i(V_j'-V_j/(2X))+U_iZ_{0,j}V_j\}\\ &-\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le N\\j+2>N}}q^{-2D+\lambda_j}Z_{0,j}^{[2]}V_j. \end{split} \tag{Z1.4} \]

For N=0 the last sum has j=0; for N≥1 it has precisely \(j=N-1,N\). This includes the entire final axial-viscosity contribution. The stress pair has only tangential divergence, so it adds no radial term to this identity.

After dividing the radial equation by r, the common radial power is \(q^{-2A-1/2+\lambda_n}\); the tangential power is \(q^{-A-1+\lambda_n}\). Division by R in the radial coefficient is regular: \(\Omega_k=X\) times the smooth function D1.7, while the pressure/centrifugal bracket has factor X. Multiplication by \(e_r\) then gives \(R e_r=(\xi_1,\xi_2,0)\), with its retained numerical factors. The angular bracket in Y4.1 has its explicit R factor and hence a smooth Cartesian angular vector. The only cylindrical factors in the stress divergence occur on \([X_a,X_b]\), away from X=0, where \(R^{-1}\) and every fixed derivative are bounded. Consequently all remaining coefficient functions are smooth Cartesian functions with finite bounds on each fixed compact profile range.

Since 0<q≤1 and 2A+1/2>A+1 for h>0, the exact powers above and Z0.3 give the concrete estimate

\[ |\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[N]})|_m \le C_{N,m}q^{2h(N+1)-(2A+1/2+m)}. \tag{Z1.5} \]

Here \(|\cdot|_m\) is the original maximum of Cartesian space-time derivatives through order m. This estimate retains every term of Z1.2–Z1.4. Its exponent loss is independent of N, and its constant may depend on N,m and the compact profile range. It proves the finite-residual assertion of original (5.25), with an explicit allowable loss. There is no additional finite-stage remainder in this application.

Z2. The actual Stokes potential and its full cutoff curl

A scalar cutoff of a divergence-free velocity usually has nonzero divergence. Cutting its vector potential supplies the precise radial term that restores the equation.

For positive order use the exact \(F_n\) from Y1.4 and \(s=r^2/2=qX\). The physical Stokes function and vector potential are

\[ S_n=q^{1-A+\lambda_n}F_n,\qquad \mathcal A_n=(S_n/r)e_\theta =\frac12q^{-A+\lambda_n}\frac{F_n}{X}(-x_2,x_1,0) =\frac12q^{1/2-A+\lambda_n}\frac{F_n}{X}(-\xi_2,\xi_1,0). \tag{Z2.1} \]

These equalities retain the factor 1/2 and both coordinate representations. The actual potential is smooth at the Cartesian axis because \(F_n\)/X is smooth. Direct curl in cylindrical coordinates gives

\[ \operatorname{curl}\mathcal A_n=-\frac{\partial_zS_n}{r}e_r+\frac{\partial_rS_n}{r}e_z, \quad \partial_sS_n=q^{-A+\lambda_n}U_n=u_{z,n}, \quad -\partial_zS_n=q^{\lambda_n}V_n=ru_{r,n}. \tag{Z2.2} \]

The last identity follows from the full expression D0.4 and \(F_n=X\mathcal A_XU_n\); it includes the derivative of \(q^{1-A+\lambda_n}\). Thus the potential is proved to give the original radial and axial fields.

Let χ be smooth, equal to one on [0,1/2] and zero on [1,∞), and let \(c_n>0\). Cutting the potential before taking curl gives the exact fields

\[ \begin{split} ru_{r,n}^{\rm cut} &=q^{\lambda_n}\left[\chi(c_nq)V_n-\frac{2\eta}{L}(c_nq)\chi'(c_nq)F_n\right],\\ u_{z,n}^{\rm cut}&=q^{-A+\lambda_n}\chi(c_nq)U_n,\qquad u_{\theta,n}^{\rm cut}=q^{-A+\lambda_n}\chi(c_nq)E_n. \end{split} \tag{Z2.3} \]

Indeed q is independent of r, while \(q_z=2\eta q^{1-D}/L\); multiplying \(c_n\chi' q_z\) by \(q^{1-A+\lambda_n}F_n\) produces \(q^{\lambda_n}(2\eta/L)(c_nq)\chi'F_n\) because A+D=1. The radial sign is negative from \(-\partial_z S_n\). Curl has zero divergence by commutation of Cartesian mixed derivatives, and the θ-independent angular field has zero divergence. This proves incompressibility through every cutoff transition, not merely where χ is constant.

The five coefficient entries \((\mathcal A_n,u_{\theta,n}e_\theta,p_n,\mathcal T_{n,\theta}^{\rm phys},\mathcal T_{n,z}^{\rm phys})\) have respectively the exact powers \(q^{-h+\lambda_n},q^{-A+\lambda_n},q^{-2A+\lambda_n},q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n},q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\) in their smooth Cartesian or annular profile representations. Since D<1/2, Z0.3 bounds every derivative through m by \(C_{n,m}q^{\lambda_n-(2A+m)}\). Thus the source's admissible common loss \(\ell_m=2A+m\) follows from the actual coefficient fields. The stress entries, pressure and potential are all included; no bound uniform in n is asserted.

Z3. One actual cutoff sequence for every required derivative

Choose one cutoff sequence from finite norms of already constructed coefficients. Each successive choice meets a finite list of derivative requirements, and their union covers every fixed derivative.

Choose the exact fixed step \(\chi(s)=1-\sigma(2s-1)\), with σ from O0.1. It equals one for s≤1/2 and zero for s≥1, is smooth and flat at the transition endpoints, and has values between zero and one. For a positive-order z,t derivative of χ(cq), repeated chain rule gives a finite sum of terms

\[ c^k\chi^{(k)}(cq)\prod_{j=1}^k\partial_z^{a_j}\partial_t^{b_j}q, \quad\sum a_j=a,\quad\sum b_j=b,\quad a_j+b_j\ge1. \tag{Z3.1} \]

Z0.2, applied repeatedly to q, gives \(|\partial_z^{a_j}\partial_t^{b_j}q|\le Cq^{1-Da_j-b_j}\). On the support of the derivative, 1/2≤cq≤1, so the factors \(c^kq^k\) are bounded independently of c. Consequently

\[ |\partial_z^a\partial_t^b\chi(cq)|\le C_{a,b}q^{-Da-b},\qquad \partial_{x_1}\chi(cq)=\partial_{x_2}\chi(cq)=0. \tag{Z3.2} \]

The undifferentiated cutoff is bounded by one. These bounds hold on the whole domain because the positive derivatives vanish outside the transition.

For the full cut tuple let

\[ W_n(c)=\left(\operatorname{curl}(\chi(cq)\mathcal A_n)+\chi(cq)u_{\theta,n}e_\theta, \quad\chi(cq)p_n,\quad\chi(cq)q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\mathcal T_n\right). \tag{Z3.3} \]

All potential, direct-field, pressure and stress terms remain. A derivative through order m of its curl uses at most m+1 derivatives in total. A term with k derivatives on χ costs at most \(q^{-k}\), and the remaining at most m+1−k derivatives on the potential cost \(q^{\lambda_n-2A-(m+1-k)}\) by Z2. The full product rule therefore gives

\[ |W_n(c)|_m\le C^{\rm phys}_{n,m}q^{2nh-\ell'_m},\qquad \ell'_m=2A+m+1, \tag{Z3.4} \]

with constants independent of c. The direct field, pressure and both stress entries obey the same bound, using fewer derivatives. All positive-order profiles have a common compact radial support, so these constants can be taken on that entire support, including its smooth zero extension. In particular the first-order stress is included by Y5.9, whose exponential beats every inverse power at its endpoint.

The additional estimates use exactly the source operators \(\mathscr D=(q\partial_q,\partial_X,\partial_\eta)\). For a multi-index I, let \(\mathscr D^I\) denote their indicated composition. They commute on functions of the independent (q,X,η). The identity

\[ (q\partial_q)^j\chi(cq)=(s\partial_s)^j\chi(s)\big|_{s=cq} \tag{Z3.5} \]

gives a uniform bound for every fixed j; the same holds with \(\chi(s)\) replaced by \(s\chi'(s)\). Each application to \(q^{2nh}\) contributes precisely 2nh. All \(\partial_X\) and \(\partial_\eta\) derivatives of the actual profiles on a fixed compact annulus are finite. Thus, for every fixed annulus, the quantities

\[ \begin{gathered} q^{2nh}\chi(cq)a_n,\qquad a_n\in\{E_n,U_n,\Pi_n,V_n/R,F_n/R\},\\ q^{2nh}\left[\chi(cq)V_n/R-\frac{2\eta}{L}(cq)\chi'(cq)F_n/R\right],\\ q^{2nh}\chi(cq)\mathcal T_n/\zeta\quad(n\ge2) \end{gathered} \tag{Z3.6} \]

have all \(\mathscr D^I\) bounds \(C_{n,I}q^{2nh}\) independent of c. In the last row Y5.2 places the stress in the interior \([X_-,X_+]\), so its quotient by ζ is smooth with bounded derivatives on the entire active annulus, extended by zero near both edges. This quotient estimate is not applied to n=1.

Here is one explicit sequence meeting every requirement. Set \(X_*=\max\{1,X_b\}\) and \(\mathcal K_k=[X_a/(k+1),(k+1)X_*]\times[-1,1]\), k≥1. These exhaust the positive radial coordinate and contain the active annulus. For each n, take \(M_n\ge1\) to be the maximum of the finitely many constants in Z3.4 for 0≤m≤n and in Z3.6 for |I|≤n and 1≤k≤n. Include the full bracket, not just its first term, and the entire stress quotient when n≥2. Each constant is defined by the finite product-rule bounds just proved for the already constructed profiles and the fixed χ; no unknown future coefficient enters. Define \(c_0=1\) and recursively

\[ c_n=1+\left\lceil\max\left\{2c_{n-1},\ 2,\ (2^nM_n)^{1/(nh)}\right\}\right\rceil. \tag{Z3.7} \]

All \(M_n\) are finite and h>0 was fixed in the actual leading construction. Hence this gives one finite positive \(c_n\) at every order and \(c_n\ge2c_{n-1}\). For \(0<q\le1/c_n\) it implies \(M_nq^{nh}\le2^{-n}\). On larger q the n-th summand and all its derivatives vanish. Consequently

\[ |W_n(c_n)|_m\le2^{-n}q^{nh-\ell'_m}\quad(m\le n), \qquad |\mathscr D^I B_n^{\rm sim}|\le2^{-n}q^{nh}\quad(|I|\le n,\ k\le n), \tag{Z3.8} \]

where \(B_n^{\rm sim}\) means each of the complete expressions in Z3.6 on \(\mathcal K_k\), including the full cutoff bracket and both stress quotients. The q derivative factors and the coefficients 2η/L are included in \(M_n\). This is an exact diagonal construction from finite norms; it requires no numerical estimate of the enormous possible cutoff sizes and no hypothesis of uniform coefficient growth.

Z4. Actual fields, exact divergence and their finite comparison

The chosen sequence now defines actual fields. Local finiteness proves smoothness away from the singular scale; the quantitative tail estimate controls the approach to that scale.

Define the fields by the actual locally finite series

\[ \begin{split} u_B&=u_0+\sum_{n\ge1}\left[\operatorname{curl}(\chi(c_nq)\mathcal A_n)+\chi(c_nq)u_{\theta,n}e_\theta\right],\\ p_B&=p_0+\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(c_nq)p_n,\\ T_{\rm phys}&=q^{-A-1/2}\mathcal T_0+\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(c_nq)q^{-A-1/2+2nh}\mathcal T_n. \end{split} \tag{Z4.1} \]

On any compact set with \(q\ge q_*>0\), \(c_nq\ge1\) for all sufficiently large n. Thus only finitely many terms and their derivatives occur locally. Every term is smooth in Cartesian coordinates at the axis by Z0–Z2, or supported away from it for the stress. Z2.3 proves exact incompressibility, including every cutoff term, and local finiteness preserves it in the sum. All added terms extend smoothly by zero for \(q\ge1/c_1\) because χ is flat at its outer endpoint.

Every positive-order velocity and pressure term is zero when \(X\ge X_+\): its potential contains \(F_n\), its cutoff curl contains only \(F_n\) and \(V_n\), and all of these, as well as \(U_n,E_n\),\(\Pi_n\), vanish there by Y3. The stress has support \([X_a,X_b]\) because its leading and higher components do, and multiplication by χ(\(c_n\)q) does not alter the radial profile support. No conclusion that the first-order stress vanishes at \(X_+\) is used.

Fix a derivative order m. For \(J\ge\max\{1,m\}\) and \(0<q<(2c_J)^{-1}\), all first J cutoffs equal one on a neighborhood, including all their vanishing derivatives. The original tuple \(\mathcal U^{[J]}\), with its uncut potentials differentiated, is therefore the first J part of Z4.1. By Z3.8,

\[ |(u_B,p_B,T_{\rm phys})-\mathcal U^{[J]}|_m \le\sum_{n>J}2^{-n}q^{nh-\ell'_m} \le2^{-J}q^{h(J+1)-\ell'_m}. \tag{Z4.2} \]

The last inequality uses q≤1 and the exact sum \(\sum_{n>J}2^{-n}=2^{-J}\). The common derivative loss is independent of J.

Z5. The complete augmented residual is flat

The nonlinear residual cannot be interchanged with an uncontrolled infinite series. Compare the actual field with one fixed finite sum and estimate every term of their exact difference.

For one fixed finite state set \(v=u^{[J]}\), \(p_*=p^{[J]}\), \(T_*=T^{[J]}\), and \(e=u_B-v\), \(\pi=p_B-p_*\), \(\tau=T_{\rm phys}-T_*\). Subtracting the full residual gives the exact identity

\[ \begin{split} \mathcal F_{\rm slow}(u_B,p_B,T_{\rm phys})-\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(v,p_*,T_*) ={}&\partial_te-\Delta e+\nabla\pi+(v\cdot\nabla)e+(e\cdot\nabla)v+(e\cdot\nabla)e\\ &+(\partial_r+2/r)\tau_\theta e_\theta+(\partial_r+1/r)\tau_ze_z. \end{split} \tag{Z5.1} \]

The last line contains both original tangential stress divergences. It is supported in the fixed active annulus. Write \(\partial_r=e_r\cdot\nabla_x\) there. A Cartesian derivative of order j of \(e_r,e_\theta\) is bounded by \(C_jr^{-j}\), and of 1/r by \(C_jr^{-1-j}\); their t,z derivatives vanish. Since \(r=\sqrt q R\) and \(\sqrt{2X_a}\le R\le\sqrt{2X_b}\), the product rule yields

\[ | (\partial_r+2/r)\tau_\theta e_\theta+(\partial_r+1/r)\tau_ze_z |_m \le C_mq^{-H_m}|\tau|_{m+1},\qquad H_m=(m+1)/2. \tag{Z5.2} \]

Terms with fewer frame derivatives obey the same bound because 0<q≤1. All coefficients and supports are the original ones; no 1/r estimate is used at the axis.

For the three nonlinear terms in Z5.1, every differentiated component is a finite sum \(\partial^I(v_k\partial_ke_i)=\sum_{J'\le I}\binom I{J'}(\partial^{J'}v_k)(\partial^{I-J'}\partial_ke_i)\), and the other two products have their respective displayed factors. This proves the full estimate

\[ |\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(u_B,p_B,T_{\rm phys})-\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(v,p_*,T_*)|_m \le C_m\left(|e|_{m+2}+|\pi|_{m+1}+|v|_{m+1}|e|_{m+1}+|e|_{m+1}^2+q^{-H_m}|\tau|_{m+1}\right). \tag{Z5.3} \]

In particular the quadratic new-new term and the pressure term have not been discarded.

On a fixed compact profile range, Z0.1–Z0.3 and the actual leading profile give, for every finite J,

\[ |\mathcal U^{[J]}|_r\le C_{J,r}q^{-K_r},\qquad K_r=2A+r, \tag{Z5.4} \]

because all coefficient increments have factor \(q^{2nh}\)≤1 and the pressure is the most singular of the undifferentiated entries. The constants may grow with J; \(K_r\) does not. The leading stress has its already proved smooth zero extension, and its support is away from the axis.

Given physical derivative order m and desired decay order M≥0, put r=m+2 and choose one finite integer J≥max{1,r} such that

\[ \alpha=h(J+1)-\ell'_r\ge M+\max\{K_r,H_m\},\qquad 2h(J+1)-(2A+1/2+m)\ge M. \tag{Z5.5} \]

Both inequalities hold for a sufficiently large finite J because h>0 and every displayed loss is independent of J. For example the ceiling of the maximum of r, \((M+\max\{K_r,H_m\}+\ell'_r)/h-1\), and \((M+2A+1/2+m)/(2h)-1\), enlarged to at least one, suffices. Keep this J fixed and restrict \(q<(2c_J)^{-1}\). Equation Z4.2 bounds e,π,τ through order r by \(2^{-J}q^\alpha\); Z5.4 bounds v by \(C_{J,r}q^{-K_r}\). The five terms in Z5.3 have powers at least α, α, \(\alpha-K_r\), 2α and \(\alpha-H_m\), all at least M by Z5.5. The finite residual Z1.5 also has power at least M. Therefore the actual field satisfies

\[ \mathscr R(u_B,p_B)=-(\partial_r+2/r)T_{{\rm phys},\theta}e_\theta -(\partial_r+1/r)T_{{\rm phys},z}e_z+\mathcal E_B, \qquad |\mathcal E_B|_m\le C_{m,M}q^M \tag{Z5.6} \]

on the chosen compact profile range as q↓0, for every m and M. The constants and neighborhood may depend on that range and on m,M. The order of choices is (m,M), then one finite J, then its q neighborhood. This uses no infinite sum of residual remainders. It proves the actual application of Lemma 5.4 to the base, including its stress variable, rather than importing unverified finite-state data.

Z6. Every original velocity and weighted stress comparison

Keep the original factors multiplying each velocity, pressure and stress component. The first stress coefficient reaches the outer endpoint and must retain its full weight.

Fix any \(0<X_{\rm lo}<X_a<X_b<X_{\rm hi}<\infty\). Choose k so its closed profile rectangle lies in \(\mathcal K_k\). For a fixed |I|=m split the positive series into a finite initial block and a tail starting at \(n_0\ge\max\{2,k,m\}\). The finite terms in Z3.6 and their \(\mathscr D^I\) derivatives are \(O(q^{2h})\), since each has its original \(q^{2nh}\) factor and the fixed cutoff derivatives are bounded. The tail is at most

\[ \sum_{n\ge n_0}2^{-n}q^{nh}\le2^{1-n_0}q^{n_0h}\le2^{1-n_0}q^{2h}. \tag{Z6.1} \]

Use this for each complete expression in Z3.6 and then use the exact fields Z2.3. It proves all of the following, with their original factors:

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathscr D^I(q^Au_{\theta,B}-E_0)=O_I(q^{2h}),\qquad \mathscr D^I(q^Au_{z,B}-U_0)=O_I(q^{2h}),\\ \mathscr D^I(q^{1/2}u_{r,B}-V_0/\sqrt{2X})=O_I(q^{2h}),\qquad \mathscr D^I(q^Au_{r,B})=O_I(q^h),\\ \mathscr D^I(q^{2A}p_B-\Pi_0)=O_I(q^{2h}). \end{gathered} \tag{Z6.2} \]

For the fourth row, the exact identity is \(q^Au_{r,B}=q^h[V_0/\sqrt{2X}+O(q^{2h})]\); the leading term is retained. The positive-order radial contribution with that same \(q^A\) factor is \(O(q^{3h})\). All derivatives of the extra cutoff term in Z2.3 are included in the third and fourth rows. The pressure statement follows from the same included coefficient row; \(\Pi_0\) here is the full leading pressure, as in D0.

For the original stress set \(\widehat T=q^{A+1/2}T_{\rm phys}\). The exact difference is

\[ \widehat T-\mathcal T_0=\chi(c_1q)q^{2h}\mathcal T_1 +\zeta\sum_{n\ge2}\chi(c_nq)q^{2nh}(\mathcal T_n/\zeta). \tag{Z6.3} \]

For n≥2 the quotients and all derivatives are bounded on the full active annulus by Y6, and are included in Z3.6–Z3.8. Their series and every \(\mathscr D^I\) derivative are \(O(q^{2h})\) by Z6.1 and a finite initial block. For each fixed j, the full exponential ζ of Y6.1 satisfies \(|\partial_X^j\zeta|\le C_j\zeta\delta^{-M_j}\): differentiate both exponential factors, using the bounded derivatives of \(\log(X/X_a)\), \(\log(X_b/X)\) on the fixed annulus, and retain the finite resulting inverse powers. The product rule therefore bounds the second term in Z6.3 by \(O_I(q^{2h}\zeta\delta^{-N_I})\). The first term obeys the same bound using the actual first-order stress estimate Y5.9–Y6.2 and the fixed cutoff derivatives. Taking the maximum over the finitely many product-rule exponents gives

\[ |\mathscr D^I(\widehat T-\mathcal T_0)|\le C_Iq^{2h}\zeta\delta^{-N_I} \le C_Iq^h\zeta\delta^{-N_I},\qquad 0<q\le1, \tag{Z6.4} \]

uniformly for \(X_a<X<X_b\) and −1≤η≤1. This treats the whole first-order outer stress and both stress entries. It does not assume positivity of the higher stresses or replace them by their leading value.

Z6a. Exact outer stress coefficient of the actual base

On the terminal collar \(X>X_+\), Y5.2–Y5.3 give \(\mathcal T_n=0\) for \(n\ge2\) and \(\mathcal T_{1,z}=0\). Thus the actual sum Z6.3 is exactly

\[ \widehat T_\theta=e^{-4/\delta_b^2}\delta_b^{-3} [b_\theta+\chi(c_1q)q^{2h}B_1],\qquad \widehat T_z=e^{-4/\delta_b^2}\delta_b^3b_z. \tag{Z6a.1} \]

These are the full original stress components; no limiting series is interchanged here because all but one correction vanish identically on this collar. H6.6 supplies the smooth positive leading coefficient \(b_\theta\), and Y8.16–Y8.27 proves

\[ \frac{B_1(0,\eta)}{b_\theta(0,\eta)} =\frac{2X_b\eta^2}{L^2},\qquad \lim_{\delta_b\downarrow0}\delta_b^{-3} \frac{B_1(\delta_b,0)}{b_\theta(\delta_b,0)}=\frac{X_b}{8}. \tag{Z6a.2} \]

In particular the ratio \(B_1/b_\theta\) extends smoothly through the outer endpoint, despite the unbounded first-order quotient \(\mathcal T_{1,\theta}/\zeta\) at fixed nonzero \(\eta\).

The actual cutoff satisfies \(0\le\chi\le1\). At the endpoint the angular coefficient divided by \(b_\theta\) is

\[ 1+\chi(c_1q)q^{2h}\frac{2X_b\eta^2}{L^2}\ge1. \tag{Z6a.3} \]

For every fixed bounded interval of \(q\ge0\), continuity and compactness supply a common smaller terminal collar on which the full angular coefficient stays positive. The cutoff is zero for large \(c_1q\), so the same conclusion holds on any intended preterminal range. The exact direction is

\[ \frac{\widehat T}{|\widehat T|} =\frac{(1,\mathcal R_B)}{\sqrt{1+\mathcal R_B^2}},\qquad \mathcal R_B=\frac{\delta_b^6b_z} {b_\theta+\chi(c_1q)q^{2h}B_1} \longrightarrow0. \tag{Z6a.4} \]

It is smooth in \((\delta_b,\eta)\) through the endpoint for each fixed \(q>0\), with every fixed \(q\)-derivative on compact positive \(q\) intervals. The exact radial derivative bounds Y8.22–Y8.25 allow the exponent \(3k+3\) for the first-order outer stress after \(k\) radial derivatives, with arbitrary fixed parameter derivatives. This supplies an explicit exponent for that term of Z6.4; other product-rule terms retain their stated finite exponents. The actual physical stress is \(\nu q^{-A-1/2}\widehat T\) at the unchanged viscosity coordinates, so the positive scalar factor preserves the direction and all original physical factors. This proves a sharper endpoint comparison for the same base field, without altering the construction or claiming an original source error.

Z7. Formal expansion, exterior, mean patch and endpoint derivatives

The same fields recover every original coefficient order, preserve the exact heat exterior and mean-patch velocity, and have the required endpoint derivatives.

Fix a formal order N and a physical derivative order m. Take \(J\ge\max\{2N+2,m+1\}\). For sufficiently small q, the finitely many cutoffs with n≤J equal one and all their derivatives vanish. The intermediate block N<n<J then consists exactly of original coefficient terms and has powers at least 2h(N+1), with the fixed derivative losses already proved in Z0.3. The remaining tail satisfies

\[ \sum_{n\ge J}2^{-n}q^{nh-\ell'_m} \le2^{1-J}q^{Jh-\ell'_m} \le2^{1-J}q^{2h(N+1)-\ell'_m}. \tag{Z7.1} \]

The constants of the finite intermediate block may depend on N,m. This proves every fixed formal order of the original tuple, including physical derivatives with an index-independent exponent loss. For the similarity derivatives the same argument applies to Z3.6, with J also exceeding the chosen annulus index k; its tail has no physical loss. The cutoff curl vanishes in the finite initial block and remains fully present in the tail bounds. Thus the asymptotic coefficients are the original \(\mathcal U^{[N]}\), with their Stokes potentials differentiated before summation as specified in the source.

One can also retain the exact component power in this comparison. For angular or axial velocity, radial velocity, pressure, and stress respectively, let \(\beta=-A,-1/2,-2A,-A-1/2\), as in Z0.1 and Z1.1. A prescribed derivative with a transverse, k axial and ℓ time derivatives has exact loss \(w=a/2+Dk+\ell\). Enlarge the finite split index J, if necessary, until \(hJ-\ell'_m\ge\beta+2h(N+1)-w\). The intermediate terms obey Z0.3 with this original β, and the tail obeys this strengthened choice of J in Z7.1. Therefore the component remainder after the original N-th truncation is \(O(q^{\beta+2h(N+1)-w})\) for that derivative. All five types of field have been retained; a larger finite J proves their finite list of requirements simultaneously. This proves the coefficient expansion with the actual physical powers as well as the common-loss estimate.

By Y3.5, \(E_n,U_n\),\(F_n,V_n\) vanish on the untouched mean patch for every positive n. Both terms in the radial bracket Z2.3 vanish there as well. Hence the exact base velocity on that patch is

\[ u_B=u^{(0)},\qquad u_{z,B}=0,\qquad q^Au_{\theta,B}=E_0=c_{\rm patch}(1+\eta^2)^{-1}X^{-1/2-\lambda} \quad(X\in\mathcal I_{\rm mean}). \tag{Z7.2} \]

There is no pressure-equality assertion on this earlier patch. In the exterior \(X\ge X_+\), Y3 gives all positive-order fields and potentials, including pressure, identically zero. Thus \(u_B=u^{(0)}\) and \(p_B=p^{(0)}\) there. For \(X\ge X_b\) this is precisely the actual heat swirl and its pressure from H0/H4 and V7, including \(U_0=V_0=0\), not just a field with the same asymptotic power.

For endpoint regularity fix a compact set with \(q\ge q_*>0\). Local finiteness leaves only finitely many positive-order terms. Each has every fixed profile derivative continuous up to η=±1 by D/Y; the leading term has that same one-sided smoothness by G/O/H/J/Q/V, including the heat factor at d=0. The cutoff and its derivatives are smooth functions of q. Formula Z0.2 transfers these limits to every fixed physical space-time derivative because \(L\ge1-2h>0\) and q is bounded below. The same applies to the pressure and stress, and then to \(\mathcal E_B\), which is their finite differential expression Z5.6. This proves the claimed continuous derivative extensions. It requires no claim of two-sided analytic extension of the terminal heat factor at d=0.

Z8. Original viscosity and the receiving construction

Restore the originally specified viscosity in the potentials, streamfunctions, velocities, pressure, stresses and residual. Their derivative factors must agree in the physical equation.

For the originally specified ν>0 use the exact map

\[ \begin{gathered} x_\nu=\sqrt\nu x,\quad t_\nu=t,\quad q_\nu-(z_\nu^2/\nu)q_\nu^{2h}=1-t,\quad X_\nu=r_\nu^2/(2\nu q_\nu),\quad \eta_\nu=z_\nu/(\sqrt\nu q_\nu^D),\\ u_{B,\nu}=\sqrt\nu\,u_B(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t),\quad p_{B,\nu}=\nu p_B(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t),\quad T_{{\rm phys},\nu}=\nu T_{\rm phys}(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t),\\ \mathcal A_{n,\nu}=\nu\mathcal A_n(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t),\qquad S_{n,\nu}=\nu^{3/2}S_n(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t),\qquad \mathcal E_{B,\nu}=\sqrt\nu\mathcal E_B(x_\nu/\sqrt\nu,t). \end{gathered} \tag{Z8.1} \]

The potential and streamfunction factors follow from \(r_\nu=\sqrt\nu r\) and \(\operatorname{curl}_\nu=\nu^{-1/2}\operatorname{curl}\); they give exactly the mapped velocity including every cutoff curl. Each momentum term has the factor \(\sqrt\nu\): one spatial derivative costs \(\nu^{-1/2}\), pressure and stress have factor ν, and \(\nu\Delta_\nu u_\nu\) has \(\nu\cdot\nu^{-1}\cdot\sqrt\nu\). Thus

\[ \partial_tu_{B,\nu}-\nu\Delta_\nu u_{B,\nu}+(u_{B,\nu}\cdot\nabla_\nu)u_{B,\nu}+\nabla_\nu p_{B,\nu} =-\operatorname{div}_{\nu,\rm tan}T_{{\rm phys},\nu}+\mathcal E_{B,\nu}. \tag{Z8.2} \]

Here the tangential divergence is exactly the two operators \((\partial_{r_\nu}+2/r_\nu)T_{\nu,\theta}e_\theta+(\partial_{r_\nu}+1/r_\nu)T_{\nu,z}e_z\). All residual derivative bounds gain only the fixed factors \(\nu^{(1-|\alpha|)/2}\) for |α| spatial derivatives; time is unchanged. They are therefore flat to every order in the same original \(q_\nu\). Stress support, endpoint extensions and exterior and mean-patch equalities pass through this exact coordinate map. No different viscosity or spatial scale has replaced the original problem.

Z9. Five worked exercises

Exercise 1. Find the exact divergence defect and the unique regular radial repair

Compare cutting the physical positive-order velocity directly with taking the curl of its cut potential. Prove the correction is uniquely determined among regular radial fields, and retain the original viscosity.

Solution. Write \(s=c_nq\), only as the argument of the already fixed cutoff. Since \(\operatorname{div}u_n=0\), \(q\) is independent of \(r\), and \(q_z=2\eta q^{1-D}/L\),

\[ \operatorname{div}[\chi(c_nq)u_n] =c_n\chi'(c_nq)q_z u_{z,n} =\frac{2\eta}{L}s\chi'(s)q^{\lambda_n-1}U_n. \tag{Z9.1} \]

Here \(A+D=1\) gives the final exponent. The angular component contributes no divergence. The extra radial component in Z2.3 is

\[ w_{r,n}=-\frac{2\eta}{L}s\chi'(s)\frac{q^{\lambda_n}F_n}{r}. \tag{Z9.2} \]

At fixed \(z,t\), every factor outside \(F_n/r\) is independent of \(r\), while \(\partial_rF_n=(r/q)U_n\). Hence

\[ \frac1r\partial_r(rw_{r,n}) =-\frac{2\eta}{L}s\chi'(s)q^{\lambda_n-1}U_n. \tag{Z9.3} \]

This proves the cancellation with its exact sign. Moreover \(F_n/X\) is smooth and \(X=r^2/(2q)\); thus \(w_{r,n}e_r\) is smooth in the Cartesian variables. In fact the positive-order zero axis trace gives \(F_n=O(X^2)\), so this correction is \(O(r^3)\) at fixed \(z,t\).

Any other radial solution of the same divergence equation differs by \(a(z,t)/r\). Smoothness at the axis forces \(a=0\). Equivalently, integrating \(\partial_r(rw)=-r\,\operatorname{div}[\chi u_n]\) from zero gives precisely Z9.2, because \(F_n(0)=0\). This proves uniqueness in the specified class. The common compact support and the zero mean-patch value follow from those of \(F_n\).

For the original viscosity, \(r_\nu=\sqrt\nu r\), \(w_{r,n,\nu}=\sqrt\nu w_{r,n}\), and

\[ r_\nu w_{r,n,\nu} =-\nu\frac{2\eta_\nu}{L_\nu}(c_nq_\nu)\chi'(c_nq_\nu) q_\nu^{\lambda_n}F_n(X_\nu,\eta_\nu). \tag{Z9.4} \]

In the divergence, the spatial factor \(\nu^{-1/2}\) cancels the velocity factor \(\sqrt\nu\); Z9.1 and Z9.3 retain exactly their coefficient-one values at \((X_\nu,\eta_\nu,q_\nu)\). In the curl, the potential has factor \(\nu\), so its mapped curl has factor \(\sqrt\nu\), as Z8.1 requires.

Exercise 2. Compute the entire residual of the first finite sum

Set \(N=1\) in the actual tuple Z1.1. List every remaining radial and tangential term, with its physical power. In particular identify both surviving radial axial-viscosity terms.

Solution. The tangential product condition \(i+j>1\), with \(0\le i,j\le1\), leaves only \((1,1)\). The last retained axial-viscosity term has index one. Consequently

\[ \begin{split} (\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[1]}))_\theta &=q^{-A-1+4h}\frac R{\mathsf C} \left[V_1(\phi_1'+\phi_1/X)+U_1Z_{b,1}\phi_1 -Z_{b,1}^{[2]}\phi_1\right],\\ (\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[1]}))_z &=q^{-A-1+4h} \left[V_1U_1'+U_1Z_{c,1}U_1-Z_{c,1}^{[2]}U_1\right]. \end{split} \tag{Z9.5} \]

All functions retain their actual \(X,\eta\) dependence. The operators have the original shifts: \(Z_{\beta,1}^{[2]}=Z_{\beta+2h-D}Z_{\beta+2h}\).

For radial transport the condition is \(i+j+1>1\). It leaves \((0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\). The radial axial-viscosity condition \(j+2>1\) leaves both \(j=0\) and \(j=1\). Group only terms with identical original powers:

\[ \begin{split} G_2={}&-\frac{2X}{\mathsf C^2}\phi_1^2 +T_{0,1}V_1-2XV_1''\\ &+V_0(V_1'-V_1/(2X))+V_1(V_0'-V_0/(2X))\\ &+U_0Z_{0,1}V_1+U_1Z_{0,0}V_0-Z_{0,0}^{[2]}V_0,\\ G_3={}&V_1(V_1'-V_1/(2X))+U_1Z_{0,1}V_1 -Z_{0,1}^{[2]}V_1. \end{split} \tag{Z9.6} \]

The full radial expression is

\[ r(\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[1]}))_r =q^{-2A+4h}G_2+q^{-2A+6h}G_3. \tag{Z9.7} \]

Indeed \(-1+2h=-2A+4h=-2D\), whereas \(-1+4h=-2A+6h=-2D+2h\). These identities place the two radial axial derivatives in orders two and three respectively. They also place the radial time and transverse-viscosity terms in order two. Every coefficient and both middle transport products remain in Z9.6.

Each \(G_j/X\) is smooth at \(X=0\): substitute \(V_i=Xv_i\) into every term and use the operator identities \(T_\beta(Xf)=XT_{\beta-1}f\), \(Z_\beta(Xf)=XZ_{\beta-1}f\). Thus division by \(r=\sqrt qR\) gives the smooth Cartesian radial vector with its exact factor \(X/R=R/2\). On a fixed compact profile range, the derivative estimate Z0.3 gives

\[ |\mathcal F_{\rm slow}(\mathcal U^{[1]})|_m \le C_m q^{4h-(2A+1/2+m)}. \tag{Z9.8} \]

This is a bound for the displayed finite residual. It does not discard the order-three term or equate a finite truncation with the actual infinite base. For viscosity \(\nu\), the entire vector in Z9.5–Z9.7 is multiplied by \(\sqrt\nu\) and evaluated at \(x=x_\nu/\sqrt\nu\); an additional spatial derivative contributes \(\nu^{-1/2}\).

Exercise 3. Compare two admissible cutoff sequences exactly

Suppose \(c_n\) and \(\widetilde c_n\) are two sequences constructed by Z3 from the same actual coefficients, each satisfying all displayed estimates. Determine their exact field difference and prove that it is flat in \(q\), including a weighted stress statement on the full active annulus.

Solution. Put \(\Delta\chi_n(q)=\chi(c_nq)-\chi(\widetilde c_nq)\). The exact difference is

\[ \begin{split} \Delta u_B&=\sum_{n\ge1} \left[\operatorname{curl}(\Delta\chi_n\mathcal A_n) +\Delta\chi_n u_{\theta,n}e_\theta\right],\\ \Delta p_B&=\sum_{n\ge1}\Delta\chi_n p_n,\\ \Delta T_{\rm phys}&=\sum_{n\ge1} \Delta\chi_n q^{-A-1/2+2nh}\mathcal T_n. \end{split} \tag{Z9.9} \]

Both sums are locally finite. Their difference is divergence-free by the full curl identity, and its velocity and pressure vanish outside \(X_+\). Its velocity vanishes on the unchanged mean patch. The stress difference has support in \([X_a,X_b]\).

Fix a derivative order \(m\) and decay order \(M\). Choose \(J\ge\max\{1,m\}\) with \(h(J+1)-\ell'_m\ge M\). For

\[ 0<q<\min\{(2c_J)^{-1},(2\widetilde c_J)^{-1}\}, \tag{Z9.10} \]

both sets of first \(J\) cutoffs are identically one. Apply Z4.2 to each base relative to the same finite tuple. The exact triangle inequality gives

\[ |(\Delta u_B,\Delta p_B,\Delta T_{\rm phys})|_m \le2^{1-J}q^{h(J+1)-\ell'_m} \le2^{1-J}q^M. \tag{Z9.11} \]

The constants and the neighborhood are permitted to depend on \(m,M\). This proves equality of every formal coefficient with a flat difference, rather than equality of the actual fields.

There is a stronger stress comparison after retaining its original multiplier. Define \(\Delta\widehat T=q^{A+1/2}\Delta T_{\rm phys}\). For \(q\) as in Z9.10 with \(J\ge\max\{2,|I|\}\), the first-order term vanishes exactly. Every remaining stress coefficient is supported in the fixed interior \([X_-,X_+]\); its quotient by \(\zeta\) is smooth. The two bounds Z3.8 therefore give

\[ \left|\mathscr D^I\left(\frac{\Delta\widehat T}{\zeta}\right)\right| \le2\sum_{n>J}2^{-n}q^{nh} \le2^{1-J}q^{h(J+1)} \quad(X_a<X<X_b). \tag{Z9.12} \]

Choose \(J\) also so that \(h(J+1)\ge M\). This is flat uniformly through the whole active annulus and every fixed similarity derivative, with no inverse distance factor. The quotient extends by zero near both endpoints because the remaining supports lie in that fixed interior. The exact original physical relation is \(\Delta T_{{\rm phys},\nu}=\nu q_\nu^{-A-1/2}\Delta\widehat T\); no stress multiplier has been removed from the physical conclusion.

Exercise 4. Compute the exact axis residual of the actual base

Track the first cutoff through the axis cancellation in D7. Prove an exact identity for \(\mathcal E_{B,\nu}\) on the axis and retain the growing axial velocity there.

Solution. Use the actual traces and slopes already derived from the full coefficient equations:

\[ \begin{gathered} U_*=4\eta+j_0,\qquad c=-A,\qquad \mathscr Z_\beta f=\frac{2\beta\eta f+(1-\eta^2)f'}{1-2h\eta^2},\\ U_n(0,\eta)=\Pi_n(0,\eta)=0\quad(n\ge1),\\ \alpha(\eta):=U_{1,X}(0,\eta) =-\tfrac12\mathscr Z_{c-D}\mathscr Z_cU_*, \qquad U_{n,X}(0,\eta)=0\quad(n\ge2). \end{gathered} \tag{Z9.13} \]

These are D7.10–D7.15; the global moment corrections preserve the protected axis interval. At any fixed \(q_\nu>0\) only finitely many base terms occur. The axial components in Z2.3 have the factor \(\chi(c_nq_\nu)\), which is independent of \(r_\nu\). Their zero axis traces remain zero under every time and axial derivative. Their pressure derivatives in \(z_\nu\) also have zero trace.

Every positive-order horizontal velocity, including the additional radial cutoff term, is \(O(r_\nu^3)\), and the positive-order axial velocity is \(O(r_\nu^2)\). Hence all extra axial convection terms vanish at the axis. Only the transverse Laplacian of the first positive-order axial component contributes there. Its exact value is
